README — Qdrant** (read: _quadrant_) is a vector similarity search engine and vector database.
README — It provides a production-ready service with a convenient API to store, search, and manage points—vectors with an additional payload
README — Qdrant is tailored to extended filtering support. It makes it useful for all sorts of neural-network or semantic-based matching, faceted search, and other applications.
README — Qdrant is written in Rust 🦀, which makes it fast and reliable even under high load. See [benchmarks](https://qdrant.tech/benchmarks/).
README — With Qdrant, embeddings or neural network encoders can be turned into full-fledged applications for matching, searching, recommending, and much more!
README — Qdrant is also available as a fully managed **[Qdrant Cloud](https://cloud.qdrant.io/)** ⛅ including a **free tier**.

README — Features
README — Filtering and Payload
README — Qdrant can attach any JSON payloads to vectors, allowing for both the storage and filtering of data based on the values in these payloads.
README — Payload supports a wide range of data types and query conditions, including keyword matching, full-text filtering, numerical ranges, geo-locations, and more.
README — Filtering conditions can be combined in various ways, including `should`, `must`, and `must_not` clauses,
README — ensuring that you can implement any desired business logic on top of similarity matching.
README — Hybrid Search with Sparse Vectors
README — To address the limitations of vector embeddings when searching for specific keywords, Qdrant introduces support for sparse vectors in addition to the regular dense ones.
README — Sparse vectors can be viewed as an generalization of BM25 or TF-IDF ranking. They enable you to harness the capabilities of transformer-based neural networks to weigh individual tokens effectively.
README — Vector Quantization and On-Disk Storage
README — Qdrant provides multiple options to make vector search cheaper and more resource-efficient.
README — Built-in vector quantization reduces RAM usage by up to 97% and dynamically manages the trade-off between search speed and precision.
README — Distributed Deployment
README — Qdrant offers comprehensive horizontal scaling support through two key mechanisms:
README — Size expansion via sharding and throughput enhancement via replication
README — Zero-downtime rolling updates and seamless dynamic scaling of the collections
README — Highlighted Features
README — Query Planning and Payload Indexes** - leverages stored payload information to optimize query execution strategy.
README — SIMD Hardware Acceleration** - utilizes modern CPU x86-x64 and Neon architectures to deliver better performance.
README — Async I/O** - uses `io_uring` to maximize disk throughput utilization even on a network-attached storage.
README — Write-Ahead Logging** - ensures data persistence with update confirmation, even during power outages.

PRETRAIN — Pre-training MAE
PRETRAIN — To pre-train ViT-Large (recommended default) with **multi-node distributed training**, run the following on 8 nodes with 8 GPUs each:
PRETRAIN — Here the effective batch size is 64 (`batch_size` per gpu) * 8 (`nodes`) * 8 (gpus per node) = 4096. If memory or # gpus is limited, use `--accum_iter` to maintain the effective batch size, which is `batch_size` (per gpu) * `nodes` * 8 (gpus per node) * `accum_iter`.
PRETRAIN — `blr` is the base learning rate. The actual `lr` is computed by the [linear scaling rule](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.02677): `lr` = `blr` * effective batch size / 256.
PRETRAIN — Here we use `--norm_pix_loss` as the target for better representation learning. To train a baseline model (e.g., for visualization), use pixel-based construction and turn off `--norm_pix_loss`.
PRETRAIN — The exact same hyper-parameters and configs (initialization, augmentation, etc.) are used as our TF/TPU implementation. In our sanity checks, this PT/GPU re-implementation can reproduce the TF/TPU results within reasonable random variation. We get 85.5% [fine-tuning](FINETUNE.md) accuracy by pre-training ViT-Large for 800 epochs (85.4% in paper Table 1d with TF/TPU).
PRETRAIN — Training time is ~42h in 64 V100 GPUs (800 epochs).
PRETRAIN — To train ViT-Base or ViT-Huge, set `--model mae_vit_base_patch16` or `--model mae_vit_huge_patch14`.

README — Masked Autoencoders: A PyTorch Implementation
README — <p align="center">
README — <img src="https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/11435359/146857310-f258c86c-fde6-48e8-9cee-badd2b21bd2c.png" width="480">
README — This is a PyTorch/GPU re-implementation of the paper [Masked Autoencoders Are Scalable Vision Learners](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.06377):
README — The original implementation was in TensorFlow+TPU. This re-implementation is in PyTorch+GPU.
README — This repo is a modification on the [DeiT repo](https://github.com/facebookresearch/deit). Installation and preparation follow that repo.
README — This repo is based on [`timm==0.3.2`](https://github.com/rwightman/pytorch-image-models), for which a [fix](https://github.com/rwightman/pytorch-image-models/issues/420#issuecomment-776459842) is needed to work with PyTorch 1.8.1+.

FINETUNE — Fine-tuning
FINETUNE — Get our pre-trained checkpoints from [here](https://github.com/fairinternal/mae/#pre-trained-checkpoints).
FINETUNE — To fine-tune with **multi-node distributed training**, run the following on 4 nodes with 8 GPUs each:
FINETUNE — Install submitit (`pip install submitit`) first.
FINETUNE — Here the effective batch size is 32 (`batch_size` per gpu) * 4 (`nodes`) * 8 (gpus per node) = 1024.
FINETUNE — `blr` is the base learning rate. The actual `lr` is computed by the [linear scaling rule](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.02677): `lr` = `blr` * effective batch size / 256.
FINETUNE — We have run 4 trials with different random seeds. The resutls are 83.63, 83.66, 83.52, 83.46 (mean 83.57 and std 0.08).
FINETUNE — Training time is ~7h11m in 32 V100 GPUs.
FINETUNE — Script for ViT-Large:
FINETUNE — We have run 4 trials with different random seeds. The resutls are 85.95, 85.87, 85.76, 85.88 (mean 85.87 and std 0.07).
FINETUNE — Training time is ~8h52m in 32 V100 GPUs.
FINETUNE — Script for ViT-Huge:
FINETUNE — Training time is ~13h9m in 64 V100 GPUs.
FINETUNE — To fine-tune our pre-trained ViT-Base with **single-node training**, run the following on 1 node with 8 GPUs:
FINETUNE — Here the effective batch size is 32 (`batch_size` per gpu) * 4 (`accum_iter`) * 8 (gpus) = 1024. `--accum_iter 4` simulates 4 nodes.
FINETUNE — The [pre-trained models we provide](https://github.com/fairinternal/mae/#pre-trained-checkpoints) are trained with *normalized* pixels `--norm_pix_loss` (1600 epochs, Table 3 in paper). The fine-tuning hyper-parameters are slightly different from the default baseline using *unnormalized* pixels.
FINETUNE — The original MAE implementation was in TensorFlow+TPU with no explicit mixed precision. This re-implementation is in PyTorch+GPU with automatic mixed precision (`torch.cuda.amp`). We have observed different numerical behavior between the two platforms. In this repo, we use `--global_pool` for fine-tuning; using `--cls_token` performs similarly, but there is a chance of producing NaN when fine-tuning ViT-Huge in GPUs. We did not observe this issue in TPUs. Turning off amp could solve this issue, but is slower.
FINETUNE — Here we use RandErase following DeiT: `--reprob 0.25`. Its effect is smaller than random variance.
FINETUNE — Linear Probing
FINETUNE — Run the following on 4 nodes with 8 GPUs each:
FINETUNE — Here the effective batch size is 512 (`batch_size` per gpu) * 4 (`nodes`) * 8 (gpus per node) = 16384.
FINETUNE — `blr` is the base learning rate. The actual `lr` is computed by the [linear scaling rule](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.02677): `lr` = `blr` * effective batch size / 256.
FINETUNE — Training time is ~2h20m for 90 epochs in 32 V100 GPUs.
FINETUNE — To run single-node training, follow the instruction in fine-tuning.
FINETUNE — To train ViT-Large or ViT-Huge, set `--model vit_large_patch16` or `--model vit_huge_patch14`. It is sufficient to train 50 epochs `--epochs 50`.
FINETUNE — This PT/GPU code produces *better* results for ViT-L/H (see the table below). This is likely caused by the system difference between TF and PT.

README — Towards Robust Monocular Depth Estimation: Mixing Datasets for Zero-shot Cross-dataset Transfer
README — This repository contains code to compute depth from a single image. It accompanies our [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.01341v3):
README — Towards Robust Monocular Depth Estimation: Mixing Datasets for Zero-shot Cross-dataset Transfer
README — René Ranftl, Katrin Lasinger, David Hafner, Konrad Schindler, Vladlen Koltun
README — and our [preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.13413):
README — Vision Transformers for Dense Prediction
README — René Ranftl, Alexey Bochkovskiy, Vladlen Koltun
README — For the latest release MiDaS 3.1, a [technical report](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2307.14460.pdf) and [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UjaeNNFf9sE&t=3s) are available.
README — MiDaS was trained on up to 12 datasets (ReDWeb, DIML, Movies, MegaDepth, WSVD, TartanAir, HRWSI, ApolloScape, BlendedMVS, IRS, KITTI, NYU Depth V2) with
README — multi-objective optimization.
README — The original model that was trained on 5 datasets (`MIX 5` in the paper) can be found [here](https://github.com/isl-org/MiDaS/releases/tag/v2).
README — The figure below shows an overview of the different MiDaS models; the bubble size scales with number of parameters.
README — ![](figures/Improvement_vs_FPS.png)
README — Pick one or more models and download the corresponding weights to the `weights` folder:
README — MiDaS 3.1
README — For highest quality: [dpt_beit_large_512](https://github.com/isl-org/MiDaS/releases/download/v3_1/dpt_beit_large_512.pt)
README — For moderately less quality, but better speed-performance trade-off: [dpt_swin2_large_384](https://github.com/isl-org/MiDaS/releases/download/v3_1/dpt_swin2_large_384.pt)
README — For embedded devices: [dpt_swin2_tiny_256](https://github.com/isl-org/MiDaS/releases/download/v3_1/dpt_swin2_tiny_256.pt), [dpt_levit_224](https://github.com/isl-org/MiDaS/releases/download/v3_1/dpt_levit_224.pt)
README — For inference on Intel CPUs, OpenVINO may be used for the small legacy model: openvino_midas_v21_small [.xml](https://github.com/isl-org/MiDaS/releases/download/v3_1/openvino_midas_v21_small_256.xml), [.bin](https://github.com/isl-org/MiDaS/releases/download/v3_1/openvino_midas_v21_small_256.bin)
README — MiDaS 3.0: Legacy transformer models [dpt_large_384](https://github.com/isl-org/MiDaS/releases/download/v3/dpt_large_384.pt) and [dpt_hybrid_384](https://github.com/isl-org/MiDaS/releases/download/v3/dpt_hybrid_384.pt)
README — MiDaS 2.1: Legacy convolutional models [midas_v21_384](https://github.com/isl-org/MiDaS/releases/download/v2_1/midas_v21_384.pt) and [midas_v21_small_256](https://github.com/isl-org/MiDaS/releases/download/v2_1/midas_v21_small_256.pt)

README — optional
README — By default, the inference resizes the height of input images to the size of a model to fit into the encoder. This
README — size is given by the numbers in the model names of the [accuracy table](#accuracy). Some models do not only support a single
README — inference height but a range of different heights. Feel free to explore different heights by appending the extra
README — command line argument `--height`. Unsupported height values will throw an error. Note that using this argument may
README — decrease the model accuracy.
README — By default, the inference keeps the aspect ratio of input images when feeding them into the encoder if this is
README — supported by a model (all models except for Swin, Swin2, LeViT). In order to resize to a square resolution,
README — disregarding the aspect ratio while preserving the height, use the command line argument `--square`.

README — Accuracy
README — We provide a **zero-shot error** $\epsilon_d$ which is evaluated for 6 different datasets
README — (see [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.01341v3)). **Lower error values are better**.

README — &ast; No zero-shot error, because models are also trained on KITTI and NYU Depth V2\
README — $\square$ Validation performed at **square resolution**, either because the transformer encoder backbone of a model
README — does not support non-square resolutions (Swin, Swin2, LeViT) or for comparison with these models. All other
README — validations keep the aspect ratio. A difference in resolution limits the comparability of the zero-shot error and the
README — improvement, because these quantities are averages over the pixels of an image and do not take into account the
README — advantage of more details due to a higher resolution.\
README — Best values per column and same validation height in bold
README — Improvement
README — The improvement in the above table is defined as the relative zero-shot error with respect to MiDaS v3.0
README — DPT<sub>L-384</sub> and averaging over the datasets. So, if $\epsilon_d$ is the zero-shot error for dataset $d$, then
README — the $\color{green}{\textsf{improvement}}$ is given by $100(1-(1/6)\sum_d\epsilon_d/\epsilon_{d,\rm{DPT_{L-384}}})$%.
README — Note that the improvements of 10% for MiDaS v2.0 &rarr; v2.1 and 21% for MiDaS v2.1 &rarr; v3.0 are not visible from the
README — improvement column (Imp.) in the table but would require an evaluation with respect to MiDaS v2.1 Large<sub>384</sub>
README — and v2.0 Large<sub>384</sub> respectively instead of v3.0 DPT<sub>L-384</sub>.

README — Applications
README — MiDaS is used in the following other projects from Intel Labs:
README — [ZoeDepth](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2302.12288.pdf) (code available [here](https://github.com/isl-org/ZoeDepth)): MiDaS computes the relative depth map given an image. For metric depth estimation, ZoeDepth can be used, which combines MiDaS with a metric depth binning module appended to the decoder.
README — [LDM3D](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2305.10853.pdf) (Hugging Face model available [here](https://huggingface.co/Intel/ldm3d-4c)): LDM3D is an extension of vanilla stable diffusion designed to generate joint image and depth data from a text prompt. The depth maps used for supervision when training LDM3D have been computed using MiDaS.
README — Changelog
README — [Dec 2022] Released [MiDaS v3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2307.14460.pdf):
README — New models based on 5 different types of transformers ([BEiT](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.08254.pdf), [Swin2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2111.09883.pdf), [Swin](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.14030.pdf), [Next-ViT](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.05501.pdf), [LeViT](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2104.01136.pdf))
README — Training datasets extended from 10 to 12, including also KITTI and NYU Depth V2 using [BTS](https://github.com/cleinc/bts) split
README — Best model, BEiT<sub>Large 512</sub>, with resolution 512x512, is on average about [28% more accurate](#Accuracy) than MiDaS v3.0
README — Integrated live depth estimation from camera feed
README — [Sep 2021] Integrated to [Huggingface Spaces](https://huggingface.co/spaces) with [Gradio](https://github.com/gradio-app/gradio). See [Gradio Web Demo](https://huggingface.co/spaces/akhaliq/DPT-Large).

README — Below Colabs run both with GPUs, and TPUs (8 cores, data parallelism).
README — The first Colab demonstrates the JAX code of Vision Transformers and MLP Mixers.
README — This Colab allows you to edit the files from the repository directly in the
README — Colab UI and has annotated Colab cells that walk you through the code step by
README — step, and lets you interact with the data.
README — https://colab.research.google.com/github/google-research/vision_transformer/blob/main/vit_jax.ipynb
README — The second Colab allows you to explore the >50k Vision Transformer and hybrid
README — checkpoints that were used to generate the data of the third paper "How to train
README — your ViT? ...". The Colab includes code to explore and select checkpoints, and
README — to do inference both using the JAX code from this repo, and also using the
README — popular [`timm`] PyTorch library that can directly load these checkpoints as
README — well. Note that a handful of models are also available directly from TF-Hub:
README — [sayakpaul/collections/vision_transformer] (external contribution by [Sayak
README — The second Colab also lets you fine-tune the checkpoints on any tfds dataset
README — and your own dataset with examples in individual JPEG files (optionally directly
README — reading from Google Drive).
README — https://colab.research.google.com/github/google-research/vision_transformer/blob/main/vit_jax_augreg.ipynb
README — Note**: As for now (6/20/21) Google Colab only supports a single GPU (Nvidia
README — Tesla T4), and TPUs (currently TPUv2-8) are attached indirectly to the Colab VM
README — and communicate over slow network, which leads to pretty bad training speed. You
README — would usually want to set up a dedicated machine if you have a non-trivial
README — amount of data to fine-tune on. For details see the
README — [Running on cloud](#running-on-cloud) section.

README — Installation
README — Make sure you have `Python>=3.10` installed on your machine.
README — Install JAX and python dependencies by running:
README — For newer versions of [JAX](https://github.com/google/jax), follow the instructions
README — provided in the corresponding repository linked here. Note that installation
README — instructions for CPU, GPU and TPU differs slightly.
README — Install [Flaxformer](https://github.com/google/flaxformer), follow the instructions
README — provided in the corresponding repository linked here.
README — For more details refer to the section [Running on cloud](#running-on-cloud)
README — Fine-tuning a model
README — You can run fine-tuning of the downloaded model on your dataset of interest. All
README — models share the same command line interface.
README — For example for fine-tuning a ViT-B/16 (pre-trained on imagenet21k) on CIFAR10
README — (note how we specify `b16,cifar10` as arguments to the config, and how we
README — instruct the code to access the models directly from a GCS bucket instead of
README — first downloading them into the local directory):
README — In order to fine-tune a Mixer-B/16 (pre-trained on imagenet21k) on CIFAR10:
README — The "How to train your ViT? ..." paper added >50k checkpoints that you can
README — fine-tune with the [`configs/augreg.py`] config. When you only specify the model
README — name (the `config.name` value from [`configs/model.py`]), then the best i21k
README — checkpoint by upstream validation accuracy ("recommended" checkpoint, see
README — section 4.5 of the paper) is chosen. To make up your mind which model you want
README — to use, have a look at Figure 3 in the paper. It's also possible to choose a
README — different checkpoint (see Colab [`vit_jax_augreg.ipynb`]) and then specify the
README — value from the `filename` or `adapt_filename` column, which correspond to the
README — filenames without `.npz` from the [`gs://vit_models/augreg`] directory.
README — Currently, the code will automatically download CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets.
README — Other public or custom datasets can be easily integrated, using [tensorflow
README — datasets library](https://github.com/tensorflow/datasets/). Note that you will
README — also need to update `vit_jax/input_pipeline.py` to specify some parameters about
README — any added dataset.
README — Note that our code uses all available GPUs/TPUs for fine-tuning.
README — To see a detailed list of all available flags, run `python3 -m vit_jax.train
README — Notes on memory:
README — Different models require different amount of memory. Available memory also
README — depends on the accelerator configuration (both type and count). If you
README — encounter an out-of-memory error you can increase the value of
README — `--config.accum_steps=8` -- alternatively, you could also decrease the
README — `--config.batch=512` (and decrease `--config.base_lr` accordingly).
README — The host keeps a shuffle buffer in memory. If you encounter a host OOM (as
README — opposed to an accelerator OOM), you can decrease the default
README — `--config.shuffle_buffer=50000`.
README — Vision Transformer
README — by Alexey Dosovitskiy\*†, Lucas Beyer\*, Alexander Kolesnikov\*, Dirk
README — Weissenborn\*, Xiaohua Zhai\*, Thomas Unterthiner, Mostafa Dehghani, Matthias
README — Minderer, Georg Heigold, Sylvain Gelly, Jakob Uszkoreit and Neil Houlsby\*†.
README — (\*) equal technical contribution, (†) equal advising.
README — ![Figure 1 from paper](vit_figure.png)
README — Overview of the model: we split an image into fixed-size patches, linearly embed
README — each of them, add position embeddings, and feed the resulting sequence of
README — vectors to a standard Transformer encoder. In order to perform classification,
README — we use the standard approach of adding an extra learnable "classification token"
README — to the sequence.
README — Available ViT models
README — We provide a variety of ViT models in different GCS buckets. The models can be
README — downloaded with e.g.:
README — The model filenames (without the `.npz` extension) correspond to the
README — `config.model_name` in [`vit_jax/configs/models.py`]
README — [`gs://vit_models/imagenet21k`] - Models pre-trained on ImageNet-21k.
README — [`gs://vit_models/imagenet21k+imagenet2012`] - Models pre-trained on
README — ImageNet-21k and fine-tuned on ImageNet.
README — [`gs://vit_models/augreg`] - Models pre-trained on ImageNet-21k,
README — applying varying amounts of [AugReg]. Improved performance.
README — [`gs://vit_models/sam`] - Models pre-trained on ImageNet with [SAM].
README — [`gs://vit_models/gsam`] - Models pre-trained on ImageNet with [GSAM].

README — the best pre-training metrics:

README — MLP-Mixer
README — by Ilya Tolstikhin\*, Neil Houlsby\*, Alexander Kolesnikov\*, Lucas Beyer\*,
README — Xiaohua Zhai, Thomas Unterthiner, Jessica Yung, Andreas Steiner, Daniel Keysers,
README — Jakob Uszkoreit, Mario Lucic, Alexey Dosovitskiy.
README — (\*) equal contribution.
README — ![Figure 1 from paper](mixer_figure.png)
README — MLP-Mixer (*Mixer* for short) consists of per-patch linear embeddings, Mixer
README — layers, and a classifier head. Mixer layers contain one token-mixing MLP and one
README — channel-mixing MLP, each consisting of two fully-connected layers and a GELU
README — nonlinearity. Other components include: skip-connections, dropout, and linear
README — classifier head.
README — For installation follow [the same steps](#installation) as above.
README — Available Mixer models
README — We provide the Mixer-B/16 and Mixer-L/16 models pre-trained on the ImageNet and
README — ImageNet-21k datasets. Details can be found in Table 3 of the Mixer paper. All
README — the models can be found at:
README — https://console.cloud.google.com/storage/mixer_models/
README — Note that these models are also available directly from TF-Hub:
README — [sayakpaul/collections/mlp-mixer] (external contribution by [Sayak
README — [sayakpaul/collections/mlp-mixer]: https://tfhub.dev/sayakpaul/collections/mlp-mixer

README — LiT models
README — For details, refer to the Google AI blog post
README — [LiT: adding language understanding to image models](http://ai.googleblog.com/2022/04/locked-image-tuning-adding-language.html),
README — or read the CVPR paper "LiT: Zero-Shot Transfer with Locked-image text Tuning"
README — (https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.07991).
README — We published a Transformer B/16-base model with an ImageNet zeroshot accuracy of
README — %, and a L/16-large model with an ImageNet zeroshot accuracy of 75.7%. For
README — more details about these models, please refer to the
README — [LiT model card](model_cards/lit.md).
README — We provide a in-browser demo with small text encoders for interactive use (the
README — smallest models should even run on a modern cell phone):
README — https://google-research.github.io/vision_transformer/lit/
README — And finally a Colab to use the JAX models with both image and text encoders:
README — https://colab.research.google.com/github/google-research/vision_transformer/blob/main/lit.ipynb
README — Note that none of above models support multi-lingual inputs yet, but we're
README — working on publishing such models and will update this repository once they
README — become available.
README — This repository only contains evaluation code for LiT models. You can find the
README — training code in the `big_vision` repository:
README — https://github.com/google-research/big_vision/tree/main/big_vision/configs/proj/image_text
README — Expected zeroshot results from [`model_cards/lit.md`] (note that the zeroshot
README — evaluation is slightly different from the simplified evaluation in the Colab):
README — | Model | B16B_2 | L16L |
README — | :--- | ---: | ---: |
README — | ImageNet zero-shot | 73.9% | 75.7% |
README — | ImageNet v2 zero-shot | 65.1% | 66.6% |
README — | CIFAR100 zero-shot | 79.0% | 80.5% |
README — | Pets37 zero-shot | 83.3% | 83.3% |
README — | Resisc45 zero-shot | 25.3% | 25.6% |
README — | MS-COCO Captions image-to-text retrieval | 51.6% | 48.5% |
README — | MS-COCO Captions text-to-image retrieval | 31.8% | 31.1% |

README — While above [colabs](#colab) are pretty useful to get started, you would usually
README — want to train on a larger machine with more powerful accelerators.

README — Changelog
README — In reverse chronological order:
README — : Added LiT-B16B_2 model that was trained for 60k steps
README — (LiT_B16B: 30k) without linear head on the image side (LiT_B16B: 768) and has
README — better performance.
README — : Added the ViT and Mixer models trained from scratch using
README — [GSAM] on ImageNet without strong data augmentations. The resultant ViTs
README — outperform those of similar sizes trained using AdamW optimizer or the
README — original [SAM] algorithm, or with strong data augmentations.
README — : Added models and Colab for [LiT models](#lit-models).
README — : Added ViT-B/8 AugReg models (3 upstream checkpoints and adaptations
README — with resolution=224).
README — : Added the "When Vision Transformers Outperform
README — ResNets..." paper
README — : Added [SAM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.01412)
README — (Sharpness-Aware Minimization) optimized ViT and MLP-Mixer checkpoints.
README — : Added the "How to train your ViT? ..." paper, and a new
README — Colab to explore the >50k pre-trained and fine-tuned checkpoints mentioned in
README — the paper.
README — : This repository was rewritten to use Flax Linen API and
README — `ml_collections.ConfigDict` for configuration.
README — : With publication of the "How to train your ViT? ..."
README — paper, we added more than 50k ViT and hybrid models pre-trained on ImageNet and
README — ImageNet-21k with various degrees of data augmentation and model regularization,
README — and fine-tuned on ImageNet, Pets37, Kitti-distance, CIFAR-100, and Resisc45.
README — Check out [`vit_jax_augreg.ipynb`] to navigate this treasure trove of models!
README — For example, you can use that Colab to fetch the filenames of recommended
README — pre-trained and fine-tuned checkpoints from the `i21k_300` column of Table 3 in
README — the paper.
README — : Added the R50+ViT-B/16 hybrid model (ViT-B/16 on
README — top of a Resnet-50 backbone). When pretrained on imagenet21k, this model
README — achieves almost the performance of the L/16 model with less than half the
README — computational finetuning cost. Note that "R50" is somewhat modified for the
README — B/16 variant: The original ResNet-50 has [3,4,6,3] blocks, each reducing the
README — resolution of the image by a factor of two. In combination with the ResNet
README — stem this would result in a reduction of 32x so even with a patch size of
README — (1,1) the ViT-B/16 variant cannot be realized anymore. For this reason we
README — instead use [3,4,9] blocks for the R50+B/16 variant.
README — : Added the ViT-L/16 model.
README — : Added ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16 models pretrained
README — on ImageNet-21k and then fine-tuned on ImageNet at 224x224 resolution (instead
README — of default 384x384). These models have the suffix "-224" in their name.
README — They are expected to achieve 81.2% and 82.7% top-1 accuracies respectively.

CONTRIBUTING — How to Contribute
CONTRIBUTING — We'd love to accept your patches and contributions to this project. There are
CONTRIBUTING — just a few small guidelines you need to follow.
CONTRIBUTING — Contributor License Agreement
CONTRIBUTING — Contributions to this project must be accompanied by a Contributor License
CONTRIBUTING — Agreement (CLA). You (or your employer) retain the copyright to your
CONTRIBUTING — contribution; this simply gives us permission to use and redistribute your
CONTRIBUTING — contributions as part of the project. Head over to
CONTRIBUTING — <https://cla.developers.google.com/> to see your current agreements on file or
CONTRIBUTING — to sign a new one.
CONTRIBUTING — You generally only need to submit a CLA once, so if you've already submitted one
CONTRIBUTING — (even if it was for a different project), you probably don't need to do it
CONTRIBUTING — Code reviews
CONTRIBUTING — All submissions, including submissions by project members, require review. We
CONTRIBUTING — use GitHub pull requests for this purpose. Consult
CONTRIBUTING — [GitHub Help](https://help.github.com/articles/about-pull-requests/) for more
CONTRIBUTING — information on using pull requests.
CONTRIBUTING — Community Guidelines
CONTRIBUTING — This project follows
CONTRIBUTING — [Google's Open Source Community Guidelines](https://opensource.google/conduct/).
awesome-transformers — Awesome projects built with Transformers
awesome-transformers — This page lists awesome projects built on top of Transformers. Transformers is more than a toolkit to use pretrained
awesome-transformers — models: it's a community of projects built around it and the Hugging Face Hub. We want Transformers to enable
awesome-transformers — developers, researchers, students, professors, engineers, and anyone else to build their dream projects.
awesome-transformers — In this list, we showcase incredibly impactful and novel projects that have pushed the field forward. We celebrate
awesome-transformers — of these projects as we reach the milestone of 100k stars as a community; but we're very open to pull requests
awesome-transformers — adding other projects to the list. If you believe a project should be here and it's not, then please, open a PR
awesome-transformers — to add it.
awesome-transformers — [gpt4all](https://github.com/nomic-ai/gpt4all)
awesome-transformers — [gpt4all](https://github.com/nomic-ai/gpt4all) is an ecosystem of open-source chatbots trained on massive collections of clean assistant data including code, stories and dialogue. It offers open-source, large language models such as LLaMA and GPT-J trained in an assistant-style.
awesome-transformers — Keywords: Open-source, LLaMa, GPT-J, instruction, assistant
awesome-transformers — [recommenders](https://github.com/recommenders-team/recommenders)
awesome-transformers — This repository contains examples and best practices for building recommendation systems, provided as Jupyter notebooks. It goes over several aspects required to build efficient recommendation systems: data preparation, modeling, evaluation, model selection & optimization, as well as operationalization
awesome-transformers — Keywords: Recommender systems, AzureML
awesome-transformers — [IOPaint](https://github.com/Sanster/IOPaint)
awesome-transformers — Image inpainting tool powered by Stable Diffusion. Remove any unwanted object, defect, people from your pictures or erase and replace anything on your pictures.
awesome-transformers — Keywords: inpainting, SD, Stable Diffusion

awesome-transformers — FLAIR is a powerful PyTorch NLP framework, covering several important tasks: NER, sentiment-analysis, part-of-speech tagging, text and document embeddings, among other things.
awesome-transformers — Keywords: NLP, text embedding, document embedding, biomedical, NER, PoS, sentiment-analysis

awesome-transformers — MindsDB is a low-code ML platform, which automates and integrates several ML frameworks into the data stack as "AI Tables" to streamline the integration of AI into applications, making it accessible to developers of all skill levels.

awesome-transformers — [sentence-transformers](https://github.com/UKPLab/sentence-transformers)
awesome-transformers — This framework provides an easy method to compute dense vector representations for sentences, paragraphs, and images. The models are based on transformer networks like BERT / RoBERTa / XLM-RoBERTa etc. and achieve state-of-the-art performance in various task. Text is embedding in vector space such that similar text is close and can efficiently be found using cosine similarity.
awesome-transformers — Keywords: Dense vector representations, Text embeddings, Sentence embeddings

SECURITY — Security Policy
SECURITY — Hugging Face Hub, remote artefacts, and remote code
SECURITY — Transformers is open-source software that is tightly coupled to the Hugging Face Hub. While you have the ability to use it
SECURITY — offline with pre-downloaded model weights, it provides a very simple way to download, use, and manage models locally.
SECURITY — When downloading artefacts that have been uploaded by others on any platform, you expose yourself to risks. Please
SECURITY — read below for the security recommendations in order to keep your runtime and local environment safe.
SECURITY — Remote artefacts
SECURITY — Models uploaded on the Hugging Face Hub come in different formats. We heavily recommend uploading and downloading
SECURITY — models in the [`safetensors`](https://github.com/huggingface/safetensors) format (which is the default prioritized
SECURITY — by the transformers library), as developed specifically to prevent arbitrary code execution on your system.
SECURITY — To avoid loading models from unsafe formats (e.g. [pickle](https://docs.python.org/3/library/pickle.html), you should use the `use_safetensors` parameter. If doing so, in the event that no .safetensors file is present, transformers will error when loading the model.
SECURITY — Remote code
SECURITY — Modeling
SECURITY — Transformers supports many model architectures, but is also the bridge between your Python runtime and models that
SECURITY — are stored in model repositories on the Hugging Face Hub.
SECURITY — These models require the `trust_remote_code=True` parameter to be set when using them; please **always** verify
SECURITY — the content of the modeling files when using this argument. We recommend setting a revision in order to ensure you
SECURITY — protect yourself from updates on the repository.
SECURITY — Reporting a Vulnerability
SECURITY — Feel free to submit vulnerability reports to [security@huggingface.co](mailto:security@huggingface.co), where someone from the HF security team will review and recommend next steps. If reporting a vulnerability specific to open source, please note [Huntr](https://huntr.com) is a vulnerability disclosure program for open source software.
AGENTS — AGENTS.md Guide for Hugging Face Transformers
AGENTS — This AGENTS.md file provides guidance for code agents working with this codebase.
AGENTS — Core Project Structure
AGENTS — `/src/transformers`: This contains the core source code for the library
AGENTS — `/models`: Code for individual models. Models inherit from base classes in the root `/src/transformers` directory.
AGENTS — `/tests`: This contains the core test classes for the library. These are usually inherited rather than directly run.
AGENTS — `/models`: Tests for individual models. Model tests inherit from common tests in the root `/tests` directory.
AGENTS — `/docs`: This contains the documentation for the library, including guides, tutorials, and API references.
AGENTS — Coding Conventions for Hugging Face Transformers
AGENTS — PRs should be as brief as possible. Bugfix PRs in particular can often be only one or two lines long, and do not need large comments, docstrings or new functions in this case. Aim to minimize the size of the diff.
AGENTS — When writing tests, they should be added to an existing file. The only exception is for PRs to add a new model, when a new test directory should be created for that model.
AGENTS — Code style is enforced in the CI. You can install the style tools with `pip install -e .[quality]`. You can then run `make fixup` to apply style and consistency fixes to your code.
AGENTS — Copying and inheritance
AGENTS — Many models in the codebase have similar code, but it is not shared by inheritance because we want each model file to be self-contained.
AGENTS — We use two mechanisms to keep this code in sync:
AGENTS — "Copied from" syntax. Functions or entire classes can have a comment at the top like this: `# Copied from transformers.models.llama.modeling_llama.rotate_half` or `# Copied from transformers.models.t5.modeling_t5.T5LayerNorm with T5->MT5`
AGENTS — These comments are actively checked by the style tools, and copies will automatically be updated when the base code is updated. If you need to update a copied function, you should
AGENTS — either update the base function and use `make fixup` to propagate the change to all copies, or simply remove the `# Copied from` comment if that is inappropriate.
AGENTS — "Modular" files. These files briefly define models by composing them using inheritance from other models. They are not meant to be used directly. Instead, the style tools
AGENTS — automatically generate a complete modeling file, like `modeling_bert.py`, from the modular file like `modular_bert.py`. If a model has a modular file, the modeling file
AGENTS — should never be edited directly! Instead, changes should be made in the modular file, and then you should run `make fixup` to update the modeling file automatically.
AGENTS — When adding new models, you should prefer `modular` style.
AGENTS — After making changes, you should usually run `make fixup` to ensure any copies and modular files are updated, and then test all affected models. This includes both
AGENTS — the model you made the changes in and any other models that were updated by `make fixup`. Tests can be run with `pytest tests/models/[name]/test_modeling_[name].py`
AGENTS — If your changes affect code in other classes like tokenizers or processors, you should run those tests instead, like `test_processing_[name].py` or `test_tokenization_[name].py`.
AGENTS — In order to run tests, you may need to install dependencies. You can do this with `pip install -e .[testing]`. You will probably also need to `pip install torch accelerate` if your environment does not already have them.

CODE OF CONDUCT — size, visible or invisible disability, ethnicity, sex characteristics, gender
CODE OF CONDUCT — identity and expression, level of experience, education, socio-economic status,

CODE OF CONDUCT — Giving and gracefully accepting constructive feedback
CODE OF CONDUCT — Accepting responsibility and apologizing to those affected by our mistakes,
CODE OF CONDUCT — and learning from the experience
CODE OF CONDUCT — Focusing on what is best not just for us as individuals, but for the overall
CODE OF CONDUCT — community

CODE OF CONDUCT — any kind

ISSUES — How To Request Support
ISSUES — This is an Open Source Project so please be mindful that like in any other project of this kind there is no obligation to answer all requests for help.
ISSUES — However, we want to encourage you to ask for help whenever you think it's needed! We are happy about every question we get because it allows us to better understand your needs, possible misunderstandings, and most importantly a way for you to help us make this library better. That being said, this document's main purpose is to provide guidelines at how you can formulate your requests to increase your chances to be understood and to get support.
ISSUES — There are two main venues to receive support: [the forums](https://discuss.huggingface.co/) and [the GitHub issues](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/issues).
ISSUES — The Forums
ISSUES — [The user forums](https://discuss.huggingface.co/) are supported by the wide community of the library users and backed up by developers when needed.
ISSUES — If you have a difficulty with deploying this library or some questions, or you'd like to discuss a new feature, please first consider discussing those things at the forums. Only when you feel your subject matter has been crystallized and you still need support from the library developers do proceed to file an [issue](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/issues).
ISSUES — In particular all "Please explain" questions or objectively very user-specific feature requests belong to the forums. Here are some example of such questions:
ISSUES — "I would like to use a BertModel within a RL-Agent for a customer support service. How can I use a BertForMaskedLM in my ChatBotModel?"
ISSUES — "Could you please explain why T5 has no positional embedding matrix under T5Model?"
ISSUES — "How should I set my generation parameters for translation?"
ISSUES — "How to train T5 on De->En translation?"
ISSUES — The GitHub Issues
ISSUES — Everything which hints at a bug should be opened as an [issue](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/issues).
ISSUES — You are not required to read the following guidelines before opening an issue. However, if you notice that your issue doesn't get any replies, chances are that the developers have one or several difficulties with its quality. In this case, reading the following points and adjusting your issue accordingly could help.
ISSUES — Before posting an issue, first search for already posted issues, since chances are someone has already asked a similar question before you.
ISSUES — If you use Google your search query should be:
ISSUES — The first two quoted words tell Google to limit the search to the context of the Huggingface Transformers. The remainder is your query - most commonly this would be the error message the software fails with. We will go deeper into details shortly.
ISSUES — The results of such a query will typically match GitHub issues, Hugging Face forums, StackExchange, and blogs.
ISSUES — If you find relevant hints, you may choose to continue the discussion there if you have follow up questions.
ISSUES — If what you found is similar but doesn't quite answer your problem, please, post a new issue and do include links to similar issues or forum discussions you may have found.
ISSUES — Let's look at some examples:
ISSUES — The error message, often referred to as an assertion, tells us what went wrong. Here is an example of an assertion:
ISSUES — and it typically includes a traceback, so that we can see the full stack of calls the program made before it fails. This gives us the context to know why the program failed.
ISSUES — Going back to the above example. If you received this error search, look at the very last line of the error which is:
ISSUES — And now we can use it to do the searching on your favorite search engine:
ISSUES — first for `"huggingface" "transformers" "ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'tqdm.auto'"`
ISSUES — if you don't find relevant results, then search for just `"ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'tqdm.auto'"`
ISSUES — and finally if nothing still comes up, then remove the outside quotes: `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'tqdm.auto'`
ISSUES — If the error includes any messages that include bits unique to your filesystem, always remove those in the search query since other users will not have the same filesystem as yours. For example:
ISSUES — Here you'd search for just: `"FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory"`
ISSUES — If the local information that you removed were inside the error message and you removed them you may need to remove double quotes since your query is no longer exact. So if the error message was something like:
ISSUES — then you'd search for `"ValueError" "cannot be found"`
ISSUES — As you search you will notice that when you don't use quotes often the search engines will return a variety of unrelated hits, which may or may not be what you want.
ISSUES — Experiment with different ways and find which approach gives the most satisfactory results.
ISSUES — Keep the issue short, providing the information that you think will aid the developers to understand your situation. Put yourself in the shoes of the person who has never seen your code or knows anything about your custom setup. This mental exercise will help to develop an intuition to what/what not to share"
ISSUES — If there is a software failure, always provide the full traceback, for example:
ISSUES — As compared to providing just the last line of the error message, e.g.:
ISSUES — which is not sufficient.
ISSUES — If your application is running on more than one GPU (e.g. under `DistributedDataParallel`) and typically getting every log and traceback printed multiple times, please make sure that you paste only one copy of it. At times the traceback from parallel processes may get interleaved - so either disentangle these or change the loggers to log only for `local_rank==0` so that only one process logs things.
ISSUES — When quoting a traceback, command line instructions and any type of code always enclose it in triple backticks inside the editor window, that is:
ISSUES — git clone https://github.com/huggingface/transformers
ISSUES — cd transformers
ISSUES — pip install .
ISSUES — If it's a command line with a long argument list, please consider breaking it down using backslashes and new lines. Here is an example of a good command line quote:
ISSUES — If you don't break it up, one has to scroll horizontally which often makes it quite difficult to quickly see what's happening.
ISSUES — The backslashes allow us to copy the command directly into the console to run it, without needing to edit it.
ISSUES — Include only the important information that you think will help the developer to quickly identify the problem.
ISSUES — For example applications often create huge amounts of logs. Ask yourself whether providing all or parts of the log is useful.
ISSUES — Pasting a 100-1000 lines of log into the issue is an immediate turn off, since it will take a lot of time to figure out where the pertinent parts of the log are.
ISSUES — Attaching a full log can be helpful if it's done as an attachment, if it's enclosed in the following html code in the comment editor window:
ISSUES — which would result in the following entry, which can be opened if desired, but otherwise takes little space.
ISSUES — <details>
ISSUES — <summary>Full log</summary>
ISSUES — </details>
ISSUES — You could also provide a link to a pastebin service, but this is less beneficial since those links tend to expire quickly and future readers of your issue might not be able to access that log file anymore and may lack some context.
ISSUES — If this is an issue in your code, do try to reduce that code to a minimal example that still demonstrates the problem. Please ask at the forums if you have a hard time figuring how to do that. Please realize that we don't have the luxury of having time to try and understand all of your custom code.
ISSUES — If you really tried to make a short reproducible code but couldn't figure it out, it might be that having a traceback will give the developer enough information to know what's going on. But if it is not enough and we can't reproduce the problem, we can't really solve it.
ISSUES — Do not despair if you can't figure it out from the beginning, just share what you can and perhaps someone else will be able to help you at the forums.
ISSUES — If your setup involves any custom datasets, the best way to help us reproduce the problem is to create a [Google Colab notebook](https://colab.research.google.com/) that demonstrates the issue and once you verify that the issue still exists, include a link to that notebook in the Issue. Just make sure that you don't copy and paste the location bar url of the open notebook - as this is private and we won't be able to open it. Instead, you need to click on `Share` in the right upper corner of the notebook, select `Get Link` and then copy and paste the public link it will give to you.
ISSUES — If you forked off some of this project's code or example applications, please, do not ask us to go into your code repository and figure out what you may have done. The code is already very complex and unless there is an easy way to do a diff and it's a small diff, it won't be possible to find someone with time on their hands to make a lengthy investigation. Albeit, you might find someone at the forums who will be generous to do this for you.
ISSUES — Before reporting an issue, first, always try to update your environment to the latest official version of this library. We have no resources to go and debug older revisions, which could easily have bugs that have been fixed in the latest released version.
ISSUES — We understand that this is not always possible, especially when APIs change, in which case file an issue against the highest library version your environment can support.
ISSUES — Of course, if you upgrade the library, always retest that the problem is still there.
ISSUES — Please do not ask us to reproduce an issue with your custom data, since we don't have it. So, either you should use some existing dataset supported by HF datasets or you need to supply a code that generates a small sample on the fly, or some another quick and simple way to get it.
ISSUES — Please do not send us any non-public domain data that may require a license or a permission to be used.
ISSUES — Do not tag multiple developers on the issue unless you know this is expected, either because you asked them and they gave you an explicit permission to tag them or the issue template instructs you to do so.
ISSUES — The "who to tag for what domain" part of the issue template is there to help users direct their questions to the right developers who are designated maintainers of project's specific domains. They can then decide at their own discretion to tag other developers if they feel it'd help move the issue forward.
ISSUES — We currently don't have a triage service and we trust your capacity to identify the right domain and thus the persons to tag in your issue. If you are not sure, please use the forums to ask for guidance.
ISSUES — When in doubt, err on the side of not tagging a given person. If you tag multiple people out of context or permission don't be surprised if you get no response at all. Please remember that every time you tag someone, they get a notification and you're taking their time without their permission. Please be sensitive to that.
ISSUES — If you got helped by one of the developers in the past please don't tag them in future issues, unless they are listed in the issue template for the domain you are asking about or that developer gave you an explicit permission to tag them in future issues.
ISSUES — If you see a certain developer doing multiple and/or recent commits into a specific area of the project that you feel is relevant to your issue, it is not a good reason to tag them. Various developers may be fixing things that prevent them from moving forward, but often their work is focused on a totally different domain. And while they may or may not know how to help you with the problem at hand, it would benefit the whole community much more if they focus on the domain of their unique expertise.
ISSUES — Use the Edit button. Take your time, and re-read and improve the wording and formatting to make your posts and comments as easy to understand as possible.
ISSUES — Avoid posting multiple comments in a row, as each comment generates a notification for the developers tagged in that issue. If you happened to post multiple comments in a row, and nobody followed up yet - consider merging those into one or a few comments while editing the combined content to be coherent.
ISSUES — If you choose to edit your older comments after others posted follow up comments you need to be aware that your modifications might not be noticed, so if it's not a typo fixing, try to write a new comment flagging that something has been changed in the previous comments.
ISSUES — For example, the very first comment is the most important one. If while the thread unfolds you realize that things aren't as they seemed to you originally you may want to edit the first post to reflect the up-to-date understanding of the issue at hand so that it helps those who read your issue in the future quickly understand what's going on and not need to sift through dozens of comments. It also helps to indicate that the post was edited. So, those reading the thread later can understand why there might be certain discontinuity in the information flow.
ISSUES — Use bullets and items if you have lists of items and the outcome improves overall readability.
ISSUES — Use backticks to refer to class and function names, e.g. `BartModel` and `generate` as these stand out and improve the speed of a reader's comprehension.
ISSUES — Try not use italics and bold text too much as these often make the text more difficult to read.
ISSUES — If you are cross-referencing a specific comment in a given thread or another issue, always link to that specific comment, rather than using the issue link. If you do the latter it could be quite impossible to find which specific comment you're referring to.
ISSUES — To get the link to the specific comment do not copy the url from the location bar of your browser, but instead, click the `...` icon in the upper right corner of the comment and then select "Copy Link".
ISSUES — For example the first link is a link to an issue, and the second to a specific comment in the same issue:
ISSUES — https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/issues/9257
ISSUES — https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/issues/9257#issuecomment-749945162
ISSUES — If you are replying to a last comment, it's totally fine to make your reply with just your comment in it. The readers can follow the information flow here.
ISSUES — But if you're replying to a comment that happened some comments back it's always a good practice to quote just the relevant lines you're replying it. The `>` is used for quoting, or you can always use the menu to do so. For example your editor box will look like:
ISSUES — If you are addressing multiple comments, quote the relevant parts of each before your answer. Some people use the same comment to do multiple replies, others separate them into separate comments. Either way works. The latter approach helps for linking to a specific comment.
ISSUES — In general the best way to figure out what works the best is learn from issues posted by other people - see which issues get great responses and which get little to no response - observe what the posters who received great responses did differently from those who did not.
ISSUES — Thank you for reading this somewhat lengthy document. We would like to conclude that these are not absolute rules, but a friendly advice that will help maximize the chances for us to understand what you are trying to communicate, reproduce the problem then resolve it to your satisfaction and the benefit of the whole community.
ISSUES — If after reading this document there are remaining questions on how and why or there is a need for further elucidation, please, don't hesitate to ask your question in [this thread](https://discuss.huggingface.co/t/how-to-request-support/3128).

README — <h3 align="center">
README — <p>State-of-the-art pretrained models for inference and training</p>
README — <h3 align="center">
README — <img src="https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/transformers/transformers_as_a_model_definition.png"/>
README — Transformers acts as the model-definition framework for state-of-the-art machine learning models in text, computer
README — vision, audio, video, and multimodal model, for both inference and training.
README — It centralizes the model definition so that this definition is agreed upon across the ecosystem. `transformers` is the
README — pivot across frameworks: if a model definition is supported, it will be compatible with the majority of training
README — frameworks (Axolotl, Unsloth, DeepSpeed, FSDP, PyTorch-Lightning, ...), inference engines (vLLM, SGLang, TGI, ...),
README — and adjacent modeling libraries (llama.cpp, mlx, ...) which leverage the model definition from `transformers`.
README — We pledge to help support new state-of-the-art models and democratize their usage by having their model definition be
README — simple, customizable, and efficient.
README — There are over 1M+ Transformers [model checkpoints](https://huggingface.co/models?library=transformers&sort=trending) on the [Hugging Face Hub](https://huggingface.com/models) you can use.
README — Explore the [Hub](https://huggingface.com/) today to find a model and use Transformers to help you get started right away.
README — Installation
README — Transformers works with Python 3.9+ [PyTorch](https://pytorch.org/get-started/locally/) 2.1+, [TensorFlow](https://www.tensorflow.org/install/pip) 2.6+, and [Flax](https://flax.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) 0.4.1+.
README — Create and activate a virtual environment with [venv](https://docs.python.org/3/library/venv.html) or [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), a fast Rust-based Python package and project manager.
README — Install Transformers in your virtual environment.
README — Install Transformers from source if you want the latest changes in the library or are interested in contributing. However, the *latest* version may not be stable. Feel free to open an [issue](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/issues) if you encounter an error.
README — Quickstart
README — Get started with Transformers right away with the [Pipeline](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/pipeline_tutorial) API. The `Pipeline` is a high-level inference class that supports text, audio, vision, and multimodal tasks. It handles preprocessing the input and returns the appropriate output.
README — Instantiate a pipeline and specify model to use for text generation. The model is downloaded and cached so you can easily reuse it again. Finally, pass some text to prompt the model.
README — To chat with a model, the usage pattern is the same. The only difference is you need to construct a chat history (the input to `Pipeline`) between you and the system.
README — You can also chat with a model directly from the command line.
README — ```shell
README — transformers chat Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct

README — Why should I use Transformers?
README — Easy-to-use state-of-the-art models:
README — High performance on natural language understanding & generation, computer vision, audio, video, and multimodal tasks.
README — Low barrier to entry for researchers, engineers, and developers.
README — Few user-facing abstractions with just three classes to learn.
README — A unified API for using all our pretrained models.
README — Lower compute costs, smaller carbon footprint:
README — Share trained models instead of training from scratch.
README — Reduce compute time and production costs.
README — Dozens of model architectures with 1M+ pretrained checkpoints across all modalities.
README — Choose the right framework for every part of a models lifetime:
README — Train state-of-the-art models in 3 lines of code.
README — Move a single model between PyTorch/JAX/TF2.0 frameworks at will.
README — Pick the right framework for training, evaluation, and production.
README — Easily customize a model or an example to your needs:
README — We provide examples for each architecture to reproduce the results published by its original authors.
README — Model internals are exposed as consistently as possible.
README — Model files can be used independently of the library for quick experiments.
README — <a target="_blank" href="https://huggingface.co/enterprise">
README — <img alt="Hugging Face Enterprise Hub" src="https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/247fb16d-d251-4583-96c4-d3d76dda4925">
README — </a><br>
README — Why shouldn't I use Transformers?
README — This library is not a modular toolbox of building blocks for neural nets. The code in the model files is not refactored with additional abstractions on purpose, so that researchers can quickly iterate on each of the models without diving into additional abstractions/files.
README — The training API is optimized to work with PyTorch models provided by Transformers. For generic machine learning loops, you should use another library like [Accelerate](https://huggingface.co/docs/accelerate).
README — The [example scripts](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/tree/main/examples) are only *examples*. They may not necessarily work out-of-the-box on your specific use case and you'll need to adapt the code for it to work.
README — projects using Transformers
README — Transformers is more than a toolkit to use pretrained models, it's a community of projects built around it and the
README — Hugging Face Hub. We want Transformers to enable developers, researchers, students, professors, engineers, and anyone
README — else to build their dream projects.
README — In order to celebrate Transformers 100,000 stars, we wanted to put the spotlight on the
README — community with the [awesome-transformers](./awesome-transformers.md) page which lists 100
README — incredible projects built with Transformers.
README — If you own or use a project that you believe should be part of the list, please open a PR to add it!

CONTRIBUTING — Contribute to 🤗 Transformers
CONTRIBUTING — Everyone is welcome to contribute, and we value everybody's contribution. Code
CONTRIBUTING — contributions are not the only way to help the community. Answering questions, helping
CONTRIBUTING — others, and improving the documentation are also immensely valuable.
CONTRIBUTING — It also helps us if you spread the word! Reference the library in blog posts
CONTRIBUTING — about the awesome projects it made possible, shout out on Twitter every time it has
CONTRIBUTING — helped you, or simply ⭐️ the repository to say thank you.
CONTRIBUTING — However you choose to contribute, please be mindful and respect our
CONTRIBUTING — [code of conduct](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).
CONTRIBUTING — This guide was heavily inspired by the awesome [scikit-learn guide to contributing](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md).**
CONTRIBUTING — Ways to contribute
CONTRIBUTING — There are several ways you can contribute to 🤗 Transformers:
CONTRIBUTING — Fix outstanding issues with the existing code.
CONTRIBUTING — Submit issues related to bugs or desired new features.
CONTRIBUTING — Implement new models.
CONTRIBUTING — Contribute to the examples or to the documentation.
CONTRIBUTING — If you don't know where to start, there is a special [Good First
CONTRIBUTING — Issue](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/contribute) listing. It will give you a list of
CONTRIBUTING — open issues that are beginner-friendly and help you start contributing to open-source. The best way to do that is to open a Pull Request and link it to the issue that you'd like to work on. We try to give priority to opened PRs as we can easily track the progress of the fix, and if the contributor does not have time anymore, someone else can take the PR over.
CONTRIBUTING — For something slightly more challenging, you can also take a look at the [Good Second Issue](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/labels/Good%20Second%20Issue) list. In general though, if you feel like you know what you're doing, go for it and we'll help you get there! 🚀
CONTRIBUTING — All contributions are equally valuable to the community. 🥰
CONTRIBUTING — Fixing outstanding issues
CONTRIBUTING — If you notice an issue with the existing code and have a fix in mind, feel free to [start contributing](#create-a-pull-request) and open a Pull Request!
CONTRIBUTING — Submitting a bug-related issue or feature request
CONTRIBUTING — Do your best to follow these guidelines when submitting a bug-related issue or a feature
CONTRIBUTING — request. It will make it easier for us to come back to you quickly and with good
CONTRIBUTING — feedback.
CONTRIBUTING — Did you find a bug?
CONTRIBUTING — The 🤗 Transformers library is robust and reliable thanks to users who report the problems they encounter.
CONTRIBUTING — Before you report an issue, we would really appreciate it if you could **make sure the bug was not
CONTRIBUTING — already reported** (use the search bar on GitHub under Issues). Your issue should also be related to bugs in the library itself, and not your code. If you're unsure whether the bug is in your code or the library, please ask in the [forum](https://discuss.huggingface.co/) or on our [discord](https://discord.com/invite/hugging-face-879548962464493619) first. This helps us respond quicker to fixing issues related to the library versus general questions.
CONTRIBUTING — We have a [docs bot](https://huggingface.co/spaces/huggingchat/hf-docs-chat), and we highly encourage you to ask all your questions there. There is always a chance your bug can be fixed with a simple flag 👾🔫
CONTRIBUTING — Once you've confirmed the bug hasn't already been reported, please include the following information in your issue so we can quickly resolve it:
CONTRIBUTING — Your **OS type and version** and **Python**, and **PyTorch** versions when applicable.
CONTRIBUTING — A short, self-contained, code snippet that allows us to reproduce the bug in
CONTRIBUTING — less than 30s.
CONTRIBUTING — The *full* traceback if an exception is raised.
CONTRIBUTING — Attach any other additional information, like screenshots, you think may help.
CONTRIBUTING — To get the OS and software versions automatically, run the following command:
CONTRIBUTING — You can also run the same command from the root of the repository:
CONTRIBUTING — Do you want a new feature?
CONTRIBUTING — If there is a new feature you'd like to see in 🤗 Transformers, please open an issue and describe:
CONTRIBUTING — What is the *motivation* behind this feature? Is it related to a problem or frustration with the library? Is it a feature related to something you need for a project? Is it something you worked on and think it could benefit the community?
CONTRIBUTING — Whatever it is, we'd love to hear about it!
CONTRIBUTING — Describe your requested feature in as much detail as possible. The more you can tell us about it, the better we'll be able to help you.
CONTRIBUTING — Provide a *code snippet* that demonstrates the features usage.
CONTRIBUTING — If the feature is related to a paper, please include a link.
CONTRIBUTING — If your issue is well written we're already 80% of the way there by the time you create it.
CONTRIBUTING — We have added [templates](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/tree/main/templates) to help you get started with your issue.
CONTRIBUTING — Do you want to implement a new model?
CONTRIBUTING — New models are constantly released and if you want to implement a new model, please provide the following information:
CONTRIBUTING — A short description of the model and a link to the paper.
CONTRIBUTING — Link to the implementation if it is open-sourced.
CONTRIBUTING — Link to the model weights if they are available.
CONTRIBUTING — If you are willing to contribute the model yourself, let us know so we can help you add it to 🤗 Transformers!
CONTRIBUTING — We have a technical guide for [how to add a model to 🤗 Transformers](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/add_new_model).
CONTRIBUTING — Do you want to add documentation?
CONTRIBUTING — We're always looking for improvements to the documentation that make it more clear and accurate. Please let us know how the documentation can be improved such as typos and any content that is missing, unclear or inaccurate. We'll be happy to make the changes or help you make a contribution if you're interested!
CONTRIBUTING — For more details about how to generate, build, and write the documentation, take a look at the documentation [README](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/tree/main/docs).
CONTRIBUTING — Create a Pull Request
CONTRIBUTING — Before writing any code, we strongly advise you to search through the existing PRs or
CONTRIBUTING — issues to make sure nobody is already working on the same thing. If you are
CONTRIBUTING — unsure, it is always a good idea to open an issue to get some feedback.
CONTRIBUTING — You will need basic `git` proficiency to contribute to

CONTRIBUTING — manual. Type `git --help` in a shell and enjoy! If you prefer books, [Pro
CONTRIBUTING — Git](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2) is a very good reference.

CONTRIBUTING — Pull request checklist
CONTRIBUTING — ☐ The pull request title should summarize your contribution.<br>
CONTRIBUTING — ☐ If your pull request addresses an issue, please mention the issue number in the pull
CONTRIBUTING — request description to make sure they are linked (and people viewing the issue know you
CONTRIBUTING — are working on it).<br>
CONTRIBUTING — ☐ To indicate a work in progress please prefix the title with `[WIP]`. These are
CONTRIBUTING — useful to avoid duplicated work, and to differentiate it from PRs ready to be merged.<br>
CONTRIBUTING — ☐ Make sure existing tests pass.<br>
CONTRIBUTING — ☐ If adding a new feature, also add tests for it.<br>
CONTRIBUTING — If you are adding a new model, make sure you use
CONTRIBUTING — `ModelTester.all_model_classes = (MyModel, MyModelWithLMHead,...)` to trigger the common tests.
CONTRIBUTING — If you are adding new `@slow` tests, make sure they pass using
CONTRIBUTING — `RUN_SLOW=1 python -m pytest tests/models/my_new_model/test_my_new_model.py`.
CONTRIBUTING — If you are adding a new tokenizer, write tests and make sure
CONTRIBUTING — `RUN_SLOW=1 python -m pytest tests/models/{your_model_name}/test_tokenization_{your_model_name}.py` passes.
CONTRIBUTING — CircleCI does not run the slow tests, but GitHub Actions does every night!<br>
CONTRIBUTING — ☐ All public methods must have informative docstrings (see
CONTRIBUTING — [`modeling_bert.py`](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/main/src/transformers/models/bert/modeling_bert.py)
CONTRIBUTING — for an example).<br>
CONTRIBUTING — ☐ Due to the rapidly growing repository, don't add any images, videos and other
CONTRIBUTING — non-text files that'll significantly weigh down the repository. Instead, use a Hub
CONTRIBUTING — repository such as [`hf-internal-testing`](https://huggingface.co/hf-internal-testing)
CONTRIBUTING — to host these files and reference them by URL. We recommend placing documentation
CONTRIBUTING — related images in the following repository:
CONTRIBUTING — [huggingface/documentation-images](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images).
CONTRIBUTING — You can open a PR on this dataset repository and ask a Hugging Face member to merge it.
CONTRIBUTING — For more information about the checks run on a pull request, take a look at our [Checks on a Pull Request](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/pr_checks) guide.
CONTRIBUTING — An extensive test suite is included to test the library behavior and several examples. Library tests can be found in
CONTRIBUTING — the [tests](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/tree/main/tests) folder and examples tests in the
CONTRIBUTING — [examples](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/tree/main/examples) folder.
CONTRIBUTING — We like `pytest` and `pytest-xdist` because it's faster. From the root of the
CONTRIBUTING — repository, specify a *path to a subfolder or a test file* to run the test:
CONTRIBUTING — Similarly, for the `examples` directory, specify a *path to a subfolder or test file* to run the test. For example, the following command tests the text classification subfolder in the PyTorch `examples` directory:
CONTRIBUTING — In fact, this is actually how our `make test` and `make test-examples` commands are implemented (not including the `pip install`)!
CONTRIBUTING — You can also specify a smaller set of tests in order to test only the feature
CONTRIBUTING — you're working on.
CONTRIBUTING — By default, slow tests are skipped but you can set the `RUN_SLOW` environment variable to
CONTRIBUTING — `yes` to run them. This will download many gigabytes of models so make sure you
CONTRIBUTING — have enough disk space, a good internet connection or a lot of patience!
CONTRIBUTING — <Tip warning={true}>
CONTRIBUTING — Remember to specify a *path to a subfolder or a test file* to run the test. Otherwise, you'll run all the tests in the `tests` or `examples` folder, which will take a very long time!
CONTRIBUTING — Like the slow tests, there are other environment variables available which are not enabled by default during testing:
CONTRIBUTING — `RUN_CUSTOM_TOKENIZERS`: Enables tests for custom tokenizers.
CONTRIBUTING — More environment variables and additional information can be found in the [testing_utils.py](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/main/src/transformers/testing_utils.py).
CONTRIBUTING — 🤗 Transformers uses `pytest` as a test runner only. It doesn't use any
CONTRIBUTING — `pytest`-specific features in the test suite itself.
CONTRIBUTING — This means `unittest` is fully supported. Here's how to run tests with
CONTRIBUTING — `unittest`:
CONTRIBUTING — Style guide
CONTRIBUTING — For documentation strings, 🤗 Transformers follows the [Google Python Style Guide](https://google.github.io/styleguide/pyguide.html).
CONTRIBUTING — Check our [documentation writing guide](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/tree/main/docs#writing-documentation---specification)
CONTRIBUTING — for more information.
CONTRIBUTING — Develop on Windows
CONTRIBUTING — On Windows (unless you're working in [Windows Subsystem for Linux](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/) or WSL), you need to configure git to transform Windows `CRLF` line endings to Linux `LF` line endings:
CONTRIBUTING — One way to run the `make` command on Windows is with MSYS2:
CONTRIBUTING — [Download MSYS2](https://www.msys2.org/), and we assume it's installed in `C:\msys64`.
CONTRIBUTING — Open the command line `C:\msys64\msys2.exe` (it should be available from the **Start** menu).
CONTRIBUTING — Run in the shell: `pacman -Syu` and install `make` with `pacman -S make`.
CONTRIBUTING — Add `C:\msys64\usr\bin` to your PATH environment variable.
CONTRIBUTING — You can now use `make` from any terminal (PowerShell, cmd.exe, etc.)! 🎉
CONTRIBUTING — Sync a forked repository with upstream main (the Hugging Face repository)
CONTRIBUTING — When updating the main branch of a forked repository, please follow these steps to avoid pinging the upstream repository which adds reference notes to each upstream PR, and sends unnecessary notifications to the developers involved in these PRs.
CONTRIBUTING — When possible, avoid syncing with the upstream using a branch and PR on the forked repository. Instead, merge directly into the forked main.
CONTRIBUTING — If a PR is absolutely necessary, use the following steps after checking out your branch:

README — MuZero General
README — A commented and [documented](https://github.com/werner-duvaud/muzero-general/wiki/MuZero-Documentation) implementation of MuZero based on the Google DeepMind [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.08265) (Schrittwieser et al., Nov 2019) and the associated [pseudocode](https://arxiv.org/src/1911.08265v2/anc/pseudocode.py).
README — It is designed to be easily adaptable for every games or reinforcement learning environments (like [gym](https://github.com/openai/gym)). You only need to add a [game file](https://github.com/werner-duvaud/muzero-general/tree/master/games) with the hyperparameters and the game class. Please refer to the [documentation](https://github.com/werner-duvaud/muzero-general/wiki/MuZero-Documentation) and the [example](https://github.com/werner-duvaud/muzero-general/blob/master/games/cartpole.py).
README — This implementation is primarily for educational purpose.\
README — [Explanatory video of MuZero](https://youtu.be/We20YSAJZSE)
README — MuZero is a state of the art RL algorithm for board games (Chess, Go, ...) and Atari games.
README — It is the successor to [AlphaZero](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.01815) but without any knowledge of the environment underlying dynamics. MuZero learns a model of the environment and uses an internal representation that contains only the useful information for predicting the reward, value, policy and transitions. MuZero is also close to [Value prediction networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.03497). See [How it works](https://github.com/werner-duvaud/muzero-general/wiki/How-MuZero-works).
README — Features
README — [x] Residual Network and Fully connected network in [PyTorch](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch)
README — [x] Multi-Threaded/Asynchronous/[Cluster](https://docs.ray.io/en/latest/cluster-index.html) with [Ray](https://github.com/ray-project/ray)
README — [X] Multi GPU support for the training and the selfplay
README — [x] TensorBoard real-time monitoring
README — [x] Model weights automatically saved at checkpoints
README — [x] Single and two player mode
README — [x] Commented and [documented](https://github.com/werner-duvaud/muzero-general/wiki/MuZero-Documentation)
README — [x] Easily adaptable for new games
README — [x] [Examples](https://github.com/werner-duvaud/muzero-general/blob/master/games/cartpole.py) of board games, Gym and Atari games (See [list of implemented games](https://github.com/werner-duvaud/muzero-general#games-already-implemented))
README — [x] [Pretrained weights](https://github.com/werner-duvaud/muzero-general/tree/master/results) available
README — [ ] Windows support (Experimental / Workaround: Use the [notebook](https://github.com/werner-duvaud/muzero-general/blob/master/notebook.ipynb) in [Google Colab](https://colab.research.google.com))

README — Atari Breakout
README — Tests are done on Ubuntu with 16 GB RAM / Intel i7 / GTX 1050Ti Max-Q. We make sure to obtain a progression and a level which ensures that it has learned. But we do not systematically reach a human level. For certain environments, we notice a regression after a certain time. The proposed configurations are certainly not optimal and we do not focus for now on the optimization of hyperparameters. Any help is welcome.

README — :star: Explanations/Tips for Grounding DINO Inputs and Outputs
README — Grounding DINO accepts an `(image, text)` pair as inputs.
README — It outputs `900` (by default) object boxes. Each box has similarity scores across all input words. (as shown in Figures below.)
README — We defaultly choose the boxes whose highest similarities are higher than a `box_threshold`.
README — We extract the words whose similarities are higher than the `text_threshold` as predicted labels.
README — If you want to obtain objects of specific phrases, like the `dogs` in the sentence `two dogs with a stick.`, you can select the boxes with highest text similarities with `dogs` as final outputs.
README — Note that each word can be split to **more than one** tokens with different tokenlizers. The number of words in a sentence may not equal to the number of text tokens.
README — We suggest separating different category names with `.` for Grounding DINO.
