README — If you would like to specify the phrases to detect, here is a demo:
README — The token_spans specify the start and end positions of a phrases. For example, the first phrase is `[[9, 10], [11, 14]]`. `"There is a cat and a dog in the image ."[9:10] = 'a'`, `"There is a cat and a dog in the image ."[11:14] = 'cat'`. Hence it refers to the phrase `a cat` . Similarly, the `[[19, 20], [21, 24]]` refers to the phrase `a dog`.

README — :sauropod: Model: Grounding DINO
README — Includes: a text backbone, an image backbone, a feature enhancer, a language-guided query selection, and a cross-modality decoder.
README — ![arch](.asset/arch.png)
README — :hearts: Acknowledgement
README — Our model is related to [DINO](https://github.com/IDEA-Research/DINO) and [GLIP](https://github.com/microsoft/GLIP). Thanks for their great work!
README — We also thank great previous work including DETR, Deformable DETR, SMCA, Conditional DETR, Anchor DETR, Dynamic DETR, DAB-DETR, DN-DETR, etc. More related work are available at [Awesome Detection Transformer](https://github.com/IDEACVR/awesome-detection-transformer). A new toolbox [detrex](https://github.com/IDEA-Research/detrex) is available as well.
README — Thanks [Stable Diffusion](https://github.com/Stability-AI/StableDiffusion) and [GLIGEN](https://github.com/gligen/GLIGEN) for their awesome models.

CODE OF CONDUCT — contributors and maintainers pledge to make participation in our project and
CODE OF CONDUCT — our community a harassment-free experience for everyone, regardless of age, body
CODE OF CONDUCT — size, disability, ethnicity, sex characteristics, gender identity and expression,
CODE OF CONDUCT — level of experience, education, socio-economic status, nationality, personal
CODE OF CONDUCT — appearance, race, religion, or sexual identity and orientation.
CODE OF CONDUCT — Our Standards
CODE OF CONDUCT — Examples of behavior that contributes to creating a positive environment
CODE OF CONDUCT — include:
CODE OF CONDUCT — Using welcoming and inclusive language
CODE OF CONDUCT — Being respectful of differing viewpoints and experiences
CODE OF CONDUCT — Gracefully accepting constructive criticism
CODE OF CONDUCT — Focusing on what is best for the community
CODE OF CONDUCT — Showing empathy towards other community members
CODE OF CONDUCT — Examples of unacceptable behavior by participants include:
CODE OF CONDUCT — The use of sexualized language or imagery and unwelcome sexual attention or
CODE OF CONDUCT — advances
CODE OF CONDUCT — Trolling, insulting/derogatory comments, and personal or political attacks
CODE OF CONDUCT — Public or private harassment
CODE OF CONDUCT — Publishing others' private information, such as a physical or electronic
CODE OF CONDUCT — address, without explicit permission
CODE OF CONDUCT — Other conduct which could reasonably be considered inappropriate in a
CODE OF CONDUCT — professional setting
CODE OF CONDUCT — Our Responsibilities
CODE OF CONDUCT — Project maintainers are responsible for clarifying the standards of acceptable
CODE OF CONDUCT — behavior and are expected to take appropriate and fair corrective action in
CODE OF CONDUCT — response to any instances of unacceptable behavior.
CODE OF CONDUCT — Project maintainers have the right and responsibility to remove, edit, or
CODE OF CONDUCT — reject comments, commits, code, wiki edits, issues, and other contributions
CODE OF CONDUCT — that are not aligned to this Code of Conduct, or to ban temporarily or
CODE OF CONDUCT — permanently any contributor for other behaviors that they deem inappropriate,
CODE OF CONDUCT — threatening, offensive, or harmful.
CODE OF CONDUCT — This Code of Conduct applies within all project spaces, and it also applies when
CODE OF CONDUCT — an individual is representing the project or its community in public spaces.
CODE OF CONDUCT — Examples of representing a project or community include using an official
CODE OF CONDUCT — project e-mail address, posting via an official social media account, or acting
CODE OF CONDUCT — as an appointed representative at an online or offline event. Representation of
CODE OF CONDUCT — a project may be further defined and clarified by project maintainers.
CODE OF CONDUCT — This Code of Conduct also applies outside the project spaces when there is a
CODE OF CONDUCT — reasonable belief that an individual's behavior may have a negative impact on
CODE OF CONDUCT — the project or its community.
CODE OF CONDUCT — Enforcement
CODE OF CONDUCT — Instances of abusive, harassing, or otherwise unacceptable behavior may be
CODE OF CONDUCT — reported by contacting the project team at <opensource-conduct@meta.com>. All
CODE OF CONDUCT — complaints will be reviewed and investigated and will result in a response that
CODE OF CONDUCT — is deemed necessary and appropriate to the circumstances. The project team is
CODE OF CONDUCT — obligated to maintain confidentiality with regard to the reporter of an incident.
CODE OF CONDUCT — Further details of specific enforcement policies may be posted separately.
CODE OF CONDUCT — Project maintainers who do not follow or enforce the Code of Conduct in good
CODE OF CONDUCT — faith may face temporary or permanent repercussions as determined by other
CODE OF CONDUCT — members of the project's leadership.
CODE OF CONDUCT — Attribution
CODE OF CONDUCT — This Code of Conduct is adapted from the [Contributor Covenant][homepage], version 1.4,
CODE OF CONDUCT — available at https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/1/4/code-of-conduct.html
CODE OF CONDUCT — [homepage]: https://www.contributor-covenant.org
CODE OF CONDUCT — For answers to common questions about this code of conduct, see
CODE OF CONDUCT — https://www.contributor-covenant.org/faq

README — DINOv2: Learning Robust Visual Features without Supervision
README — [Meta AI Research, FAIR](https://ai.facebook.com/research/)**
README — Maxime Oquab,
README — Timothée Darcet,
README — Théo Moutakanni,
README — Huy V. Vo,
README — Marc Szafraniec,
README — Vasil Khalidov,
README — Patrick Labatut,
README — Armand Joulin,
README — Piotr Bojanowski
README — [[`Paper #1`](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.07193)] [`Paper #2`](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16588)] [[`Blog`](https://ai.facebook.com/blog/dino-v2-computer-vision-self-supervised-learning/)] [[`Demo`](https://dinov2.metademolab.com)] [[`BibTeX`](#citing-dinov2)]
README — PyTorch implementation and pretrained models for DINOv2. For details, see the papers: **[DINOv2: Learning Robust Visual Features without Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.07193)** and **[Vision Transformers Need Registers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16588)**.
README — DINOv2 models produce high-performance visual features that can be directly employed with classifiers as simple as linear layers on a variety of computer vision tasks; these visual features are robust and perform well across domains without any requirement for fine-tuning. The models were pretrained on a dataset of 142 M images without using any labels or annotations.
README — https://github.com/facebookresearch/dinov2/assets/60359573/f168823e-7922-415a-b429-578badf5c356

README — Installation
README — The training and evaluation code requires PyTorch 2.0 and [xFormers](https://github.com/facebookresearch/xformers) 0.0.18 as well as a number of other 3rd party packages. Note that the code has only been tested with the specified versions and also expects a Linux environment. To setup all the required dependencies for training and evaluation, please follow the instructions below:
README — [conda](https://docs.conda.io/projects/conda/en/latest/user-guide/getting-started.html)* **(Recommended)** - Clone the repository and then create and activate a `dinov2` conda environment using the provided environment definition:
README — [pip](https://pip.pypa.io/en/stable/getting-started/)* - Clone the repository and then use the provided `requirements.txt` to install the dependencies:
README — For dense tasks (depth estimation and semantic segmentation), there are additional dependencies (specific versions of `mmcv` and `mmsegmentation`) which are captured in the `extras` dependency specifications:
README — [conda](https://docs.conda.io/projects/conda/en/latest/user-guide/getting-started.html)* **(Recommended)**:
README — [pip](https://pip.pypa.io/en/stable/getting-started/)*:
README — Data preparation
README — ImageNet-1k
README — The root directory of the dataset should hold the following contents:
README — `<ROOT>/test/ILSVRC2012_test_00000001.JPEG`
README — `<ROOT>/test/[..]`
README — `<ROOT>/test/ILSVRC2012_test_00100000.JPEG`
README — `<ROOT>/train/n01440764/n01440764_10026.JPEG`
README — `<ROOT>/train/[...]`
README — `<ROOT>/train/n15075141/n15075141_9993.JPEG`

README — Training
README — Fast setup: training DINOv2 ViT-L/16 on ImageNet-1k
README — Run DINOv2 training on 4 A100-80GB nodes (32 GPUs) in a SLURM cluster environment with submitit:
README — Training time is approximately 1 day and the resulting checkpoint should reach 81.6% on k-NN eval and 82.9% on linear eval.
README — The training code saves the weights of the teacher in the `eval` folder every 12500 iterations for evaluation.
README — Long setup: training DINOv2 ViT-L/14 on ImageNet-22k
README — Run DINOv2 training on 12 A100-80GB nodes (96 GPUs) in a SLURM cluster environment with submitit:
README — Training time is approximately 3.3 days and the resulting checkpoint should reach 82.0% on k-NN eval and 84.5% on linear eval.
README — The training code saves the weights of the teacher in the `eval` folder every 12500 iterations for evaluation.

MODEL CARD — Model Card for DINOv2-S/B/L/g
MODEL CARD — These are Vision Transformer models trained following the method described in the papers:
MODEL CARD — "DINOv2: Learning Robust Visual Features without Supervision"
MODEL CARD — "Vision Transformers Need Registers".
MODEL CARD — We provide 8 models:
MODEL CARD — ViT-g trained from scratch with 3 ViT-S/B/L models distilled from the ViT-g, without registers.
MODEL CARD — ViT-g trained from scratch with 3 ViT-S/B/L models distilled from the ViT-g, with registers.
MODEL CARD — Model Details
MODEL CARD — The model takes an image as input and returns a class token and patch tokens, and optionally 4 register tokens.
MODEL CARD — The embedding dimension is:
MODEL CARD — for ViT-S.
MODEL CARD — for ViT-B.
MODEL CARD — for ViT-L.
MODEL CARD — for ViT-g.
MODEL CARD — The models follow a Transformer architecture, with a patch size of 14. In the case of registers, we add 4 register tokens, learned during training, to the input sequence after the patch embedding.
MODEL CARD — For a 224x224 image, this results in 1 class token + 256 patch tokens, and optionally 4 register tokens.
MODEL CARD — The models can accept larger images provided the image shapes are multiples of the patch size (14).
MODEL CARD — If this condition is not verified, the model will crop to the closest smaller multiple of the patch size.
MODEL CARD — Model Description
MODEL CARD — Developed by:** Meta AI
MODEL CARD — Model type:** Vision Transformer
MODEL CARD — License:** Apache License 2.0
MODEL CARD — Repository:** https://github.com/facebookresearch/dinov2
MODEL CARD — Paper:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.07193
MODEL CARD — Demo:** https://dinov2.metademolab.com/
MODEL CARD — The models are vision backbones providing multi-purpose features for downstream tasks.
MODEL CARD — Direct Use
MODEL CARD — The models can be used without fine-tuning, with downstream classifiers as simple as linear layers, to obtain competitive results:
MODEL CARD — on depth estimation, semantic segmentation, using linear layers.
MODEL CARD — on image classification, using k-NN classifiers on the class token.
MODEL CARD — on image classification, with logistic regression classifiers applied on the class token.
MODEL CARD — on image classification, with a linear layer applied on the class token and the average of the patch tokens.
MODEL CARD — on image retrieval using nearest neighbors.
MODEL CARD — Downstream Use
MODEL CARD — It is technically possible to perform fine-tuning on the models, for small gains (we measured +2% on ImageNet-1k classification).
MODEL CARD — We recommend keeping this as a very last step and only when necessary, as the features already provide good performance out-of-the-box.
MODEL CARD — Bias, Risks, and Limitations
MODEL CARD — Despite improvements thanks to the training method not using annotations, we still observe significant biases in our models toward rich households from Western countries.
MODEL CARD — Recommendations
MODEL CARD — We expect fine-tuning will increase the biases in the features produced by the model as they will be tuned to the fine-tuning labels.
MODEL CARD — How to Get Started with the Model
MODEL CARD — Use the code below to get started with the model.
MODEL CARD — Training Details
MODEL CARD — Training Data
MODEL CARD — Training data:** LVD-142M (see paper)
MODEL CARD — Training regime:** fp16 using PyTorch-FSDP mixed-precision.
MODEL CARD — Training Procedure
MODEL CARD — Training objective:**
MODEL CARD — DINO self-distillation loss with multi-crop
MODEL CARD — iBOT masked-image modeling loss
MODEL CARD — KoLeo regularization on [CLS] tokens
MODEL CARD — Architectures:**
MODEL CARD — ViT-S (21M params): Patch size 14, embedding dimension 384, 6 heads, MLP FFN
MODEL CARD — ViT-B (86M params): Patch size 14, embedding dimension 768, 12 heads, MLP FFN
MODEL CARD — ViT-L (0.3B params): Patch size 14, embedding dimension 1024, 16 heads, MLP FFN
MODEL CARD — ViT-g (1.1B params): Patch size 14, embedding dimension 1536, 24 heads, SwiGLU FFN
MODEL CARD — Distillation:**
MODEL CARD — Distillation follows the standard DINOv2 pretraining procedure, except the teacher is a pretrained ViT-g, frozen.
MODEL CARD — Evaluation
MODEL CARD — We refer users to the associated papers for the evaluation protocols.

TESTING RECALL — Testing recall
TESTING RECALL — Selecting HNSW parameters for a specific use case highly impacts the search quality. One way to test the quality of the constructed index is to compare the HNSW search results to the actual results (i.e., the actual `k` nearest neighbors).
TESTING RECALL — For that cause, the API enables creating a simple "brute-force" index in which vectors are stored as is, and searching for the `k` nearest neighbors to a query vector requires going over the entire index.
TESTING RECALL — Comparing between HNSW and brute-force results may help with finding the desired HNSW parameters for achieving a satisfying recall, based on the index size and data dimension.
TESTING RECALL — Brute force index API
TESTING RECALL — `hnswlib.BFIndex(space, dim)` creates a non-initialized index in space `space` with integer dimension `dim`.
TESTING RECALL — `hnswlib.BFIndex` methods:
TESTING RECALL — `init_index(max_elements)` initializes the index with no elements.
TESTING RECALL — max_elements defines the maximum number of elements that can be stored in the structure.
TESTING RECALL — `add_items(data, ids)` inserts the data (numpy array of vectors, shape:`N*dim`) into the structure.
TESTING RECALL — `ids` are optional N-size numpy array of integer labels for all elements in data.
TESTING RECALL — `delete_vector(label)` delete the element associated with the given `label` so it will be omitted from search results.
TESTING RECALL — `knn_query(data, k = 1)` make a batch query for `k `closest elements for each element of the
TESTING RECALL — `data` (shape:`N*dim`). Returns a numpy array of (shape:`N*k`).
TESTING RECALL — `load_index(path_to_index, max_elements = 0)` loads the index from persistence to the uninitialized index.
TESTING RECALL — `save_index(path_to_index)` saves the index from persistence.
TESTING RECALL — measuring recall example
README — Hnswlib - fast approximate nearest neighbor search
README — Header-only C++ HNSW implementation with python bindings, insertions and updates.
README — version 0.8.0**
README — Multi-vector document search and epsilon search (for now, only in C++)
README — By default, there is no statistic aggregation, which speeds up the multi-threaded search (it does not seem like people are using it anyway: [Issue #495](https://github.com/nmslib/hnswlib/issues/495)).
README — Various bugfixes and improvements
README — `get_items` now have `return_type` parameter, which can be either 'numpy' or 'list'
README — Full list of changes: https://github.com/nmslib/hnswlib/pull/523

README — Highlights:
README — Lightweight, header-only, no dependencies other than C++ 11
README — Interfaces for C++, Python, external support for Java and R (https://github.com/jlmelville/rcpphnsw).
README — Has full support for incremental index construction and updating the elements (thanks to the contribution by Apoorv Sharma). Has support for element deletions
README — (by marking them in index, later can be replaced with other elements). Python index is picklable.
README — Can work with custom user defined distances (C++).
README — Significantly less memory footprint and faster build time compared to current nmslib's implementation.
README — Description of the algorithm parameters can be found in [ALGO_PARAMS.md](ALGO_PARAMS.md).
README — Python bindings
README — Supported distances:
README — | Distance | parameter | Equation |
README — | ------------- |:---------------:| -----------------------:|
README — |Squared L2 |'l2' | d = sum((Ai-Bi)^2) |
README — |Inner product |'ip' | d = 1.0 - sum(Ai\*Bi) |
README — |Cosine similarity |'cosine' | d = 1.0 - sum(Ai\*Bi) / sqrt(sum(Ai\*Ai) * sum(Bi\*Bi))|
README — Note that inner product is not an actual metric. An element can be closer to some other element than to itself. That allows some speedup if you remove all elements that are not the closest to themselves from the index.
README — For other spaces use the nmslib library https://github.com/nmslib/nmslib.
README — API description
README — `hnswlib.Index(space, dim)` creates a non-initialized index an HNSW in space `space` with integer dimension `dim`.
README — `hnswlib.Index` methods:
README — `init_index(max_elements, M = 16, ef_construction = 200, random_seed = 100, allow_replace_deleted = False)` initializes the index from with no elements.
README — `max_elements` defines the maximum number of elements that can be stored in the structure(can be increased/shrunk).
README — `ef_construction` defines a construction time/accuracy trade-off (see [ALGO_PARAMS.md](ALGO_PARAMS.md)).
README — `M` defines tha maximum number of outgoing connections in the graph ([ALGO_PARAMS.md](ALGO_PARAMS.md)).
README — `allow_replace_deleted` enables replacing of deleted elements with new added ones.
README — `add_items(data, ids, num_threads = -1, replace_deleted = False)` - inserts the `data`(numpy array of vectors, shape:`N*dim`) into the structure.
README — `num_threads` sets the number of cpu threads to use (-1 means use default).
README — `ids` are optional N-size numpy array of integer labels for all elements in `data`.
README — If index already has the elements with the same labels, their features will be updated. Note that update procedure is slower than insertion of a new element, but more memory- and query-efficient.
README — `replace_deleted` replaces deleted elements. Note it allows to save memory.
README — to use it `init_index` should be called with `allow_replace_deleted=True`
README — Thread-safe with other `add_items` calls, but not with `knn_query`.
README — `mark_deleted(label)` - marks the element as deleted, so it will be omitted from search results. Throws an exception if it is already deleted.
README — `unmark_deleted(label)` - unmarks the element as deleted, so it will be not be omitted from search results.
README — `resize_index(new_size)` - changes the maximum capacity of the index. Not thread safe with `add_items` and `knn_query`.
README — `set_ef(ef)` - sets the query time accuracy/speed trade-off, defined by the `ef` parameter (
README — [ALGO_PARAMS.md](ALGO_PARAMS.md)). Note that the parameter is currently not saved along with the index, so you need to set it manually after loading.
README — `knn_query(data, k = 1, num_threads = -1, filter = None)` make a batch query for `k` closest elements for each element of the
README — `data` (shape:`N*dim`). Returns a numpy array of (shape:`N*k`).
README — `num_threads` sets the number of cpu threads to use (-1 means use default).
README — `filter` filters elements by its labels, returns elements with allowed ids. Note that search with a filter works slow in python in multithreaded mode. It is recommended to set `num_threads=1`
README — Thread-safe with other `knn_query` calls, but not with `add_items`.
README — `load_index(path_to_index, max_elements = 0, allow_replace_deleted = False)` loads the index from persistence to the uninitialized index.
README — `max_elements`(optional) resets the maximum number of elements in the structure.
README — `allow_replace_deleted` specifies whether the index being loaded has enabled replacing of deleted elements.
README — `save_index(path_to_index)` saves the index from persistence.
README — `set_num_threads(num_threads)` set the default number of cpu threads used during data insertion/querying.
README — `get_items(ids, return_type = 'numpy')` - returns a numpy array (shape:`N*dim`) of vectors that have integer identifiers specified in `ids` numpy vector (shape:`N`) if `return_type` is `list` return list of lists. Note that for cosine similarity it currently returns **normalized** vectors.
README — `get_ids_list()` - returns a list of all elements' ids.
README — `get_max_elements()` - returns the current capacity of the index
README — `get_current_count()` - returns the current number of element stored in the index
README — Read-only properties of `hnswlib.Index` class:
README — `space` - name of the space (can be one of "l2", "ip", or "cosine").
README — `dim` - dimensionality of the space.
README — `M` - parameter that defines the maximum number of outgoing connections in the graph.
README — `ef_construction` - parameter that controls speed/accuracy trade-off during the index construction.
README — `max_elements` - current capacity of the index. Equivalent to `p.get_max_elements()`.
README — `element_count` - number of items in the index. Equivalent to `p.get_current_count()`.
README — Properties of `hnswlib.Index` that support reading and writing:
README — `ef` - parameter controlling query time/accuracy trade-off.
README — `num_threads` - default number of threads to use in `add_items` or `knn_query`. Note that calling `p.set_num_threads(3)` is equivalent to `p.num_threads=3`.

ALGO PARAMS — HNSW algorithm parameters
ALGO PARAMS — Search parameters:
ALGO PARAMS — ```ef``` - the size of the dynamic list for the nearest neighbors (used during the search). Higher ```ef```
ALGO PARAMS — leads to more accurate but slower search. ```ef``` cannot be set lower than the number of queried nearest neighbors

README — [[Blog]](https://openai.com/blog/clip/) [[Paper]](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020) [[Model Card]](model-card.md) [[Colab]](https://colab.research.google.com/github/openai/clip/blob/master/notebooks/Interacting_with_CLIP.ipynb)
README — CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pre-Training) is a neural network trained on a variety of (image, text) pairs. It can be instructed in natural language to predict the most relevant text snippet, given an image, without directly optimizing for the task, similarly to the zero-shot capabilities of GPT-2 and 3. We found CLIP matches the performance of the original ResNet50 on ImageNet “zero-shot” without using any of the original 1.28M labeled examples, overcoming several major challenges in computer vision.
README — Approach
README — ![CLIP](CLIP.png)
README — First, [install PyTorch 1.7.1](https://pytorch.org/get-started/locally/) (or later) and torchvision, as well as small additional dependencies, and then install this repo as a Python package. On a CUDA GPU machine, the following will do the trick:
README — Replace `cudatoolkit=11.0` above with the appropriate CUDA version on your machine or `cpuonly` when installing on a machine without a GPU.
README — The CLIP module `clip` provides the following methods:
README — `clip.available_models()`
README — Returns the names of the available CLIP models.
README — `clip.load(name, device=..., jit=False)`
README — Returns the model and the TorchVision transform needed by the model, specified by the model name returned by `clip.available_models()`. It will download the model as necessary. The `name` argument can also be a path to a local checkpoint.
README — The device to run the model can be optionally specified, and the default is to use the first CUDA device if there is any, otherwise the CPU. When `jit` is `False`, a non-JIT version of the model will be loaded.
README — `clip.tokenize(text: Union[str, List[str]], context_length=77)`
README — Returns a LongTensor containing tokenized sequences of given text input(s). This can be used as the input to the model
README — The model returned by `clip.load()` supports the following methods:
README — `model.encode_image(image: Tensor)`
README — Given a batch of images, returns the image features encoded by the vision portion of the CLIP model.
README — `model.encode_text(text: Tensor)`
README — Given a batch of text tokens, returns the text features encoded by the language portion of the CLIP model.
README — `model(image: Tensor, text: Tensor)`
README — Given a batch of images and a batch of text tokens, returns two Tensors, containing the logit scores corresponding to each image and text input. The values are cosine similarities between the corresponding image and text features, times 100.

model-card — Model Card: CLIP
model-card — Inspired by [Model Cards for Model Reporting (Mitchell et al.)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.03993) and [Lessons from Archives (Jo & Gebru)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1912.10389.pdf), we’re providing some accompanying information about the multimodal model.
model-card — Model Details
model-card — The CLIP model was developed by researchers at OpenAI to learn about what contributes to robustness in computer vision tasks. The model was also developed to test the ability of models to generalize to arbitrary image classification tasks in a zero-shot manner. It was not developed for general model deployment - to deploy models like CLIP, researchers will first need to carefully study their capabilities in relation to the specific context they’re being deployed within.
model-card — Model Date
model-card — January 2021
model-card — Model Type
model-card — The base model uses a ResNet50 with several modifications as an image encoder and uses a masked self-attention Transformer as a text encoder. These encoders are trained to maximize the similarity of (image, text) pairs via a contrastive loss. There is also a variant of the model where the ResNet image encoder is replaced with a Vision Transformer.
model-card — Model Versions
model-card — Initially, we’ve released one CLIP model based on the Vision Transformer architecture equivalent to ViT-B/32, along with the RN50 model, using the architecture equivalent to ResNet-50.
model-card — As part of the staged release process, we have also released the RN101 model, as well as RN50x4, a RN50 scaled up 4x according to the [EfficientNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.11946) scaling rule. In July 2021, we additionally released the RN50x16 and ViT-B/16 models, and in January 2022, the RN50x64 and ViT-L/14 models were released. Lastly, the ViT-L/14@336px model was released in April 2022.
model-card — Please see the paper linked below for further details about their specification.
model-card — Documents
model-card — [Blog Post](https://openai.com/blog/clip/)
model-card — [CLIP Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020)
model-card — Model Use
model-card — Intended Use
model-card — The model is intended as a research output for research communities. We hope that this model will enable researchers to better understand and explore zero-shot, arbitrary image classification. We also hope it can be used for interdisciplinary studies of the potential impact of such models - the CLIP paper includes a discussion of potential downstream impacts to provide an example for this sort of analysis.
model-card — Primary intended uses
model-card — The primary intended users of these models are AI researchers.
model-card — We primarily imagine the model will be used by researchers to better understand robustness, generalization, and other capabilities, biases, and constraints of computer vision models.
model-card — Out-of-Scope Use Cases
model-card — Any** deployed use case of the model - whether commercial or not - is currently out of scope. Non-deployed use cases such as image search in a constrained environment, are also not recommended unless there is thorough in-domain testing of the model with a specific, fixed class taxonomy. This is because our safety assessment demonstrated a high need for task specific testing especially given the variability of CLIP’s performance with different class taxonomies. This makes untested and unconstrained deployment of the model in any use case currently potentially harmful.
model-card — Certain use cases which would fall under the domain of surveillance and facial recognition are always out-of-scope regardless of performance of the model. This is because the use of artificial intelligence for tasks such as these can be premature currently given the lack of testing norms and checks to ensure its fair use.
model-card — Since the model has not been purposefully trained in or evaluated on any languages other than English, its use should be limited to English language use cases.
model-card — The model was trained on publicly available image-caption data. This was done through a combination of crawling a handful of websites and using commonly-used pre-existing image datasets such as [YFCC100M](http://projects.dfki.uni-kl.de/yfcc100m/). A large portion of the data comes from our crawling of the internet. This means that the data is more representative of people and societies most connected to the internet which tend to skew towards more developed nations, and younger, male users.
model-card — Data Mission Statement
model-card — Our goal with building this dataset was to test out robustness and generalizability in computer vision tasks. As a result, the focus was on gathering large quantities of data from different publicly-available internet data sources. The data was gathered in a mostly non-interventionist manner. However, we only crawled websites that had policies against excessively violent and adult images and allowed us to filter out such content. We do not intend for this dataset to be used as the basis for any commercial or deployed model and will not be releasing the dataset.
model-card — Performance and Limitations
model-card — Performance
model-card — We have evaluated the performance of CLIP on a wide range of benchmarks across a variety of computer vision datasets such as OCR to texture recognition to fine-grained classification. The paper describes model performance on the following datasets:
model-card — CIFAR100
model-card — Birdsnap
model-card — Stanford Cars
model-card — FGVC Aircraft
model-card — Oxford-IIIT Pet dataset
model-card — Caltech101
model-card — Flowers102
model-card — Hateful Memes
model-card — Kinetics700
model-card — Country211
model-card — CLEVR Counting
model-card — KITTI Distance
model-card — Flickr30
model-card — ImageNet
model-card — ImageNet-A
model-card — ImageNet-R
model-card — ImageNet Sketch
model-card — ObjectNet (ImageNet Overlap)
model-card — Youtube-BB
model-card — ImageNet-Vid
model-card — Limitations
model-card — CLIP and our analysis of it have a number of limitations. CLIP currently struggles with respect to certain tasks such as fine grained classification and counting objects. CLIP also poses issues with regards to fairness and bias which we discuss in the paper and briefly in the next section. Additionally, our approach to testing CLIP also has an important limitation- in many cases we have used linear probes to evaluate the performance of CLIP and there is evidence suggesting that linear probes can underestimate model performance.
model-card — Bias and Fairness
model-card — We find that the performance of CLIP - and the specific biases it exhibits - can depend significantly on class design and the choices one makes for categories to include and exclude. We tested the risk of certain kinds of denigration with CLIP by classifying images of people from [Fairface](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.04913) into crime-related and non-human animal categories. We found significant disparities with respect to race and gender. Additionally, we found that these disparities could shift based on how the classes were constructed. (Details captured in the Broader Impacts Section in the paper).
model-card — We also tested the performance of CLIP on gender, race and age classification using the Fairface dataset (We default to using race categories as they are constructed in the Fairface dataset.) in order to assess quality of performance across different demographics. We found accuracy >96% across all races for gender classification with ‘Middle Eastern’ having the highest accuracy (98.4%) and ‘White’ having the lowest (96.5%). Additionally, CLIP averaged ~93% for racial classification and ~63% for age classification. Our use of evaluations to test for gender, race and age classification as well as denigration harms is simply to evaluate performance of the model across people and surface potential risks and not to demonstrate an endorsement/enthusiasm for such tasks.

UPDATE MILVUS API — Update Milvus API Version
UPDATE MILVUS API — This document explains how to use the `update-milvus-api` command to update the milvus-proto version across all go.mod files in the project.
UPDATE MILVUS API — Overview
UPDATE MILVUS API — The `update-milvus-api` command has been enhanced to update the milvus-proto version in all 4 go.mod files:
UPDATE MILVUS API — `go.mod` (main module)
UPDATE MILVUS API — `client/go.mod` (client module)
UPDATE MILVUS API — `pkg/go.mod` (pkg module)
UPDATE MILVUS API — `tests/go_client/go.mod` (test client module)
UPDATE MILVUS API — Update to a specific tagged version
UPDATE MILVUS API — Update to a specific commit ID
UPDATE MILVUS API — What the command does
UPDATE MILVUS API — Validates the version**: Checks if the provided version is a valid git tag or treats it as a commit ID
UPDATE MILVUS API — Updates all go.mod files**: Updates the milvus-proto dependency in all 4 go.mod files
UPDATE MILVUS API — Runs go mod tidy**: Ensures all dependencies are properly resolved
UPDATE MILVUS API — Updates the local milvus-proto repo**: Updates the third-party milvus-proto repository if it exists
UPDATE MILVUS API — Provides feedback**: Shows which files were updated
UPDATE MILVUS API — Example output
UPDATE MILVUS API — Error handling
UPDATE MILVUS API — If no version is provided, the command will show usage examples
UPDATE MILVUS API — If the milvus-proto third-party directory doesn't exist, a warning will be displayed but the go.mod updates will still proceed
UPDATE MILVUS API — If a git branch with the same name already exists, the command will checkout the commit directly
UPDATE MILVUS API — Prerequisites
UPDATE MILVUS API — Go must be installed and available in PATH
UPDATE MILVUS API — Git must be installed and available in PATH
UPDATE MILVUS API — Internet connection to fetch the milvus-proto repository
UPDATE MILVUS API — The command will automatically determine if the provided version is a git tag or commit ID
UPDATE MILVUS API — All go.mod files will be updated to the same version
UPDATE MILVUS API — The command includes proper error handling and user feedback

README CN — 欢迎来到 Milvus
README CN — Milvus 是什么
README CN — Milvus 是一款全球领先的开源向量数据库，赋能 AI 应用和向量相似度搜索，加速非结构化数据检索。用户在任何部署环境中均可获得始终如一的用户体验。
README CN — Milvus 2.0 是一款云原生向量数据库，采用存储与计算分离的架构设计。该重构版本的所有组件均为无状态组件，极大地增强了系统弹性和灵活性。更多系统架构细节，参考 [Milvus 系统架构](https://milvus.io/cn/docs/architecture_overview.md)。
README CN — Milvus 基于 [Apache 2.0 License](https://github.com/milvus-io/milvus/blob/master/LICENSE) 协议发布，于 2019 年 10 月正式开源，是 [LF AI & Data 基金会](https://lfaidata.foundation/) 的毕业项目。
README CN — <details>
README CN — <summary><b>针对万亿级向量的毫秒级搜索</b></summary>
README CN — 完成万亿条向量数据搜索的平均延迟以毫秒计。
README CN — </details>
README CN — <details>
README CN — <summary><b>简化的非结构化数据管理</b></summary>
README CN — <li>一整套专为数据科学工作流设计的 API。</li><li>无论是笔记本、本地集群还是云服务器，始终如一的跨平台用户体验。</li><li>可以在任何场景下实现实时搜索与分析。</li>
README CN — </details>
README CN — <details>
README CN — <summary><b>稳定可靠的用户体验</b></summary>
README CN — Milvus 具有故障转移和故障恢复的机制，即使服务中断，也能确保数据和应用的业务连续性。
README CN — </details>
README CN — <details>
README CN — <summary><b>高度可扩展，弹性伸缩</b></summary>
README CN — 组件级别的高扩展性，支持精准扩展。
README CN — </details>
README CN — <details>
README CN — <summary><b>混合查询</b></summary>
README CN — Milvus 2.4 引入了多向量支持和混合查询框架，用户可以将多个向量字段（最多 10 个）导入到单个 Collection 中。这些来自不同的嵌入模型或经过不同的处理方法处理的向量分别代表了不同的数据特征。混合搜索的结果使用 reranking 策略对各向量列的结果进行融合，如 Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) 和 Weighted Scoring。
README CN — 该特性尤其适用于综合搜索场景，如基于多种属性（如照片、声音、指纹等）识别向量库中最相似的人。有关更多信息，请参阅 [混合搜索](https://milvus.io/cn/docs/multi-vector-search.md)。
README CN — </details>
README CN — <details>
README CN — <summary><b>基于 Lambda 架构的流批一体式数据存储</b></summary>
README CN — Milvus 在存储数据时支持流处理和批处理两种方式，兼顾了流处理的时效性和批处理的效率。统一的对外接口使得向量相似度查询更为便捷。
README CN — </details>
README CN — <details>
README CN — <summary><b>广受社区支持和业界认可</b></summary>
README CN — Milvus 项目在 GitHub 上获星超 8000，拥有逾 1000 家企业用户，还有活跃的开源社区。Milvus 由 <a href="https://lfaidata.foundation/">LF AI & Data 基金会</a> 背书，是该基金会的毕业项目。
README CN — </details>

README CN — 注意** 主分支用于 Milvus v2.0 代码开发。Milvus v1.0 于 2021 年 3 月 9 日发布，是 Milvus 的首个长期支持（LTS）版本。如需使用 Milvus 1.0，请切换至 [1.0 分支](https://github.com/milvus-io/milvus/tree/1.0)。

README CN — 详见 [Milvus 2.0 vs. 1.x](https://github.com/milvus-io/milvus/blob/master/milvus20vs1x.md) 。

DEVELOPMENT — Building Milvus with Docker
DEVELOPMENT — Our official Milvus versions are releases as Docker images. To build Milvus Docker on your own, please follow [these instructions](https://github.com/milvus-io/milvus/blob/master/build/README.md).
DEVELOPMENT — Building Milvus on a local OS/shell environment
DEVELOPMENT — The details below outline the hardware and software requirements for building on Linux and MacOS.

DEVELOPMENT — The following specification (either physical or virtual machine resources) is recommended for Milvus to build and run from source code.
DEVELOPMENT — Software Requirements
DEVELOPMENT — All Linux distributions are available for Milvus development. However a majority of our contributor worked with Ubuntu or CentOS systems, with a small portion of Mac (both x86_64 and Apple Silicon) contributors. If you would like Milvus to build and run on other distributions, you are more than welcome to file an issue and contribute!
DEVELOPMENT — Here's a list of verified OS types where Milvus can successfully build and run:
DEVELOPMENT — Debian/Ubuntu
DEVELOPMENT — Amazon Linux
DEVELOPMENT — MacOS (x86_64)
DEVELOPMENT — MacOS (Apple Silicon)

DEVELOPMENT — CMake & Conan

DEVELOPMENT — Confirm that your `GOPATH` and `GOBIN` environment variables are correctly set as detailed in [How to Write Go Code](https://golang.org/doc/code.html) before proceeding.
DEVELOPMENT — Note: go >= 1.22 is required to build Milvus.

DEVELOPMENT — E2E Tests
DEVELOPMENT — Milvus uses Python SDK to write test cases to verify the correctness of Milvus functions. Before running E2E tests, you need a running Milvus. There are two modes of operation to build Milvus — Milvus Standalone and Milvus Cluster. Milvus Standalone operates independently as a single instance. Milvus Cluster operates across multiple nodes. All milvus instances are clustered together to form a unified system to support larger volumes of data and higher traffic loads.
DEVELOPMENT — Both include three components:
DEVELOPMENT — Milvus: The core functional component.
DEVELOPMENT — Etcd: The metadata engine. Access and store metadata of Milvus’ internal components.
DEVELOPMENT — MinIO: The storage engine. Responsible for data persistence for Milvus.
DEVELOPMENT — Milvus Cluster includes further component — Pulsar, to be distributed through Pub/Sub mechanism.
DEVELOPMENT — To run E2E tests, use these commands:
DEVELOPMENT — Test on local branch
DEVELOPMENT — With Linux and MacOS
DEVELOPMENT — After preparing deployment environment, we can start the cluster on your host machine
DEVELOPMENT — With docker
DEVELOPMENT — start the cluster on your host machine

DEVELOPMENT — Q: The go building phase fails on Apple Silicon (Mac M1) machines.

DEVELOPMENT — Q: The binary fails to open on my OS with the error "Unsupported system page size"?
DEVELOPMENT — A: This occurs when your OS uses a large memory page size, which must be explicitly declared during compilation. Follow these steps to resolve it:
DEVELOPMENT — First, check your OS page size by running the following command:
DEVELOPMENT — If the output is 65536, your system uses 64KB pages.
DEVELOPMENT — The `MILVUS_JEMALLOC_LG_PAGE` variable's primary function is to specify the size of large pages during the compilation of jemalloc. Jemalloc is a memory allocator designed to enhance the performance and efficiency of applications in a multi-threaded environment. By specifying the size of large pages, memory management and access can be optimized, thereby improving performance.
DEVELOPMENT — Large page support allows the operating system to manage and allocate memory in larger blocks, reducing the number of page table entries, thereby decreasing the time for page table lookups and improving the efficiency of memory access. This is particularly important when processing large amounts of data, as it can significantly reduce page faults and Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) misses, enhancing application performance.
DEVELOPMENT — On ARM64 architectures, different systems may support different page sizes, such as 4KB and 64KB. The `MILVUS_JEMALLOC_LG_PAGE` setting allows developers to customize the compilation of jemalloc for the target platform, ensuring it can efficiently operate on systems with varying page sizes. By specifying the `--with-lg-page` configuration option, jemalloc can utilize the optimal page size supported by the system when managing memory.
DEVELOPMENT — For example, if a system supports a 64KB page size, by setting `MILVUS_JEMALLOC_LG_PAGE` to the corresponding value (the power of 2, 64KB is 2 to the 16th power, so the value is 16), jemalloc can allocate and manage memory in 64KB units, which can improve the performance of applications running on that system.
DEVELOPMENT — Modify the make configuration file, located at: `./milvus/scripts/core_build.sh`, with the following changes:
DEVELOPMENT — Using `-DMILVUS_JEMALLOC_LG_PAGE=16` as a compilation option for jemalloc is because it specifies the size of "large pages" as 2 to the 16th power bytes, which equals 65536 bytes or 64KB. This value is set to optimize memory management and improve performance, especially on systems that support or prefer using large pages to reduce the overhead of page table management.
DEVELOPMENT — Specifying `-DMILVUS_JEMALLOC_LG_PAGE=16` during the compilation of jemalloc informs jemalloc to assume the system's large page size is 64KB. This allows jemalloc to work more efficiently with the operating system's memory manager, using large pages to optimize performance. This is crucial for ensuring optimal performance on systems with different default page sizes, particularly in environments that might have different memory management needs due to varying hardware or system configurations.

README — What is Milvus?
README — 🐦 [Milvus](https://milvus.io/) is a high-performance vector database built for scale. It powers AI applications by efficiently organizing and searching vast amounts of unstructured data, such as text, images, and multi-modal information.
README — 🧑‍💻 Written in Go and C++, Milvus implements hardware accelaration for CPU/GPU to achieve best-in-class vector search performance. Thanks to its [fully-distributed and K8s-native architecture](https://milvus.io/docs/overview.md#What-Makes-Milvus-so-Scalable), Milvus can scale horizontally, handle tens of thousands of search queries on billions of vectors, and keep data fresh with real-time streaming updates. Milvus also supports [Standalone mode](https://milvus.io/docs/install_standalone-docker.md) for single machine deployment. [Milvus Lite](https://milvus.io/docs/milvus_lite.md) is a lightweight version good for quickstart in python with `pip install`.
README — Want to use Milvus with zero setup? Try out [Zilliz Cloud ☁️](https://cloud.zilliz.com/signup?utm_source=partner&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=2024-11-04_web_github-readme_global) for free. Milvus is available as a fully managed service on Zilliz Cloud, with [Serverless](https://zilliz.com/serverless?utm_source=partner&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=2024-11-04_web_github-readme_global), [Dedicated](https://zilliz.com/cloud?utm_source=partner&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=2024-11-04_web_github-readme_global) and [BYOC](https://zilliz.com/bring-your-own-cloud?utm_source=partner&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=2024-11-04_web_github-readme_global) options available.
README — For questions about how to use Milvus, join the community on [Discord](https://discord.gg/33mfvwep3J) to get help. For reporting problems, file bugs and feature requests in GitHub [Issues](https://github.com/milvus-io/milvus/issues) or ask in [Discussions](https://github.com/milvus-io/milvus/discussions).

README — Why Milvus
README — Milvus is designed to handle vector search at scale. It stores vectors, which are learned representations of unstructured data, together with other scalar data types such as integers, strings, and JSON objects. Users can conduct efficient vector search with metadata filtering or hybrid search. Here are why developers choose Milvus as the vector database for AI applications:
README — High Performance at Scale and High Availability**
README — Milvus features a [distributed architecture](https://milvus.io/docs/architecture_overview.md ) that separates [compute](https://milvus.io/docs/data_processing.md#Data-query) and [storage](https://milvus.io/docs/data_processing.md#Data-insertion). Milvus can horizontally scale and adapt to diverse traffic patterns, achieving optimal performance by independently increasing query nodes for read-heavy workload and data node for write-heavy workload. The stateless microservices on K8s allow [quick recovery](https://milvus.io/docs/coordinator_ha.md#Coordinator-HA) from failure, ensuring high availability. The support for [replicas](https://milvus.io/docs/replica.md) further enhances fault tolerance and throughput by loading data segments on multiple query nodes. See [benchmark](https://zilliz.com/vector-database-benchmark-tool) for performance comparison.
README — Support for Various Vector Index Types and Hardware Acceleration**
README — Milvus separates the system and core vector search engine, allowing it to support all major vector index types that are optimized for different scenarios, including HNSW, IVF, FLAT (brute-force), SCANN, and DiskANN, with [quantization-based](https://milvus.io/docs/index.md?tab=floating#IVFPQ) variations and [mmap](https://milvus.io/docs/mmap.md). Milvus optimizes vector search for advanced features such as [metadata filtering](https://milvus.io/docs/scalar_index.md#Scalar-Index) and [range search](https://milvus.io/docs/single-vector-search.md#Range-search). Additionally, Milvus implements hardware acceleration to enhance vector search performance and supports GPU indexing, such as NVIDIA's [CAGRA](https://github.com/rapidsai/cuvs).
README — Flexible Multi-tenancy and Hot/Cold Storage**
README — Milvus supports [multi-tenancy](https://milvus.io/docs/multi_tenancy.md#Multi-tenancy-strategies) through isolation at database, collection, partition, or partition key level. The flexible strategies allow a single cluster to handle hundreds to millions of tenants, also ensures optimized search performance and flexible access control. Milvus enhances cost-effectiveness with hot/cold storage. Frequently accessed hot data can be stored in memory or on SSDs for better performance, while less-accessed cold data is kept on slower, cost-effective storage. This mechanism can significantly reduce costs while maintaining high performance for critical tasks.
README — Sparse Vector for Full Text Search and Hybrid Search**
README — In addition to semantic search through dense vector, Milvus also natively supports [full text search](https://milvus.io/docs/full-text-search.md) with BM25 as well as learned sparse embedding such as SPLADE and BGE-M3. Users can store sparse vector and dense vector in the same collection, and define functions to rerank results from multiple search requests. See examples of [Hybrid Search with semantic search + full text search](https://milvus.io/docs/full_text_search_with_milvus.md).
README — Data Security and Fine-grain Access Control**
README — Milvus ensures data security by implementing mandatory user authentication, TLS encryption, and Role-Based Access Control (RBAC). User authentication ensures that only authorized users with valid credentials can access the database, while TLS encryption secures all communications within the network. Additionally, RBAC allows for fine-grained access control by assigning specific permissions to users based on their roles. These features make Milvus a robust and secure choice for enterprise applications, protecting sensitive data from unauthorized access and potential breaches.
README — Milvus is trusted by AI developers to build applications such as text and image search, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and recommendation systems. Milvus powers [many mission-critical business]((https://milvus.io/use-cases)) for startups and enterprises.

README — Ecosystem and Integration
README — Milvus integrates with a comprehensive suite of [AI development tools](https://milvus.io/docs/integrations_overview.md), such as LangChain, LlamaIndex, OpenAI and HuggingFace, making it an ideal vector store for GenAI applications such as Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). Milvus works with both open-source embedding models and embedding service, in text, image and video modalities. Milvus also provides a convenient util [`pymilvus[model]`](https://milvus.io/docs/embeddings.md), users can use the simple wrapper code to transform unstructured data into vector embeddings and leverage reranking models for optimized search results. The Milvus ecosystem also includes [Attu](https://github.com/zilliztech/attu?tab=readme-ov-file#attu) for GUI-based administration, [Birdwatcher](https://milvus.io/docs/birdwatcher_overview.md) for system debugging, [Prometheus/Grafana](https://milvus.io/docs/monitor_overview.md) for monitoring, [Milvus CDC](https://milvus.io/docs/milvus-cdc-overview.md) for data synchronization, [VTS](https://github.com/zilliztech/vts?tab=readme-ov-file#vts) for data migration and data connectors for [Spark](https://milvus.io/docs/integrate_with_spark.md#Spark-Milvus-Connector-User-Guide), [Kafka](https://github.com/zilliztech/kafka-connect-milvus?tab=readme-ov-file#kafka-connect-milvus-connector), [Fivetran](https://fivetran.com/docs/destinations/milvus), and [Airbyte](https://milvus.io/docs/integrate_with_airbyte.md) to build search pipelines.
README — Check out https://milvus.io/docs/integrations_overview.md for more details.

CODE REVIEW — Milvus Code Review Guide
CODE REVIEW — All PRs are checked in automatically by the sre-robot, with the following conditions:
CODE REVIEW — DCO check passed
CODE REVIEW — All test passed and code coverage check passed, with a `ci-passed` label
CODE REVIEW — Notes: If there is a `[skip e2e]` tag in the commit message, it skips running e2e tests automatically,
CODE REVIEW — but it still runs UT tests and code checkers.
CODE REVIEW — Reviewer passed, with a `/lgtm` label
CODE REVIEW — Approver passed, with a `/approve` label
CODE REVIEW — Generally speaking, reviewer is volunteered and can be anyone in the community who is familiar with the packages the PR modifies.
CODE REVIEW — Reviewers are responsible for the logic correctness, error handling, unit test coverage and code readability.
CODE REVIEW — While Approver focuses on overall design, code readability, and ensuring the PR follows code of
CODE REVIEW — conduct(Such as meaningful title and commit message, marked with correct labels, meaningful comments). Currently,
CODE REVIEW — all Approvers are listed under OWNERS_ALIASES file.
CODE REVIEW — Things to do before review
CODE REVIEW — Read the title, commit message and related issue of the PR, if it's not easy to understand, ask for improvement
CODE REVIEW — For a bug fix PR, there should be a detailed bug description in related issue, and make sure the test cases to cover this bug.
CODE REVIEW — For a function enhancement PR, understand the function use case, make sure the functionality is reasonable.
CODE REVIEW — For a performance PR, make sure benchmark result is listed in PR.
CODE REVIEW — Think deeply about why is the solution necessary, any workaround or substitutions?
CODE REVIEW — Things to check during the review
CODE REVIEW — Does the code follow style guide?
CODE REVIEW — Does the code do exactly the same as title and commit message describe?
CODE REVIEW — Can this function and variable's behavior be inferred by its name?
CODE REVIEW — Do unit tests cover all the important code branches?
CODE REVIEW — What about the edge cases and failure handling paths?
CODE REVIEW — Do we need better layering and abstraction?
CODE REVIEW — Are there enough comments to understand the intent of the code?
CODE REVIEW — Are hacks, workarounds and temporary fixes commented?
CODE REVIEW — If `[skip e2e]` is tagged, is it safe enough to skip running e2e tests?
CODE REVIEW — Notes: it skips running e2e tests, if there is a `[skip e2e]` in the commit message.
CODE REVIEW — Does the code will generate similar logs many times in one second?
CODE REVIEW — Things to keep in mind when you are writing a review comment
CODE REVIEW — Be kind to the coder, not to the code.
CODE REVIEW — Ask questions rather than make statements.
CODE REVIEW — Treat people who know less than you with respect, deference, and patience.
CODE REVIEW — Remember to praise when the code quality exceeds your expectation.
CODE REVIEW — It isn't necessarily wrong if the coder's solution is different with yours.
CODE REVIEW — Community is not only about the product, it is about person. Help others to improve whenever possible.
CODE REVIEW — For Approvers
CODE REVIEW — Besides All the reviewer's responsibility listed above, Approvers should also maintain code of conduct.
CODE REVIEW — Be sure the pr has only one commit, author has to do a squash commit in local REPO
CODE REVIEW — Commit message starts with a capital letter and does not end with punctuation
CODE REVIEW — Commit message is clear and meaningful. You can only have title without body if the title is self explained
CODE REVIEW — PR links to the correct issue, which clearly states the problems to be solved and the planned solution
CODE REVIEW — PR sets kind label
CODE REVIEW — The variable names appearing in the source code need to be readable. Comments are necessary if it is an unusual abbreviations
CODE REVIEW — Thanks for [Code Review Guide](https://github.com/pingcap/tidb/blob/master/code_review_guide.md) from Pingcap community.
CONTRIBUTING — Contributing to Milvus
CONTRIBUTING — Contributions to Milvus are welcome from everyone. We strive to make the contribution process simple and straightforward. Up-to-date information can be found at [milvus.io](https://milvus.io/).
CONTRIBUTING — The following are a set of guidelines for contributing to Milvus. Following these guidelines makes contributing to this project easy and transparent. These are mostly guidelines, not rules. Use your best judgment, and feel free to propose changes to this document in a pull request.
CONTRIBUTING — As for everything else in the project, the contributions to Milvus are governed by our [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

CONTRIBUTING — How can you contribute?
CONTRIBUTING — Contributing code
CONTRIBUTING — If you encounter a bug, you can**
CONTRIBUTING — (**Recommended**) File an issue about the bug.
CONTRIBUTING — Provide clear and concrete ways/scripts to reproduce the bug.
CONTRIBUTING — Provide possible solutions for the bug.
CONTRIBUTING — Pull a request to fix the bug.
CONTRIBUTING — If you're interested in existing issues, you can**
CONTRIBUTING — (**Recommended**) Provide answers for issue labeled `question`.
CONTRIBUTING — Provide help for issues labeled `bug`, `improvement`, and `enhancement` by
CONTRIBUTING — (**Recommended**) Ask questions, reproduce the issue, or provide solutions.
CONTRIBUTING — Pull a request to fix the issue.
CONTRIBUTING — If you require a new feature or major enhancement, you can**
CONTRIBUTING — (**Recommended**) File an issue about the feature/enhancement with reasons.
CONTRIBUTING — Provide an MEP for the feature/enhancement.
CONTRIBUTING — Pull a request to implement the MEP.
CONTRIBUTING — If you are a reviewer/approver of Milvus, you can**
CONTRIBUTING — Participate in [PR review](CODE_REVIEW.md) process.
CONTRIBUTING — Instruct newcomers in the community to complete the PR process.
CONTRIBUTING — If you want to become a contributor of Milvus, submit your pull requests! For those just getting started, see [GitHub workflow](#github-workflow) below.
CONTRIBUTING — All submissions will be reviewed as quickly as possible.
CONTRIBUTING — There will be a reviewer to review the codes, and an approver to review everything aside the codes, see [code review](CODE_REVIEW.md) for details.
CONTRIBUTING — If everything is perfect, the reviewer will label `/lgtm`, and the approver will label `/approve`.
CONTRIBUTING — Once the 2 labels are on your PR, and all actions pass, your PR will be merged into base branch automatically by our @sre-ci-robot
CONTRIBUTING — GitHub workflow
CONTRIBUTING — Generally, we follow the "fork-and-pull" Git workflow.
CONTRIBUTING — [Fork](https://docs.github.com/en/github/getting-started-with-github/fork-a-repo) the [Milvus repo](https://github.com/milvus-io/milvus/tree/master) on GitHub.
CONTRIBUTING — Clone your fork to your local machine with `git clone git@github.com:<yourname>/milvus.git`.
CONTRIBUTING — Work in your local repo and file a PR.
CONTRIBUTING — In your local repo:
CONTRIBUTING — [Configure](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/collaborating-with-pull-requests/working-with-forks/configuring-a-remote-repository-for-a-fork) your local repo by adding the remote official repo as upstream.
CONTRIBUTING — Then you can create a branch, make changes and [commit](https://docs.github.com/en/github/collaborating-with-issues-and-pull-requests/committing-changes-to-a-pull-request-branch-created-from-a-fork).
CONTRIBUTING — Lastly, fetch upstream (and resolve merge conflicts if necessary), rebase and push the changes to origin. You can submit a [pull request](https://docs.github.com/en/github/collaborating-with-issues-and-pull-requests/about-pull-requests) to get your code reviewed.
CONTRIBUTING — Once getting approved, your code can be merged to `master`, yay!
CONTRIBUTING — Here is the process illustrated in details:
CONTRIBUTING — ![](docs/developer_guides/figs/fork-and-pull.png)
CONTRIBUTING — Remember to [sync your forked repository](https://docs.github.com/en/github/getting-started-with-github/fork-a-repo#keep-your-fork-synced) _before_ submitting proposed changes upstream. If you have an existing local repository, please update it before you start, to minimize the chance of merge conflicts.
CONTRIBUTING — ![](docs/developer_guides/figs/local-develop-steps.png)
CONTRIBUTING — General guidelines
CONTRIBUTING — Before submitting your pull requests for review, make sure that your changes are consistent with the [coding style](CONTRIBUTING.md#coding-style), and run [unit tests](CONTRIBUTING.md#run-unit-test-with-code-coverage) to check your code coverage rate.
CONTRIBUTING — Include unit tests when you contribute new features, as they help to prove that your code works correctly, and also guard against future breaking changes to lower the maintenance cost.
CONTRIBUTING — Bug fixes also require unit tests, because the presence of bugs usually indicates insufficient test coverage.
CONTRIBUTING — Keep API compatibility in mind when you change code in Milvus. Reviewers of your pull request will comment on any API compatibility issues.
CONTRIBUTING — When you contribute a new feature to Milvus, the maintenance burden is (by default) transferred to the Milvus team. This means that the benefit of the contribution must be compared against the cost of maintaining the feature.
CONTRIBUTING — Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO)
CONTRIBUTING — All contributions to this project must be accompanied by acknowledgment of, and agreement to, the [Developer Certificate of Origin](https://developercertificate.org/). Acknowledgment of and agreement to the Developer Certificate of Origin _must_ be included in the comment section of each contribution and _must_ take the form of `Signed-off-by: {{Full Name}} <{{email address}}>` (without the `{}`). Contributions without this acknowledgment will be required to add it before being accepted. If contributors are unable or unwilling to agree to the Developer Certificate of Origin, their contribution will not be included.
CONTRIBUTING — Contributors sign-off that they adhere to DCO by adding the following Signed-off-by line to commit messages:
CONTRIBUTING — Git also has a `-s` command line option to append this automatically to your commit message:
CONTRIBUTING — Coding Style
CONTRIBUTING — Keeping a consistent style for code, code comments, commit messages, and PR descriptions will greatly accelerate your PR review process.
CONTRIBUTING — We highly recommend you refer to and comply to the following style guides when you put together your pull requests:
CONTRIBUTING — Golang coding style
CONTRIBUTING — Coding style: refer to the [Effictive Go Style Guide](https://golang.org/doc/effective_go)
CONTRIBUTING — We also use `golangci-lint` to perform code check. Run the following command before submitting your pull request and make sure there is no issue reported:
CONTRIBUTING — To format code
CONTRIBUTING — C++ coding style
CONTRIBUTING — The C++ coding style used in Milvus generally follows [Google C++ Style Guide](https://google.github.io/styleguide/cppguide.html).
CONTRIBUTING — We made the following changes based on the guide:
CONTRIBUTING — spaces for indentation
CONTRIBUTING — Adopt .cpp file extension instead of .cc extension
CONTRIBUTING — character line length
CONTRIBUTING — Camel-Cased file names
CONTRIBUTING — Install clang-format
CONTRIBUTING — Check code style
CONTRIBUTING — Run unit test with code coverage
CONTRIBUTING — Before submitting your Pull Request, make sure you have run unit test, and your code coverage rate is >= 90%.
CONTRIBUTING — Run golang unit tests
CONTRIBUTING — You can run all the Golang unit tests using make.
CONTRIBUTING — You can also run unit tests in package level.
CONTRIBUTING — You can run a sub unit test.
CONTRIBUTING — In this case, we are only concerned about the tests with name "SegmentReplica" and
CONTRIBUTING — sub tests with name "segmentFlushed". When running sub tests, the coverage is not concerned.
CONTRIBUTING — Using mockery
CONTRIBUTING — It is recommended to use [Mockery](https://github.com/vektra/mockery) to generate mock implementations for unit test dependencies.
CONTRIBUTING — If your PR changes any interface definition, you shall run following commands to update all mockery implemented type before submitting it:
CONTRIBUTING — If your PR adds any new interface and related mockery types, please add a new entry under proper [Makefile](Makefile) `generate-mockery-xxx` command.
CONTRIBUTING — Run C++ unit tests
CONTRIBUTING — Install lcov
CONTRIBUTING — Run unit test and generate code for code coverage check
CONTRIBUTING — Commits and PRs
CONTRIBUTING — Commit message and PR description style: refer to [good commit messages](https://chris.beams.io/posts/git-commit)
CODE OF CONDUCT — Code of Conduct
CODE OF CONDUCT — Our Pledge
CODE OF CONDUCT — In the interest of fostering an open and welcoming environment, we as
CODE OF CONDUCT — contributors and maintainers pledge to make participation in our project and
CODE OF CONDUCT — our community a harassment-free experience for everyone, regardless of age, body
CODE OF CONDUCT — size, disability, ethnicity, sex characteristics, gender identity and expression,
CODE OF CONDUCT — level of experience, education, socio-economic status, nationality, personal
CODE OF CONDUCT — appearance, race, religion, or sexual identity and orientation.
CODE OF CONDUCT — Our Standards
CODE OF CONDUCT — Examples of behavior that contributes to creating a positive environment
CODE OF CONDUCT — include:
CODE OF CONDUCT — Using welcoming and inclusive language
CODE OF CONDUCT — Being respectful of differing viewpoints and experiences
CODE OF CONDUCT — Gracefully accepting constructive criticism
CODE OF CONDUCT — Focusing on what is best for the community
CODE OF CONDUCT — Showing empathy towards other community members
CODE OF CONDUCT — Examples of unacceptable behavior by participants include:
CODE OF CONDUCT — The use of sexualized language or imagery and unwelcome sexual attention or
CODE OF CONDUCT — advances
CODE OF CONDUCT — Trolling, insulting/derogatory comments, and personal or political attacks
CODE OF CONDUCT — Public or private harassment
CODE OF CONDUCT — Publishing others' private information, such as a physical or electronic
CODE OF CONDUCT — address, without explicit permission
CODE OF CONDUCT — Other conduct which could reasonably be considered inappropriate in a
CODE OF CONDUCT — professional setting
CODE OF CONDUCT — Our Responsibilities
CODE OF CONDUCT — Project maintainers are responsible for clarifying the standards of acceptable
CODE OF CONDUCT — behavior and are expected to take appropriate and fair corrective action in
CODE OF CONDUCT — response to any instances of unacceptable behavior.

README — Latest updates -- SAM 2: Segment Anything in Images and Videos
README — Please check out our new release on [**Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM 2)**](https://github.com/facebookresearch/segment-anything-2).
README — SAM 2 code: https://github.com/facebookresearch/segment-anything-2
README — SAM 2 demo: https://sam2.metademolab.com/
README — SAM 2 paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.00714
README — ![SAM 2 architecture](https://github.com/facebookresearch/segment-anything-2/blob/main/assets/model_diagram.png?raw=true)
README — Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM 2)** is a foundation model towards solving promptable visual segmentation in images and videos. We extend SAM to video by considering images as a video with a single frame. The model design is a simple transformer architecture with streaming memory for real-time video processing. We build a model-in-the-loop data engine, which improves model and data via user interaction, to collect [**our SA-V dataset**](https://ai.meta.com/datasets/segment-anything-video), the largest video segmentation dataset to date. SAM 2 trained on our data provides strong performance across a wide range of tasks and visual domains.

README — ![SAM design](assets/model_diagram.png?raw=true)
README — The **Segment Anything Model (SAM)** produces high quality object masks from input prompts such as points or boxes, and it can be used to generate masks for all objects in an image. It has been trained on a [dataset](https://segment-anything.com/dataset/index.html) of 11 million images and 1.1 billion masks, and has strong zero-shot performance on a variety of segmentation tasks.

CODE OF CONDUCT — Code of Conduct
CODE OF CONDUCT — Facebook has adopted a Code of Conduct that we expect project participants to adhere to. Please [read the full text](https://code.fb.com/codeofconduct) so that you can understand what actions will and will not be tolerated.
README — Faiss is a library for efficient similarity search and clustering of dense vectors. It contains algorithms that search in sets of vectors of any size, up to ones that possibly do not fit in RAM. It also contains supporting code for evaluation and parameter tuning. Faiss is written in C++ with complete wrappers for Python/numpy. Some of the most useful algorithms are implemented on the GPU. It is developed primarily at Meta's [Fundamental AI Research](https://ai.facebook.com/) group.
README — See [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) for detailed information about latest features.
README — Introduction
README — Faiss contains several methods for similarity search. It assumes that the instances are represented as vectors and are identified by an integer, and that the vectors can be compared with L2 (Euclidean) distances or dot products. Vectors that are similar to a query vector are those that have the lowest L2 distance or the highest dot product with the query vector. It also supports cosine similarity, since this is a dot product on normalized vectors.
README — Some of the methods, like those based on binary vectors and compact quantization codes, solely use a compressed representation of the vectors and do not require to keep the original vectors. This generally comes at the cost of a less precise search but these methods can scale to billions of vectors in main memory on a single server. Other methods, like HNSW and NSG add an indexing structure on top of the raw vectors to make searching more efficient.
README — The GPU implementation can accept input from either CPU or GPU memory. On a server with GPUs, the GPU indexes can be used a drop-in replacement for the CPU indexes (e.g., replace `IndexFlatL2` with `GpuIndexFlatL2`) and copies to/from GPU memory are handled automatically. Results will be faster however if both input and output remain resident on the GPU. Both single and multi-GPU usage is supported.
README — Installing
README — Faiss comes with precompiled libraries for Anaconda in Python, see [faiss-cpu](https://anaconda.org/pytorch/faiss-cpu), [faiss-gpu](https://anaconda.org/pytorch/faiss-gpu) and [faiss-gpu-cuvs](https://anaconda.org/pytorch/faiss-gpu-cuvs). The library is mostly implemented in C++, the only dependency is a [BLAS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_Linear_Algebra_Subprograms) implementation. Optional GPU support is provided via CUDA or AMD ROCm, and the Python interface is also optional. The backend GPU implementations of NVIDIA [cuVS](https://github.com/rapidsai/cuvs) can also be enabled optionally. It compiles with cmake. See [INSTALL.md](INSTALL.md) for details.
README — How Faiss works
README — Faiss is built around an index type that stores a set of vectors, and provides a function to search in them with L2 and/or dot product vector comparison. Some index types are simple baselines, such as exact search. Most of the available indexing structures correspond to various trade-offs with respect to
README — search time
README — search quality
README — memory used per index vector
README — training time
README — adding time
README — need for external data for unsupervised training
README — The optional GPU implementation provides what is likely (as of March 2017) the fastest exact and approximate (compressed-domain) nearest neighbor search implementation for high-dimensional vectors, fastest Lloyd's k-means, and fastest small k-selection algorithm known. [The implementation is detailed here](https://arxiv.org/abs/1702.08734).
README — Full documentation of Faiss
README — The following are entry points for documentation:
README — the full documentation can be found on the [wiki page](http://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/wiki), including a [tutorial](https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/wiki/Getting-started), a [FAQ](https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/wiki/FAQ) and a [troubleshooting section](https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/wiki/Troubleshooting)
README — the [doxygen documentation](https://faiss.ai/) gives per-class information extracted from code comments
README — to reproduce results from our research papers, [Polysemous codes](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.01882) and [Billion-scale similarity search with GPUs](https://arxiv.org/abs/1702.08734), refer to the [benchmarks README](benchs/README.md). For [
README — Link and code: Fast indexing with graphs and compact regression codes](https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.09996), see the [link_and_code README](benchs/link_and_code)
README — The main authors of Faiss are:
README — [Hervé Jégou](https://github.com/jegou) initiated the Faiss project and wrote its first implementation
README — [Matthijs Douze](https://github.com/mdouze) implemented most of the CPU Faiss
README — [Jeff Johnson](https://github.com/wickedfoo) implemented all of the GPU Faiss
README — [Lucas Hosseini](https://github.com/beauby) implemented the binary indexes and the build system
README — [Chengqi Deng](https://github.com/KinglittleQ) implemented NSG, NNdescent and much of the additive quantization code.
README — [Alexandr Guzhva](https://github.com/alexanderguzhva) many optimizations: SIMD, memory allocation and layout, fast decoding kernels for vector codecs, etc.
README — [Gergely Szilvasy](https://github.com/algoriddle) build system, benchmarking framework.

CHANGELOG — Support METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT for GpuIndexIVFPQ.
CHANGELOG — Support float16 coarse quantizer for GpuIndexIVFFlat and GpuIndexIVFPQ. GPU
CHANGELOG — Tensor Core operations (mixed-precision arithmetic) are enabled on supported
CHANGELOG — hardware when operating with float16 data.
CHANGELOG — Support k-means clustering with encoded vectors. This makes it possible to
CHANGELOG — train on larger datasets without decompressing them in RAM, and is especially
CHANGELOG — useful for binary datasets (see https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/blob/main/tests/test_build_blocks.py#L92).
CHANGELOG — Support weighted k-means. Weights can be associated to each training point
CHANGELOG — (see https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/blob/main/tests/test_build_blocks.py).
CHANGELOG — Serialize callback in python, to write to pipes or sockets (see
CHANGELOG — https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/wiki/Index-IO,-cloning-and-hyper-parameter-tuning).
CHANGELOG — Reconstruct arbitrary ids from IndexIVF + efficient remove of a small number
CHANGELOG — of ids. This avoids 2 inefficiencies: O(ntotal) removal of vectors and
CHANGELOG — IndexIDMap2 on top of indexIVF. Documentation here:
CHANGELOG — https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/wiki/Special-operations-on-indexes.
CHANGELOG — Support inner product as a metric in IndexHNSW (see
CHANGELOG — https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/blob/main/tests/test_index.py#L490).
CHANGELOG — Support PQ of sizes other than 8 bit in IndexIVFPQ.
CHANGELOG — Demo on how to perform searches sequentially on an IVF index. This is useful
CHANGELOG — for an OnDisk index with a very large batch of queries. In that case, it is
CHANGELOG — worthwhile to scan the index sequentially (see
CHANGELOG — https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/blob/main/tests/test_ivflib.py#L62).
CHANGELOG — Range search support for most binary indexes.
CHANGELOG — Support for hashing-based binary indexes (see
CHANGELOG — https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/wiki/Binary-indexes).
CHANGELOG — Replaced obj table in Clustering object: now it is a ClusteringIterationStats
CHANGELOG — structure that contains additional statistics.
CHANGELOG — Removed support for useFloat16Accumulator for accumulators on GPU (all
CHANGELOG — accumulations are now done in float32, regardless of whether float16 or float32
CHANGELOG — input data is used).
CHANGELOG — Some python3 fixes in benchmarks.
CHANGELOG — Fixed GpuCloner (some fields were not copied, default to no precomputed tables
CHANGELOG — with IndexIVFPQ).
CHANGELOG — Fixed support for new pytorch versions.
CHANGELOG — Serialization bug with alternative distances.
CHANGELOG — Removed test on multiple-of-4 dimensions when switching between blas and AVX
CHANGELOG — implementations.
CHANGELOG — [1.6.2] - 2020-03-10
CHANGELOG — [1.6.1] - 2019-12-04
CHANGELOG — [1.6.0] - 2019-09-24
CHANGELOG — Faiss as a codec: We introduce a new API within Faiss to encode fixed-size
CHANGELOG — vectors into fixed-size codes. The encoding is lossy and the tradeoff between
CHANGELOG — compression and reconstruction accuracy can be adjusted.
CHANGELOG — ScalarQuantizer support for GPU, see gpu/GpuIndexIVFScalarQuantizer.h. This is
CHANGELOG — particularly useful as GPU memory is often less abundant than CPU.
CHANGELOG — Added easy-to-use serialization functions for indexes to byte arrays in Python
CHANGELOG — (faiss.serialize_index, faiss.deserialize_index).
CHANGELOG — The Python KMeans object can be used to use the GPU directly, just add
CHANGELOG — gpu=True to the constuctor see gpu/test/test_gpu_index.py test TestGPUKmeans.
CHANGELOG — Change in the code layout: many C++ sources are now in subdirectories impl/
CHANGELOG — and utils/.
