CONTRIBUTING — Contributing to Faiss
CONTRIBUTING — We want to make contributing to this project as easy and transparent as
CONTRIBUTING — possible.
CONTRIBUTING — Our Development Process
CONTRIBUTING — We mainly develop Faiss within Facebook. Sometimes, we will sync the
CONTRIBUTING — github version of Faiss with the internal state.
CONTRIBUTING — Pull Requests
CONTRIBUTING — We welcome pull requests that add significant value to Faiss. If you plan to do
CONTRIBUTING — a major development and contribute it back to Faiss, please contact us first before
CONTRIBUTING — putting too much effort into it.
CONTRIBUTING — Fork the repo and create your branch from `main`.
CONTRIBUTING — If you've added code that should be tested, add tests.
CONTRIBUTING — If you've changed APIs, update the documentation.
CONTRIBUTING — Ensure the test suite passes.
CONTRIBUTING — Make sure your code lints.
CONTRIBUTING — If you haven't already, complete the Contributor License Agreement ("CLA").
CONTRIBUTING — There is a Facebook internal test suite for Faiss, and we need to run
CONTRIBUTING — all changes to Faiss through it.
CONTRIBUTING — Contributor License Agreement ("CLA")
CONTRIBUTING — In order to accept your pull request, we need you to submit a CLA. You only need
CONTRIBUTING — to do this once to work on any of Facebook's open source projects.
CONTRIBUTING — Complete your CLA here: <https://code.facebook.com/cla>
CONTRIBUTING — We use GitHub issues to track public bugs. Please ensure your description is
CONTRIBUTING — clear and has sufficient instructions to be able to reproduce the issue.
CONTRIBUTING — Facebook has a [bounty program](https://www.facebook.com/whitehat/) for the safe
CONTRIBUTING — disclosure of security bugs. In those cases, please go through the process
CONTRIBUTING — outlined on that page and do not file a public issue.
CONTRIBUTING — Coding Style
CONTRIBUTING — spaces for indentation in C++ (no tabs)
CONTRIBUTING — character line length (both for C++ and Python)
CONTRIBUTING — C++ language level: C++17
CONTRIBUTING — By contributing to Faiss, you agree that your contributions will be licensed
CONTRIBUTING — under the LICENSE file in the root directory of this source tree.
INSTALL — Installing Faiss via conda
INSTALL — The supported way to install Faiss is through [conda](https://docs.conda.io).
INSTALL — Stable releases are pushed regularly to the pytorch conda channel, as well as
INSTALL — pre-release nightly builds.
INSTALL — The CPU-only faiss-cpu conda package is currently available on Linux (x86-64 and aarch64), OSX (arm64 only), and Windows (x86-64)
INSTALL — faiss-gpu, containing both CPU and GPU indices, is available on Linux (x86-64 only) for CUDA 11.4 and 12.1
INSTALL — faiss-gpu-cuvs package containing GPU indices provided by [NVIDIA cuVS](https://github.com/rapidsai/cuvs/) version 25.08, is available on Linux (x86-64 only) for CUDA 12.4.
INSTALL — To install the latest stable release:
INSTALL — For faiss-gpu, the nvidia channel is required for CUDA, which is not published in the main anaconda channel.
INSTALL — For faiss-gpu-cuvs, the rapidsai, conda-forge and nvidia channels are required.
INSTALL — Nightly pre-release packages can be installed as follows:
INSTALL — In the above commands, pytorch-cuda=11 or pytorch-cuda=12 would select a specific CUDA version, if it’s required.
INSTALL — A combination of versions that installs GPU Faiss with CUDA and Pytorch (as of 2024-05-15):
INSTALL — Installing from conda-forge
INSTALL — Faiss is also being packaged by [conda-forge](https://conda-forge.org/), the
INSTALL — community-driven packaging ecosystem for conda. The packaging effort is
INSTALL — collaborating with the Faiss team to ensure high-quality package builds.
INSTALL — Due to the comprehensive infrastructure of conda-forge, it may even happen that
INSTALL — certain build combinations are supported in conda-forge that are not available
INSTALL — through the pytorch channel. To install, use
INSTALL — You can tell which channel your conda packages come from by using `conda list`.
INSTALL — If you are having problems using a package built by conda-forge, please raise
INSTALL — an [issue](https://github.com/conda-forge/faiss-split-feedstock/issues) on the
INSTALL — conda-forge package "feedstock".
INSTALL — Building from source
INSTALL — Faiss can be built from source using CMake.
INSTALL — Faiss is supported on x86-64 machines on Linux, OSX, and Windows. It has been
INSTALL — found to run on other platforms as well, see
INSTALL — [other platforms](https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/wiki/Related-projects#bindings-to-other-languages-and-porting-to-other-platforms).
INSTALL — The basic requirements are:
INSTALL — a C++17 compiler (with support for OpenMP support version 2 or higher),
INSTALL — a BLAS implementation (on Intel machines we strongly recommend using Intel MKL for best
INSTALL — performance).
INSTALL — The optional requirements are:
INSTALL — for GPU indices:
INSTALL — the CUDA toolkit,
INSTALL — for AMD GPUs:
INSTALL — AMD ROCm,
INSTALL — for using NVIDIA cuVS implementations:
INSTALL — libcuvs=25.08
INSTALL — for the python bindings:
INSTALL — python 3,
INSTALL — and swig.
INSTALL — Indications for specific configurations are available in the [troubleshooting
INSTALL — section of the wiki](https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/wiki/Troubleshooting).
INSTALL — Building with NVIDIA cuVS
INSTALL — [cuVS](https://docs.rapids.ai/api/cuvs/nightly/) contains state-of-the-art implementations of several algorithms for running approximate nearest neighbors and clustering on the GPU. It is built on top of the [RAPIDS RAFT](https://github.com/rapidsai/raft) library of high performance machine learning primitives. Building Faiss with cuVS enabled allows a user to choose between regular GPU implementations in Faiss and cuVS implementations for specific algorithms.
INSTALL — The libcuvs dependency should be installed via conda:
INSTALL — For more ways to install cuVS 25.08, refer to the [RAPIDS Installation Guide](https://docs.rapids.ai/install).
INSTALL — Step 1: invoking CMake
INSTALL — This generates the system-dependent configuration/build files in the `build/`
INSTALL — subdirectory.
INSTALL — Several options can be passed to CMake, among which:
INSTALL — general options:
INSTALL — `-DFAISS_ENABLE_GPU=OFF` in order to disable building GPU indices (possible
INSTALL — values are `ON` and `OFF`),
INSTALL — `-DFAISS_ENABLE_PYTHON=OFF` in order to disable building python bindings
INSTALL — (possible values are `ON` and `OFF`),
INSTALL — `-DFAISS_ENABLE_CUVS=ON` in order to use the NVIDIA cuVS implementations
INSTALL — of the IVF-Flat, IVF-PQ and [CAGRA](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2308.15136) GPU-accelerated indices (default is `OFF`, possible, values are `ON` and `OFF`).
INSTALL — Note: `-DFAISS_ENABLE_GPU` must be set to `ON` when enabling this option.
INSTALL — `-DBUILD_TESTING=OFF` in order to disable building C++ tests,
INSTALL — `-DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON` in order to build a shared library (possible values
INSTALL — are `ON` and `OFF`),
INSTALL — `-DFAISS_ENABLE_C_API=ON` in order to enable building [C API](c_api/INSTALL.md) (possible values
INSTALL — are `ON` and `OFF`),
INSTALL — optimization-related options:
INSTALL — `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release` in order to enable generic compiler
INSTALL — optimization options (enables `-O3` on gcc for instance),
INSTALL — `-DFAISS_OPT_LEVEL=avx2` in order to enable the required compiler flags to
INSTALL — generate code using optimized SIMD/Vector instructions. Possible values are below:
INSTALL — On x86-64, `generic`, `avx2`, `avx512`, and `avx512_spr` (for avx512 features available since Intel(R) Sapphire Rapids), by increasing order of optimization,
INSTALL — On aarch64, `generic` and `sve`, by increasing order of optimization,
INSTALL — `-DFAISS_USE_LTO=ON` in order to enable [Link-Time Optimization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Link-time_optimization) (default is `OFF`, possible values are `ON` and `OFF`).
INSTALL — BLAS-related options:
INSTALL — `-DBLA_VENDOR=Intel10_64_dyn -DMKL_LIBRARIES=/path/to/mkl/libs` to use the
INSTALL — Intel MKL BLAS implementation, which is significantly faster than OpenBLAS
INSTALL — (more information about the values for the `BLA_VENDOR` option can be found in
INSTALL — the [CMake docs](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/module/FindBLAS.html)),
INSTALL — GPU-related options:
INSTALL — `-DCUDAToolkit_ROOT=/path/to/cuda-10.1` in order to hint to the path of
INSTALL — the CUDA toolkit (for more information, see
INSTALL — [CMake docs](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/module/FindCUDAToolkit.html)),
INSTALL — `-DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES="75;72"` for specifying which GPU architectures
INSTALL — to build against (see [CUDA docs](https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-gpus) to
INSTALL — determine which architecture(s) you should pick),
INSTALL — `-DFAISS_ENABLE_ROCM=ON` in order to enable building GPU indices for AMD GPUs.
INSTALL — `-DFAISS_ENABLE_GPU` must be `ON` when using this option. (possible values are `ON` and `OFF`),
INSTALL — python-related options:
INSTALL — `-DPython_EXECUTABLE=/path/to/python3.7` in order to build a python
INSTALL — interface for a different python than the default one (see
INSTALL — [CMake docs](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/module/FindPython.html)).
INSTALL — Step 2: Invoking Make
INSTALL — This builds the C++ library (`libfaiss.a` by default, and `libfaiss.so` if
INSTALL — `-DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON` was passed to CMake).
INSTALL — The `-j` option enables parallel compilation of multiple units, leading to a
INSTALL — faster build, but increasing the chances of running out of memory, in which case
INSTALL — it is recommended to set the `-j` option to a fixed value (such as `-j4`).
INSTALL — If making use of optimization options, build the correct target before swigfaiss.
INSTALL — For AVX2:
INSTALL — For AVX512:
INSTALL — For AVX512 features available since Intel(R) Sapphire Rapids.
INSTALL — This will ensure the creation of neccesary files when building and installing the python package.
INSTALL — Step 3: Building the python bindings (optional)
INSTALL — The first command builds the python bindings for Faiss, while the second one
INSTALL — generates and installs the python package.
INSTALL — Step 4: Installing the C++ library and headers (optional)
INSTALL — This will make the compiled library (either `libfaiss.a` or `libfaiss.so` on
INSTALL — Linux) available system-wide, as well as the C++ headers. This step is not
INSTALL — needed to install the python package only.
INSTALL — Step 5: Testing (optional)
INSTALL — Running the C++ test suite
INSTALL — To run the whole test suite, make sure that `cmake` was invoked with
INSTALL — `-DBUILD_TESTING=ON`, and run:
INSTALL — Running the python test suite

CMakeLists — cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.15...3.25 FATAL_ERROR)
CMakeLists — project(Annoy
CMakeLists — DESCRIPTION "Approximate Nearest Neighbors Oh Yeah"
CMakeLists — VERSION 1.17.1
CMakeLists — LANGUAGES CXX)
CMakeLists — add_library(Annoy INTERFACE)
CMakeLists — add_library(Annoy::Annoy ALIAS Annoy)
CMakeLists — foreach (HEADER annoylib.h kissrandom.h mman.h)
CMakeLists — configure_file("${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/src/${HEADER}" "${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR}/include/annoy/${HEADER}" COPYONLY)
CMakeLists — endforeach ()
CMakeLists — target_include_directories(Annoy INTERFACE
CMakeLists — $<BUILD_INTERFACE:${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR}/include>
CMakeLists — $<INSTALL_INTERFACE:include>)
CMakeLists — include(GNUInstallDirs)
CMakeLists — install(DIRECTORY ${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR}/include/
CMakeLists — DESTINATION ${CMAKE_INSTALL_INCLUDEDIR})
CMakeLists — install(TARGETS Annoy
CMakeLists — EXPORT AnnoyTargets)
CMakeLists — install(EXPORT AnnoyTargets
CMakeLists — FILE AnnoyConfig.cmake
CMakeLists — NAMESPACE Annoy::
CMakeLists — DESTINATION ${CMAKE_INSTALL_LIBDIR}/cmake/annoy)
CMakeLists — export(TARGETS Annoy NAMESPACE Annoy:: FILE AnnoyConfig.cmake)
RELEASE — How to release
RELEASE — Make sure you're on master. `git checkout master && git fetch && git reset --hard origin/master`
RELEASE — Update `setup.py` to the newest version, `git add setup.py && git commit -m "version 1.2.3"`
RELEASE — `python setup.py sdist bdist_wheel`
RELEASE — `git tag -a v1.2.3 -m "version 1.2.3"`
RELEASE — `git push --tags origin master` to push the last version to Github
RELEASE — Go to https://github.com/spotify/annoy/releases and click "Draft a new release"
RELEASE — `twine upload dist/annoy-1.2.3*`

README — :alt: Annoy example
README — :align: center
README — image:: https://github.com/spotify/annoy/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg
README — :target: https://github.com/spotify/annoy/actions
README — Annoy (`Approximate Nearest Neighbors <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nearest_neighbor_search#Approximate_nearest_neighbor>`__ Oh Yeah) is a C++ library with Python bindings to search for points in space that are close to a given query point. It also creates large read-only file-based data structures that are `mmapped <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mmap>`__ into memory so that many processes may share the same data.
README — To install, simply do ``pip install --user annoy`` to pull down the latest version from `PyPI <https://pypi.python.org/pypi/annoy>`_.
README — For the C++ version, just clone the repo and ``#include "annoylib.h"``.
README — Background
README — There are some other libraries to do nearest neighbor search. Annoy is almost as fast as the fastest libraries, (see below), but there is actually another feature that really sets Annoy apart: it has the ability to **use static files as indexes**. In particular, this means you can **share index across processes**. Annoy also decouples creating indexes from loading them, so you can pass around indexes as files and map them into memory quickly. Another nice thing of Annoy is that it tries to minimize memory footprint so the indexes are quite small.
README — Why is this useful? If you want to find nearest neighbors and you have many CPU's, you only need to build the index once. You can also pass around and distribute static files to use in production environment, in Hadoop jobs, etc. Any process will be able to load (mmap) the index into memory and will be able to do lookups immediately.
README — We use it at `Spotify <http://www.spotify.com/>`__ for music recommendations. After running matrix factorization algorithms, every user/item can be represented as a vector in f-dimensional space. This library helps us search for similar users/items. We have many millions of tracks in a high-dimensional space, so memory usage is a prime concern.
README — Annoy was built by `Erik Bernhardsson <http://www.erikbern.com>`__ in a couple of afternoons during `Hack Week <http://labs.spotify.com/2013/02/15/organizing-a-hack-week/>`__.
README — Summary of features
README — `Euclidean distance <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_distance>`__, `Manhattan distance <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxicab_geometry>`__, `cosine distance <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosine_similarity>`__, `Hamming distance <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamming_distance>`__, or `Dot (Inner) Product distance <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dot_product>`__
README — Cosine distance is equivalent to Euclidean distance of normalized vectors = sqrt(2-2*cos(u, v))
README — Works better if you don't have too many dimensions (like <100) but seems to perform surprisingly well even up to 1,000 dimensions
README — Small memory usage
README — Lets you share memory between multiple processes
README — Index creation is separate from lookup (in particular you can not add more items once the tree has been created)
README — Native Python support, tested with 2.7, 3.6, and 3.7.
README — Build index on disk to enable indexing big datasets that won't fit into memory (contributed by `Rene Hollander <https://github.com/ReneHollander>`__)
README — Python code example
README — code-block:: python
README — from annoy import AnnoyIndex
README — import random
README — f = 40 # Length of item vector that will be indexed
README — t = AnnoyIndex(f, 'angular')
README — for i in range(1000):
README — v = [random.gauss(0, 1) for z in range(f)]
README — t.add_item(i, v)
README — t.build(10) # 10 trees
README — t.save('test.ann')
README — u = AnnoyIndex(f, 'angular')
README — u.load('test.ann') # super fast, will just mmap the file
README — print(u.get_nns_by_item(0, 1000)) # will find the 1000 nearest neighbors
README — Right now it only accepts integers as identifiers for items. Note that it will allocate memory for max(id)+1 items because it assumes your items are numbered 0 … n-1. If you need other id's, you will have to keep track of a map yourself.
README — Full Python API
README — ``AnnoyIndex(f, metric)`` returns a new index that's read-write and stores vector of ``f`` dimensions. Metric can be ``"angular"``, ``"euclidean"``, ``"manhattan"``, ``"hamming"``, or ``"dot"``.
README — ``a.add_item(i, v)`` adds item ``i`` (any nonnegative integer) with vector ``v``. Note that it will allocate memory for ``max(i)+1`` items.
README — ``a.build(n_trees, n_jobs=-1)`` builds a forest of ``n_trees`` trees. More trees gives higher precision when querying. After calling ``build``, no more items can be added. ``n_jobs`` specifies the number of threads used to build the trees. ``n_jobs=-1`` uses all available CPU cores.
README — ``a.save(fn, prefault=False)`` saves the index to disk and loads it (see next function). After saving, no more items can be added.
README — ``a.load(fn, prefault=False)`` loads (mmaps) an index from disk. If `prefault` is set to `True`, it will pre-read the entire file into memory (using mmap with `MAP_POPULATE`). Default is `False`.
README — ``a.unload()`` unloads.
README — ``a.get_nns_by_item(i, n, search_k=-1, include_distances=False)`` returns the ``n`` closest items. During the query it will inspect up to ``search_k`` nodes which defaults to ``n_trees * n`` if not provided. ``search_k`` gives you a run-time tradeoff between better accuracy and speed. If you set ``include_distances`` to ``True``, it will return a 2 element tuple with two lists in it: the second one containing all corresponding distances.
README — ``a.get_nns_by_vector(v, n, search_k=-1, include_distances=False)`` same but query by vector ``v``.
README — ``a.get_item_vector(i)`` returns the vector for item ``i`` that was previously added.
README — ``a.get_distance(i, j)`` returns the distance between items ``i`` and ``j``. NOTE: this used to return the *squared* distance, but has been changed as of Aug 2016.
README — ``a.get_n_items()`` returns the number of items in the index.
README — ``a.get_n_trees()`` returns the number of trees in the index.
README — ``a.on_disk_build(fn)`` prepares annoy to build the index in the specified file instead of RAM (execute before adding items, no need to save after build)
README — ``a.set_seed(seed)`` will initialize the random number generator with the given seed. Only used for building up the tree, i. e. only necessary to pass this before adding the items. Will have no effect after calling `a.build(n_trees)` or `a.load(fn)`.
README — There's no bounds checking performed on the values so be careful.
README — Annoy uses Euclidean distance of normalized vectors for its angular distance, which for two vectors u,v is equal to ``sqrt(2(1-cos(u,v)))``
README — The C++ API is very similar: just ``#include "annoylib.h"`` to get access to it.
README — Tradeoffs
README — There are just two main parameters needed to tune Annoy: the number of trees ``n_trees`` and the number of nodes to inspect during searching ``search_k``.
README — ``n_trees`` is provided during build time and affects the build time and the index size. A larger value will give more accurate results, but larger indexes.
README — ``search_k`` is provided in runtime and affects the search performance. A larger value will give more accurate results, but will take longer time to return.
README — If ``search_k`` is not provided, it will default to ``n * n_trees`` where ``n`` is the number of approximate nearest neighbors. Otherwise, ``search_k`` and ``n_trees`` are roughly independent, i.e. the value of ``n_trees`` will not affect search time if ``search_k`` is held constant and vice versa. Basically it's recommended to set ``n_trees`` as large as possible given the amount of memory you can afford, and it's recommended to set ``search_k`` as large as possible given the time constraints you have for the queries.
README — You can also accept slower search times in favour of reduced loading times, memory usage, and disk IO. On supported platforms the index is prefaulted during ``load`` and ``save``, causing the file to be pre-emptively read from disk into memory. If you set ``prefault`` to ``False``, pages of the mmapped index are instead read from disk and cached in memory on-demand, as necessary for a search to complete. This can significantly increase early search times but may be better suited for systems with low memory compared to index size, when few queries are executed against a loaded index, and/or when large areas of the index are unlikely to be relevant to search queries.
README — How does it work
README — Using `random projections <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locality-sensitive_hashing#Random_projection>`__ and by building up a tree. At every intermediate node in the tree, a random hyperplane is chosen, which divides the space into two subspaces. This hyperplane is chosen by sampling two points from the subset and taking the hyperplane equidistant from them.
README — We do this k times so that we get a forest of trees. k has to be tuned to your need, by looking at what tradeoff you have between precision and performance.
README — Hamming distance (contributed by `Martin Aumüller <https://github.com/maumueller>`__) packs the data into 64-bit integers under the hood and uses built-in bit count primitives so it could be quite fast. All splits are axis-aligned.
README — Dot Product distance (contributed by `Peter Sobot <https://github.com/psobot>`__ and `Pavel Korobov <https://github.com/pkorobov>`__) reduces the provided vectors from dot (or "inner-product") space to a more query-friendly cosine space using `a method by Bachrach et al., at Microsoft Research, published in 2014 <https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/XboxInnerProduct.pdf>`__.

README — Dreamer learns a world model that predicts ahead in a compact feature space.
README — From imagined feature sequences, it learns a policy and state-value function.
README — The value gradients are backpropagated through the multi-step predictions to
README — efficiently learn a long-horizon policy.

README — search on SIFT1B
README — The script [`bench_gpu_1bn.py`](bench_gpu_1bn.py) runs multi-gpu searches on the two 1-billion vector datasets we considered. It is more complex than the previous scripts, because it supports many search options and decomposes the dataset build process in Python to exploit the best possible CPU/GPU parallelism and GPU distribution.
README — Even on multiple GPUs, building the 1B datasets can last several hours. It is often a good idea to validate that everything is working fine on smaller datasets like SIFT1M, SIFT2M, etc.

README — search on Deep1B
README — The same script generates the GPU search results on Deep1B.
README — Here we are a bit tight on memory so we disable precomputed tables (`-noptables`) and restrict the amount of temporary memory. The `-altadd` option avoids GPU memory overflows during add.

README — The same script generates the KNN-graph on Deep1B. Note that the inverted file from above will not be re-used because the training sets are different. For the knngraph, the script will first do a pass over the whole dataset to compute the ground-truth knn for a subset of 10k nodes, for evaluation.

README — Demos for a few Faiss functionalities
README — =====================================
README — demo_auto_tune.py
README — Demonstrates the auto-tuning functionality of Faiss
README — demo_ondisk_ivf.py
README — Shows how to construct a Faiss index that stores the inverted file
README — data on disk, eg. when it does not fit in RAM. The script works on a
README — small dataset (sift1M) for demonstration and proceeds in stages:
README — : train on the dataset
README — : build 4 indexes, each containing 1/4 of the dataset. This can be
README — done in parallel on several machines
README — : merge the 4 indexes into one that is written directly to disk
README — (needs not to fit in RAM)
README — : load and test the index
README — The contrib modules
README — The contrib directory contains helper modules for Faiss for various tasks.
README — Code structure
README — The contrib directory gets compiled in the module faiss.contrib.
README — Note that although some of the modules may depend on additional modules (eg. GPU Faiss, pytorch, hdf5), they are not necessarily compiled in to avoid adding dependencies. It is the user's responsibility to provide them.
README — In contrib, we are progressively dropping python2 support.
README — List of contrib modules
README — A very simple Remote Procedure Call library, where function parameters and results are pickled, for use with client_server.py
README — client_server.py
README — The server handles requests to a Faiss index. The client calls the remote index.
README — This is mainly to shard datasets over several machines, see [Distributed index](https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/wiki/Indexes-that-do-not-fit-in-RAM#distributed-index)
README — ondisk.py
README — Encloses the main logic to merge indexes into an on-disk index.
README — See [On-disk storage](https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/wiki/Indexes-that-do-not-fit-in-RAM#on-disk-storage)
README — exhaustive_search.py
README — Computes the ground-truth search results for a dataset that possibly does not fit in RAM. Uses GPU if available.
README — Tested in `tests/test_contrib.TestComputeGT`
README — torch_utils.py
README — Interoperability functions for pytorch and Faiss: Importing this will allow pytorch Tensors (CPU or GPU) to be used as arguments to Faiss indexes and other functions. Torch GPU tensors can only be used with Faiss GPU indexes. If this is imported with a package that supports Faiss GPU, the necessary stream synchronization with the current pytorch stream will be automatically performed.
README — Numpy ndarrays can continue to be used in the Faiss python interface after importing this file. All arguments must be uniformly either numpy ndarrays or Torch tensors; no mixing is allowed.
README — Tested in `tests/test_contrib_torch.py` (CPU) and `gpu/test/test_contrib_torch_gpu.py` (GPU).
README — inspect_tools.py
README — Functions to inspect C++ objects wrapped by SWIG. Most often this just means reading
README — fields and converting them to the proper python array.
README — ivf_tools.py
README — A few functions to override the coarse quantizer in IVF, providing additional flexibility for assignment.
README — datasets.py
README — (may require h5py)
README — Definition of how to access data for some standard datasets.
README — factory_tools.py
README — Functions related to factory strings.
README — evaluation.py
README — A few non-trivial evaluation functions for search results
README — clustering.py
README — Contains:
README — a Python implementation of kmeans, that can be used for special datatypes (eg. sparse matrices).
README — a 2-level clustering routine and a function that can apply it to train an IndexIVF
README — big_batch_search.py
README — Search IVF indexes with one centroid after another. Useful for large
README — databases that do not fit in RAM *and* a large number of queries.

CMakeLists — LICENSE file in the root directory of this source tree.

INSTALL — Faiss C API
INSTALL — ===========
INSTALL — Faiss provides a pure C interface, which can subsequently be used either in pure C programs or to produce bindings for programming languages with Foreign Function Interface (FFI) support. Although this is not required for the Python interface, some other programming languages (e.g. Rust and Julia) do not have SWIG support.
INSTALL — Compilation instructions
INSTALL — The full contents of the pure C API are in the ["c_api"](c_api/) folder.
INSTALL — Please be sure to follow the instructions on [building the main C++ library](../INSTALL.md#step-1-compiling-the-c-faiss) first.
INSTALL — Include `-DFAISS_ENABLE_C_API=ON` to the cmake command.
INSTALL — `make -C build`
INSTALL — This builds the dynamic library "faiss_c", containing the full implementation of Faiss and the necessary wrappers for the C interface. It does not depend on libfaiss.a or the C++ standard library.
INSTALL — To build the example program, you should run `make -C build example_c` at the top level of
INSTALL — the faiss repo. The example program will be in `build/c_api/example_c` .
INSTALL — Using the API
INSTALL — The C API is composed of:
INSTALL — A set of C header files comprising the main Faiss interfaces, converted for use in C. Each file follows the format `«name»_c.h`, where `«name»` is the respective name from the C++ API. For example, the file [Index_c.h](./Index_c.h) file corresponds to the base `Index` API. Functions are declared with the `faiss_` prefix (e.g. `faiss_IndexFlat_new`), whereas new types have the `Faiss` prefix (e.g. `FaissIndex`, `FaissMetricType`, ...).
INSTALL — A dynamic library, compiled from the sources in the same folder, encloses the implementation of the library and wrapper functions.
INSTALL — The index factory is available via the `faiss_index_factory` function in `AutoTune_c.h`:
INSTALL — Most operations that you would find as member functions are available with the format `faiss_«classname»_«member»`.
INSTALL — Since this is C, the index needs to be freed manually in the end:
INSTALL — Error handling is done by examining the error code returned by operations with recoverable errors.
INSTALL — The code identifies the type of exception that rose from the implementation. Fetching the
INSTALL — corresponding error message can be done by calling the function `faiss_get_last_error()` from
INSTALL — `error_c.h`. Getter functions and `free` functions do not return an error code.
INSTALL — An example is included, which is built automatically for the target `all`. It can also be built separately:
INSTALL — `make bin/example_c`
INSTALL — Building with GPU support
INSTALL — For GPU support, a separate dynamic library in the "c_api/gpu" directory needs to be built.
INSTALL — The "gpufaiss_c" dynamic library contains the GPU and CPU implementations of Faiss, which means that
INSTALL — it can be used in place of "faiss_c". The same library will dynamically link with the CUDA runtime
INSTALL — and cuBLAS.
INSTALL — Using the GPU with the C API
INSTALL — A standard GPU resources object can be obtained by the name `FaissStandardGpuResources`:
INSTALL — Similarly to the C++ API, a CPU index can be converted to a GPU index:
INSTALL — A more complete example is available by the name `bin/example_gpu_c`.

CMakeLists — LICENSE file in the root directory of this source tree.

CMakeLists — set(THREADS_AND_WARPS
CMakeLists — "128|1024|8"
CMakeLists — "128|1|1"
CMakeLists — "128|128|3"
CMakeLists — "128|256|4"
CMakeLists — "128|32|2"

CMakeLists — Traverse through the Cartesian product of X and Y
CMakeLists — foreach(sub_codec ${SUB_CODEC_TYPE})
CMakeLists — foreach(metric_type ${SUB_METRIC_TYPE})
CMakeLists — foreach(threads_and_warps_str ${THREADS_AND_WARPS})
CMakeLists — string(REPLACE "|" ";" threads_and_warps ${threads_and_warps_str})
CMakeLists — list(GET threads_and_warps 0 sub_threads)
CMakeLists — list(GET threads_and_warps 1 sub_num_warp_q)
CMakeLists — list(GET threads_and_warps 2 sub_num_thread_q)
CMakeLists — Define the output file name
CMakeLists — set(filename "template_${sub_codec}_${metric_type}_${sub_threads}_${sub_num_warp_q}_${sub_num_thread_q}")
CMakeLists — Remove illegal characters from filename
CMakeLists — string(REGEX REPLACE "[^A-Za-z0-9_]" "" filename ${filename})
CMakeLists — set(output_file "${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR}/${filename}.${GPU_EXT_PREFIX}")
CMakeLists — Read the template file
CMakeLists — file(READ "${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/impl/scan/IVFInterleavedScanKernelTemplate.${GPU_EXT_PREFIX}" template_content)
CMakeLists — Replace the placeholders
CMakeLists — string(REPLACE "SUB_CODEC_TYPE" "${sub_codec}" template_content "${template_content}")
CMakeLists — string(REPLACE "SUB_METRIC_TYPE" "${metric_type}" template_content "${template_content}")
CMakeLists — string(REPLACE "SUB_THREADS" "${sub_threads}" template_content "${template_content}")
CMakeLists — string(REPLACE "SUB_NUM_WARP_Q" "${sub_num_warp_q}" template_content "${template_content}")
CMakeLists — string(REPLACE "SUB_NUM_THREAD_Q" "${sub_num_thread_q}" template_content "${template_content}")
CMakeLists — Write the modified content to the output file
CMakeLists — file(WRITE "${output_file}" "${template_content}")
CMakeLists — Add the file to the sources
CMakeLists — list(APPEND FAISS_GPU_SRC "${output_file}")
CMakeLists — endforeach()
CMakeLists — endforeach()
CMakeLists — endforeach()
CMakeLists — Propagate modified variable to the parent scope
CMakeLists — set(FAISS_GPU_SRC "${FAISS_GPU_SRC}" PARENT_SCOPE)
CMakeLists — endfunction()

CMakeLists — global 'public' functions that also exist in libcuvs.so
CMakeLists — This ensures that faiss functions will call the local version
CMakeLists — inside libfaiss.so . This is needed to ensure that things
CMakeLists — like raft cublas resources are created and used within the same
CMakeLists — dynamic library + CUDA runtime context which are requirements
CMakeLists — for valid execution
CMakeLists — To still allow these classes to be used by consumers, the
CMakeLists — respective classes/types in the headers are explicitly marked
CMakeLists — as 'public' so they can be used by consumers

README — Offline IVF
README — This folder contains the code for the offline ivf algorithm powered by faiss big batch search.
README — Create a conda env:
README — `conda create --name oivf python=3.10`
README — `conda activate oivf`
README — `conda install -c pytorch/label/nightly -c nvidia faiss-gpu=1.7.4`

README — Run book
README — Optionally shard your dataset (see create_sharded_dataset.py) and create the corresponding yaml file `config_ssnpp.yaml`. You can use `generate_config.py` by specifying the root directory of your dataset and the files with the data shards
README — `python generate_config`
README — Run the train index command
README — `python run.py --command train_index --config config_ssnpp.yaml --xb ssnpp_1B`
README — Run the index-shard command so it produces sharded indexes, required for the search step
README — `python run.py --command index_shard --config config_ssnpp.yaml --xb ssnpp_1B`
README — Send jobs to the cluster to run search
README — `python run.py --command search --config config_ssnpp.yaml --xb ssnpp_1B --cluster_run --partition <PARTITION-NAME>`
README — Remarks about the `search` command: it is assumed that the database vectors are the query vectors when performing the search step.
README — a. If the query vectors are different than the database vectors, it should be passed in the xq argument
README — b. A new dataset needs to be prepared (step 1) before passing it to the query vectors argument `–xq`
README — `python run.py --command search --config config_ssnpp.yaml --xb ssnpp_1B --xq <QUERIES_DATASET_NAME>`
README — We can always run the consistency-check for sanity checks!
README — `python run.py --command consistency_check--config config_ssnpp.yaml --xb ssnpp_1B`

README — Distributed on-disk index for 1T-scale datasets
README — This is code corresponding to the description in [Indexing 1T vectors](https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/wiki/Indexing-1T-vectors).
README — All the code is in python 3 (and not compatible with Python 2).
README — The current code uses the Deep1B dataset for demonstration purposes, but can scale to 1000x larger.
README — To run it, download the Deep1B dataset as explained [here](../#getting-deep1b), and edit paths to the dataset in the scripts.
README — The cluster commands are written for the Slurm batch scheduling system.
README — Hopefully, changing to another type of scheduler should be quite straightforward.
README — Distributed k-means
README — To cluster 500M vectors to 10M centroids, it is useful to have a distributed k-means implementation.
README — The distribution simply consists in splitting the training vectors across machines (servers) and have them do the assignment.
README — The master/client then synthesizes the results and updates the centroids.
README — The distributed k-means implementation here is based on 3 files:
README — [`distributed_kmeans.py`](distributed_kmeans.py) contains the k-means implementation.
README — The main loop of k-means is re-implemented in python but follows closely the Faiss C++ implementation, and should not be significantly less efficient.
README — It relies on a `DatasetAssign` object that does the assignment to centroids, which is the bulk of the computation.
README — The object can be a Faiss CPU index, a GPU index or a set of remote GPU or CPU indexes.
README — [`run_on_cluster.bash`](run_on_cluster.bash) contains the shell code to run the distributed k-means on a cluster.
README — The distributed k-means works with a Python install that contains faiss and scipy (for sparse matrices).
README — It clusters the training data of Deep1B, this can be changed easily to any file in fvecs, bvecs or npy format that contains the training set.
README — The training vectors may be too large to fit in RAM, but they are memory-mapped so that should not be a problem.
README — The file is also assumed to be accessible from all server machines with eg. a distributed file system.
README — Local tests
README — Edit `distributed_kmeans.py` to point `testdata` to your local copy of the dataset.
README — Then, 4 levels of sanity check can be run:
README — The output should look like [This gist](https://gist.github.com/mdouze/ffa01fe666a9325761266fe55ead72ad).
README — Distributed sanity check
README — To run the distributed k-means, `distributed_kmeans.py` has to be run both on the servers (`--server` option) and client sides (`--client` option).
README — Edit the top of `run_on_cluster.bash` to set the path of the data to cluster.
README — Sanity checks can be run with
README — The test `test_kmeans_2` simulates a distributed run on a single machine by starting one server process per GPU and connecting to the servers via the rpc protocol.
README — The output should look like [this gist](https://gist.github.com/mdouze/5b2dc69b74579ecff04e1686a277d32e).
README — Distributed run
README — The way the script can be distributed depends on the cluster's scheduling system.
README — Here we use Slurm, but it should be relatively easy to adapt to any scheduler that can allocate a set of machines and start the same executable on all of them.
README — The command
README — asks SLURM for 5 machines with 4 GPUs each with the `srun` command.
README — All 5 machines run the script with the `slurm_within_kmeans_server` option.
README — They determine the number of servers and their own server id via the `SLURM_NPROCS` and `SLURM_PROCID` environment variables.
README — All machines start `distributed_kmeans.py` in server mode for the slice of the dataset they are responsible for.
README — In addition, the machine #0 also starts the client.
README — The client knows who are the other servers via the variable `SLURM_JOB_NODELIST`.
README — It connects to all clients and performs the clustering.
README — The output should look like [this gist](https://gist.github.com/mdouze/8d25e89fb4af5093057cae0f917da6cd).
README — Run used for deep1B
README — For the real run, we run the clustering on 50M vectors to 1M centroids.
README — This is just a matter of using as many machines / GPUs as possible in setting the output centroids with the `--out filename` option.
README — Then run
README — The last lines of output read like:
README — This means that the total training time was 899s, of which 876s were used for computation.
README — However, the computation includes the I/O overhead to the assignment servers.
README — In this implementation, the overhead of transmitting the data is non-negligible and so is the centroid computation stage.
README — This is due to the inefficient Python implementation and the RPC protocol that is not optimized for broadcast / gather (like MPI).
README — However, it is a simple implementation that should run on most clusters.
README — Making the trained index
README — After the centroids are obtained, an empty trained index must be constructed.
README — This is done by:
README — applying a pre-processing stage (a random rotation) to balance the dimensions of the vectors. This can be done after clustering, the clusters are just rotated as well.
README — wrapping the centroids into a HNSW index to speed up the CPU-based assignment of vectors
README — training the 6-bit scalar quantizer used to encode the vectors
README — This is performed by the script [`make_trained_index.py`](make_trained_index.py).
README — Building the index by slices
README — We call the slices "vslices" as they are vertical slices of the big matrix, see explanation in the wiki section [Split across database partitions](https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/wiki/Indexing-1T-vectors#split-across-database-partitions).
README — The script [make_index_vslice.py](make_index_vslice.py) makes an index for a subset of the vectors of the input data and stores it as an independent index.
README — There are 200 slices of 5M vectors each for Deep1B.
README — It can be run in a brute-force parallel fashion, there is no constraint on ordering.
README — To run the script in parallel on a slurm cluster, use:
README — For a real dataset, the data would be read from a DBMS.
README — In that case, reading the data and indexing it in parallel is worthwhile because reading is very slow.
README — Splitting across inverted lists
README — The 200 slices need to be merged together.
README — This is done with the script [merge_to_ondisk.py](merge_to_ondisk.py), that memory maps the 200 vertical slice indexes, extracts a subset of the inverted lists and writes them to a contiguous horizontal slice.
README — We slice the inverted lists into 50 horizontal slices.
README — This is run with
README — Querying the index
README — At this point the index is ready.
README — The horizontal slices need to be loaded in the right order and combined into an index to be usable.
README — This is done in the [combined_index.py](combined_index.py) script.
README — It provides a `CombinedIndexDeep1B` object that contains an index object that can be searched.
README — To test, run:
README — The output should look like:
README — ie. searching is a lot slower than from RAM.
README — Distributed query
README — To reduce the bandwidth required from the machine that does the queries, it is possible to split the search across several search servers.
README — This way, only the effective results are returned to the main machine.
README — The search client and server are implemented in [`search_server.py`](search_server.py).
README — It can be used as a script to start a search server for `CombinedIndexDeep1B` or as a module to load the clients.
README — The search servers can be started with
README — (adjust to the number of servers that can be used).
README — Then an example of search client is [`distributed_query_demo.py`](distributed_query_demo.py).
README — It connects to the servers and assigns subsets of inverted lists to visit to each of them.
README — A typical output is [this gist](https://gist.github.com/mdouze/1585b9854a9a2437d71f2b2c3c05c7c5).
README — The number in MiB indicates the amount of data that is read from disk to perform the search.
README — In this case, the scale of the dataset is too small for the distributed search to have much impact, but on datasets > 10x larger, the difference becomes more significant.
README — Conclusion
README — This code contains the core components to make an index that scales up to 1T vectors.
README — There are a few simplifications wrt. the index that was effectively used in [Indexing 1T vectors](https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/wiki/Indexing-1T-vectors).
README — Benchmark of IVF variants
README — This is a benchmark of IVF index variants, looking at compression vs. speed vs. accuracy.
README — The results are in [this wiki chapter](https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/wiki/Indexing-1G-vectors)
README — The code is organized as:
README — `datasets.py`: code to access the datafiles, compute the ground-truth and report accuracies
README — `bench_all_ivf.py`: evaluate one type of inverted file
README — `run_on_cluster_generic.bash`: call `bench_all_ivf.py` for all tested types of indices.
README — Since the number of experiments is quite large the script is structured so that the benchmark can be run on a cluster.
README — `parse_bench_all_ivf.py`: make nice tradeoff plots from all the results.
README — The code depends on Faiss and can use 1 to 8 GPUs to do the k-means clustering for large vocabularies.
README — It was run in October 2018 for the results in the wiki.
README — README for the link & code implementation
README — =========================================
README — What is this?
README — Link & code is an indexing method that combines HNSW indexing with
README — compression and exploits the neighborhood structure of the similarity
README — graph to improve the reconstruction. It is described in
README — ArXiV [here](https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.09996)
README — The necessary code for this paper was removed from Faiss in version 1.8.0.
README — For a functioning verinsion, use Faiss 1.7.4.

README — Building Milvus with Docker
README — Building Milvus is easy if you take advantage of the containerized build environment. This document will guide you through this build process.
README — Docker, using one of the following configurations:
README — macOS** Install Docker for Mac. See installation instructions [here](https://docs.docker.com/docker-for-mac/).
README — Note**: You will want to set the Docker VM to have at least 2 vCPU and 8GB of initial memory or building will likely fail.
README — Linux with local Docker** Install Docker according to the [instructions](https://docs.docker.com/installation/#installation) for your OS.
README — Windows with Docker Desktop WSL2 backend** Install Docker according to the [instructions](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/windows/wsl/). Be sure to store your sources in the local Linux file system, not the Windows remote mount at `/mnt/c`.
README — Optional** [Google Cloud SDK](https://developers.google.com/cloud/sdk/)
README — You must install and configure Google Cloud SDK if you want to upload your release to Google Cloud Storage and may safely omit this otherwise.
README — Overview
README — While it is possible to build Milvus using a local golang installation, we have a build process that runs in a Docker container. This simplifies initial set up and provides a very consistent build and test environment.
README — Before You Begin
README — Before building Milvus, you must check the eligibility of Docker, Docker Compose, and hardware in line with Milvus' requirements.
README — <details><summary>Check Docker and Docker Compose version</summary>
README — <li>Docker version 19.03 or higher is required. </li>
README — <div class="alert note">
README — Follow <a href="https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/">Get Docker</a> to install Docker on your system.
README — <li>Docker Compose version 1.25.1 or higher is required. </li>
README — <div class="alert note">
README — See <a href="https://docs.docker.com/compose/install/">Install Docker Compose</a> for Docker Compose installation guide.
README — </details>
README — <details><summary>Check whether your CPU supports SIMD extension instruction set</summary>
README — Milvus' computing operations depend on CPU’s support for SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) extension instruction set. Whether your CPU supports SIMD extension instruction set is crucial to index building and vector similarity search within Milvus. Ensure that your CPU supports at least one of the following SIMD instruction sets:
README — Run the lscpu command to check if your CPU supports the SIMD instruction sets mentioned above:
README — Check Wikipedia [CPU with AVX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Vector_Extensions#CPUs_with_AVX) for more details.

README — [`build/builder.sh`](builder.sh): Run a command in a build docker container. Common invocations are:
README — `build/builder.sh make`: Build just linux binary in the container. Pass options and packages as necessary.
README — `build/builder.sh make verifiers`: Run all pre-submission verification check.
README — `build/builder.sh make unittest`: Run all unit tests.
README — `build/builder.sh make clean`: Clean up all the generated files.

README — Basic Flow
README — The scripts under [`build/`](.) are used to build and test. They will ensure that the `builder` Docker image is built (based on [`build/docker/builder`] ) and then execute the appropriate command in that container. These scripts will both ensure that the right data is cached from run to run for incremental builds and will copy the results back out of the container. You can specify a different registry/name for `builder` by setting `IMAGE_REPO` which defaults to `milvusdb`.
README — The `builder.sh` is executed by first creating a “docker volume“ directory in `.docker/`. The `.docker/` directory is used to cache the third-party package and compiler cache data. It speeds up recompilation by caching previous compilations and detecting when the same compilation is being done again.

README — Integrate with VS Code
README — The working principle is as follows: mount the local file system to the workspace inside the container, or copy it to the container. The extension of vs code is installed inside the container and runs in it, so that the vs Code of the host can fully access the tools, platforms and file systems inside the container. This means that you just need to connect to different containers to switch the entire development environment seamlessly.
README — ![image](../docs/imgs/vscode.png)
README — Taking the Milvus project as an example, there is a file named **.devcontainer.json** in the root directory of the project. This file describes how vs code accesses (or creates) a development container environment, and defines the container environment, working directory, extension tool set, etc.
README — The steps to configure the development environment are as follows:
README — Start VS Code，in the command panel ( F1 ) input **“Remote-Containers: Open Folder in Container”** , then select the project folder which contains devcontainer.json file.
README — or click right-bottom corner button > < , choose **“Remote-Containers: Open Folder in Container”**，then select the project folder which contains devcontainer.json file.
README — ![image](../docs/imgs/remote.png)
README — VS Code begin load and construct Devcontainer, the progress bar display the construction state.
README — ![image](../docs/imgs/bar.png)
README — After Construction, VS Code automatically connects to the container. Now you can code and debug in VS Code, just like developing in your host machine.
README — You can also use terminal of VS Code to enter the Dev container to do something. Choose **Terminal >> New Terminal** in the navigation bar, then you can enter the container:
README — ![image](../docs/imgs/terminal.png)
README — Modify vscode go setups if necessary, the setting path is **code -> preference -> settings**
README — ![image](../docs/imgs/settings.png)

README — Overview
README — Milvus 2.2 has changed the meta structure for segment index. To upgrade a Milvus cluster of 2.1.x version you have installed, run this script to migrate the meta and upgrade the Milvus image version.
README — This script only applies to Milvus installed on a K8s cluster which has storageclass.
README — You can verify storageclass by running `kubectl get storageclass`. If you don't have a
README — default storageclass, you need specify a storageclass via `-c <storage-class>` when running
README — this script.
README — This script only supports upgrading from Milvus v2.1.x to v2.2.0.
README — If your milvus cluster use an external etcd service (which isn't installed with milvus),
README — you need specify etcd service explicitly via `-e <etcd-service-ip:etcd-service-port>` otherwise
README — we use the default etcd service which installed with milvus.
README — Parameters
README — | Parameters | Description | Default value | Required |
README — | ------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------| -------------------------------- | ----------------------- |
README — | `i` | The Milvus instance name. | `None` | True |
README — | `n` | The namespace that Milvus is installed in. | `default` | False |
README — | `s` | The source Milvus version. | `None` | True |
README — | `t` | The target Milvus version. | `None` | True |
README — | `r` | The root path of Milvus meta. | `by-dev` | False |
README — | `w` | The new Milvus image tag. | `milvusdb/milvus:v2.2.0` | False |
README — | `m` | The meta migration image tag. | `milvusdb/meta-migration:v2.2.0-bugfix-20220112` | False |
README — | `o` | The meta migration operation. | `migrate` | False |
README — | `d` | Whether to cleanup after migration is completed. | `false` | False |
README — | `c` | The storage class for meta migration pvc. | `default storage class` | False |
README — | `e` | The endpoints for etcd which used by milvus. | `etcd svc installed with milvus` | False |
README — By default, the script only applies to migration from v2.1.x to v2.2.x. Rollback to the older version with the `rollback` operation first if an error occurs.
README — Overview of migration procedures
README — Stop the Milvus components. Any live session in the Milvus Etcd can cause the migration to fail.
README — Create a backup for Milvus meta.
README — Migrate the Milvus meta.
README — Start Milvus components with a new image.
README — Migration guide
README — Specify Milvus instance name, source Milvus version, and target Milvus version.
README — Specify namespace with `-n` if your Milvus is not installed in the default K8s namespace.
README — Specify rootpath with `-r` if your Milvus is installed with the custom `rootpath`.
README — Specify the image tag with `-w` if your Milvus is installed with custom `image`.
README — Set `-d true` if you want to automatically remove the migration pod after the migration is completed.
README — Rollback and migrate again if the migration fails.
README — Specify the storage class explicitly.

README — Milvus 2.2.3 supports rolling update. This script helps you to perform a rolling update with zero downtime.
README — Milvus version must be after 2.2.0.
README — This script only applies to update Milvus installed with Helm and does not apply to Milvus installed with Milvus Operator.
README — This script only supports update operation now.
README — Rolling update is **not supported** in Milvus standalone with **RocksMQ**.

README — Check all deployments of the Milvus instance. Make sure no deployment is blocked.
README — Update the deployments one by one. The update order is hard-coded for now.
README — Specify the namespace, Milvus instance name, target Milvus version, and target image in the script.
README — Run the script. The following script updates Milvus to 2.2.3.
README — This script update the deployment by `kubectl patch` and watch the deployment's status by `kubectl rollout status`.
README — The `target version` is the deployment's label `app.kubernetes.io/version` and is updated by `kubectl patch`.

README — Milvus Metrics Dashboard
README — Milvus outputs a list of detailed time-series metrics during runtime. You can use [Prometheus](https://prometheus.io/) and [Grafana](https://grafana.com/) to visualize the metrics. This topic introduces the monitoring metrics displayed in the Grafana Milvus Dashboard.
README — We recommend reading [Milvus monitoring framework overview](monitor_overview.md) to understand Prometheus metrics first.
README — The time unit in this topic is millisecond.
README — And "99th percentile" in this topic refers to the fact that 99 percent of the time statistics are controlled within certain value.
README — <details><summary>Proxy</summary>
README — | Panel | Panel description | PromQL (Prometheus query language) | The Milvus metrics used | Milvus metrics description |
README — |---|---|---|---|---|
README — | Search Vector Count Rate | The average number of vectors queried per second by each proxy within the past two minutes. | ``` sum(increase(milvus_proxy_search_vectors_count{app_kubernetes_io_instance=~"$instance", app_kubernetes_io_name="$app_name", namespace="$namespace"}[2m])/120) by (pod, node_id) ``` | `milvus_proxy_search_vectors_count` | The accumulated number of vectors queried. |
README — | Insert Vector Count Rate | The average number of vectors inserted per second by each proxy within the past two minutes. | ``` sum(increase(milvus_proxy_insert_vectors_count{app_kubernetes_io_instance=~"$instance", app_kubernetes_io_name="$app_name", namespace="$namespace"}[2m])/120) by (pod, node_id) ``` | `milvus_proxy_insert_vectors_count` | The accumulated number of vectors inserted. |
README — | Search Latency | The average latency and the 99th percentile of the latency of receiving search and query requests by each proxy within the past two minutes. | p99: <br/> ``` histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, query_type, pod, node_id) (rate(milvus_proxy_sq_latency_bucket{app_kubernetes_io_instance=~"$instance", app_kubernetes_io_name="$app_name", namespace="$namespace"}[2m]))) ``` <br/> avg: <br/> ``` sum(increase(milvus_proxy_sq_latency_sum{app_kubernetes_io_instance=~"$instance", app_kubernetes_io_name="$app_name", namespace="$namespace"}[2m])) by (pod, node_id, query_type) / sum(increase(milvus_proxy_sq_latency_count{app_kubernetes_io_instance=~"$instance", app_kubernetes_io_name="$app_name", namespace="$namespace"}[2m])) by (pod, node_id, query_type) ``` | `milvus_proxy_sq_latency` | The latency of search and query requests. |
README — | Wait Search Result Latency | The average latency and the 99th percentile of the latency between sending search and query requests and receiving results by proxy within the past two minutes. | p99: <br/> ``` histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, query_type, pod, node_id) (rate(milvus_proxy_sq_wait_result_latency_bucket{app_kubernetes_io_instance=~"$instance", app_kubernetes_io_name="$app_name", namespace="$namespace"}[2m]))) ``` <br/> avg: <br/> ``` sum(increase(milvus_proxy_sq_wait_result_latency_sum{app_kubernetes_io_instance=~"$instance", app_kubernetes_io_name="$app_name", namespace="$namespace"}[2m])) by (pod, node_id, query_type) / sum(increase(milvus_proxy_sq_wait_result_latency_count{app_kubernetes_io_instance=~"$instance", app_kubernetes_io_name="$app_name", namespace="$namespace"}[2m])) by (pod, node_id, query_type) ``` | `milvus_proxy_sq_wait_result_latency` | The latency between sending search and query requests and receiving results. |

proxy-reduce — How Proxy Reduces the Multiple Search Results?
proxy-reduce — Search Results Organized format
proxy-reduce — For a specified Search request, with nq = 2 and topk = 10, Proxy receives 4 search results from query nodes.
proxy-reduce — Each Search Result is nq * topk two-dimensional structure, as the illustration below. The result indicates that the user input nq vectors and wanted to obtain the topk similar vectors to these nq vectors respectively.
proxy-reduce — ![search_result_format](./figs/nq_topk_search_results.png)
proxy-reduce — For each query, the topk hit results are in descending order of score. The larger the score, the more similar the hit result is to the vector to be queried. The hit results of different queries are independent of each other.
proxy-reduce — Therefore, we will only discuss how Proxy merges the results for one query result. For nq query results, we can loop through nq or process them in parallel.
proxy-reduce — So the problem degenerates to how to get the maximum number of 10 (topk) results from these four sorted arrays. As shown in the figure below:
proxy-reduce — ![final_result](./figs/reduce_results.png)
proxy-reduce — K-Way Merge Algorithm
proxy-reduce — The pseudocode of this algorithm is shown below:
proxy-reduce — This algorithm is originated from the merging phase of merge sort. The common point of the two is that the results have been sorted when merging, and the difference is that merge sort merges two-way results, proxy reduces merges multiple results.
proxy-reduce — In contrast, in merge sort, two pointers are used to record the offsets of the two-way results, and proxy reduces uses multiple pointers `locs` to record the offsets of the `k-way` results.
proxy-reduce — In our specific situation, n indicates that there are 4 results to be merged, `multiple_results` is an array of four `topk`, and each `choiceOffset` in `locs` records the offset of each way being merged.
proxy-reduce — The `score_this_way` corresponding to this offset records the maximum value of the current way, so when you take a larger `score`, you only need to pick one of the four maximum values.
proxy-reduce — This ensures that the result we take each time is the largest among the remaining results.
proxy-reduce — This algorithm will scan all Search Results linearly at most, hence the time complexity of this algorithm is n \* topk.
how-guarantee-ts-works — Guarantee Timestamp in Search Requests
how-guarantee-ts-works — [中文文档](./how-guarantee-ts-works-cn.md)
how-guarantee-ts-works — Users and developers may feel confused by so many parameters in the search requests, especially for those developers
how-guarantee-ts-works — who develop the SDK client for Milvus.
how-guarantee-ts-works — This document will explain a special parameter in the search request-"Guarantee Timestamp", hereinafter referred to as
how-guarantee-ts-works — "GuaranteeTs".
how-guarantee-ts-works — Milvus Clock Mechanism
how-guarantee-ts-works — Like most distributed systems, Milvus will assign a timestamp to each record that enters the system.
how-guarantee-ts-works — At the same time, Milvus is a system that separates storage and computing.
how-guarantee-ts-works — The DataNodes handle the data persistence load, and the data will eventually be flushed to MinIO/S3 or other distributed
how-guarantee-ts-works — object storage.
how-guarantee-ts-works — QueryNodes handle the computing(read) requests. The reading link will process two types of data at the same time--batch
how-guarantee-ts-works — data and streaming data.
how-guarantee-ts-works — Among them, the batch data will no longer be changed, and the search request will see all the data in the batch data.
how-guarantee-ts-works — QueryNodes and DataNodes consume user insert requests through the same subscription mechanism, which constitute the
how-guarantee-ts-works — streaming data.
how-guarantee-ts-works — Due to the network delays, QueryNodes often do not hold all the latest streaming data. Without other control mechanisms,
how-guarantee-ts-works — some unconsumed data will be invisible and thus reduce the query accuracy. At this time, let's introduce the
how-guarantee-ts-works — "GuaranteeTs".
how-guarantee-ts-works — Milvus uses timestamp and timetick watermark to ensure the consistency of the read link.
how-guarantee-ts-works — As shown in the figure below, when inserting data into the message queue, Milvus will not only time stamp these inserted
how-guarantee-ts-works — records, but also insert timetick continuously. Taking "syncTs1" in the figure as an example, when downstream consumers
how-guarantee-ts-works — (such as QueryNodes) see syncTs1, it means that all the data which is earlier than syncTs1 has been consumed. In
how-guarantee-ts-works — other words, the inserted record with a timestamp smaller than syncTs1 will no longer appear in the message queue.
how-guarantee-ts-works — ![ts-watermask](./figs/guarantee-ts-ts-mask.png)
how-guarantee-ts-works — Guarantee Timestamp
how-guarantee-ts-works — As mentioned above, QueryNodes will continue to get insert records and timetick from the message queue. Every time a
how-guarantee-ts-works — timetick is consumed, QueryNodes will update this timetick as the serviceable time-"ServiceTime". With the above figure,
how-guarantee-ts-works — it is easy to understand that QueryNodes can see all the data before ServiceTime.
how-guarantee-ts-works — With ServiceTime, Milvus provides GuaranteeTs according to the needs of different users for consistency and
how-guarantee-ts-works — availability. Users can specify GuaranteeTs to inform QueryNodes that the search request must see all the data before
how-guarantee-ts-works — GuaranteeTs.
how-guarantee-ts-works — As shown in the figure below, if GuaranteeTs is less than ServiceTime, QueryNodes can execute search request
how-guarantee-ts-works — immediately.
how-guarantee-ts-works — ![do-search-right-now](./figs/guarantee-ts-do-search-right-now.png)
how-guarantee-ts-works — If GuaranteeTs is greater than ServiceTime, QueryNodes must continue to consume timetick from the message queue. Search
how-guarantee-ts-works — request cannot be executed until ServiceTime is greater than GuaranteeTs.
how-guarantee-ts-works — ![wait-for-service-time](./figs/guarantee-ts-wait-for-service-time.png)
how-guarantee-ts-works — If users want to obtain high query accuracy, have higher requirements for consistency, and are not sensitive to query
how-guarantee-ts-works — delay, then GuaranteeTs should be set to the latest wall clock; on the contrary, if users have higher requirements for
how-guarantee-ts-works — availability, in other words, if they want to get the search results as soon as possible, then GuaranteeTs may not be
how-guarantee-ts-works — set very large.
how-guarantee-ts-works — As shown in the figure below, different GuaranteeTs correspond to four different consistency levels:
how-guarantee-ts-works — ![relationship-between-consistency-and-guaranteeTs](./figs/guarantee-ts-consistency-relationship.png)
how-guarantee-ts-works — Strong consistency: GuaranteeTs is set to the newest timestamp of the system, QueryNodes will wait for the ServiceTime
how-guarantee-ts-works — to be greater than or equal to the GuaranteeTs;
how-guarantee-ts-works — Eventual consistency: Set GuaranteeTs to a very small value (for example 1) and skip the check, QueryNodes will
how-guarantee-ts-works — execute search requests immediately;
how-guarantee-ts-works — Bounded Staleness: Set GuaranteeTs to an older timestamp, such as 1 minute ago, the query can be executed immediately
how-guarantee-ts-works — within a tolerable range;
how-guarantee-ts-works — Read your own write (Session): Set GuaranteeTs to the client last write, in this way, every client will see all their
how-guarantee-ts-works — own data.
how-guarantee-ts-works — Milvus provides bounded staleness consistency by default.
chap08 binlog — InsertBinlog、DeleteBinlog、DDLBinlog
chap08 binlog — Binlog is stored in a columnar storage format, every column in schema is stored in an individual file.
chap08 binlog — Timestamp, schema, row id and primary key allocated by system are four special columns.
chap08 binlog — Schema column records the DDL of the collection.
chap08 binlog — Event format
chap08 binlog — Binlog file consists of 4 bytes magic number and a series of events. The first event must be a descriptor event.
chap08 binlog — Event format
chap08 binlog — Descriptor Event format
chap08 binlog — `ExtraBytes` is in json format.
chap08 binlog — `ExtraBytes` stores the extra information of the binlog file.
chap08 binlog — In binlog file, we have stored many common fields in fixed part, such as `CollectionID`, `PartitionID` and etc.
chap08 binlog — However, different binlog files have some other different information which differs from each other.
chap08 binlog — So, `ExtraBytes` was designed to store this different information.
chap08 binlog — For example, for index binlog file, we will store `indexID`, `indexBuildID`, `indexID` and other index-related
chap08 binlog — information to `ExtraBytes`.
chap08 binlog — In addition, `ExtraBytes` was also designed to extend binlog. Then we can add new features to binlog file without
chap08 binlog — breaking the compatibility.
chap08 binlog — For example, we can store the memory size of original content(before encoding) to `ExtraBytes`.
chap08 binlog — The key in `ExtraBytes` is `original_size`. For now, `original_size` is required, not optional.
chap08 binlog — Type code
chap08 binlog — DESCRIPTOR_EVENT must appear in all column files and always be the first event.
chap08 binlog — INSERT_EVENT may appear in any column binlog except DDL binlog files.
chap08 binlog — DELETE_EVENT can only be used in primary key's binlog files（currently we can only delete by primary key).
chap08 binlog — CREATE_COLLECTION_EVENT、DROP_COLLECTION_EVENT、CREATE_PARTITION_EVENT、DROP_PARTITION_EVENT only appears in DDL binlog files.
chap08 binlog — Event data part
chap08 binlog — ​ string | int | float(optional) | vector(512)
chap08 binlog — Request:
chap08 binlog — ​ InsertRequest rows(1W)
chap08 binlog — ​ DeleteRequest pk=1
chap08 binlog — ​ DropPartition partitionTag="abc"
chap08 binlog — insert binlogs:
chap08 binlog — ​ rowid, pk, ts, string, int, float, vector 6 files
chap08 binlog — ​ all events are INSERT_EVENT
chap08 binlog — ​ float column file contains some NULL value
chap08 binlog — delete binlogs:
chap08 binlog — ​ pk, ts 2 files
chap08 binlog — ​ pk's events are DELETE_EVENT, ts's events are INSERT_EVENT
chap08 binlog — DDL binlogs:
chap08 binlog — ​ ddl, ts
chap08 binlog — ​ ddl's event is DROP_PARTITION_EVENT, ts's event is INSERT_EVENT
chap08 binlog — C++ interface
appendix b api reference — Appendix B. API Reference
appendix b api reference — In this section, we introduce the RPCs of milvus service. A brief description of the RPCs is listed as follows.
appendix b api reference — | RPC | description |
appendix b api reference — | :---------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
appendix b api reference — | CreateCollection | create a collection based on schema statement |
appendix b api reference — | DropCollection | drop a collection |
appendix b api reference — | HasCollection | check whether a collection exists |
appendix b api reference — | LoadCollection | load collection to memory for future search |
appendix b api reference — | ReleaseCollection | release the collection from memory |
appendix b api reference — | DescribeCollection | show a collection's schema and its descriptive statistics |
appendix b api reference — | GetCollectionStatistics | show a collection's statistics |
appendix b api reference — | ShowCollections | list all collections |
appendix b api reference — | CreatePartition | create a partition |
appendix b api reference — | DropPartition | drop a partition |
appendix b api reference — | HasPartition | check whether a partition exists |

appendix b api reference — | ReleasePartitions | release partitions from memory |
appendix b api reference — | GetPartitionStatistics | show a partition's statistics |
appendix b api reference — | ShowPartitions | list a collection's all partitions |
appendix b api reference — | CreateIndex | create an index for a field in the collection |
appendix b api reference — | DescribeIndex | get index details for a field in the collection |
appendix b api reference — | GetIndexStates | get build index state |
appendix b api reference — | DropIndex | drop a specific index for a field in the collection |
appendix b api reference — | Insert | insert a batch of rows into a collection or a partition |
appendix b api reference — | Search | query the columns of a collection or a partition with ANNS statements and boolean expressions |
appendix b api reference — | Flush | Perform persistent storage of data in memory |
appendix b api reference — MsgBase** is a base struct in each request.
appendix b api reference — MsgType** is the enum to distinguish different message types in message queue, such as insert msg, search msg, etc. **msgID** is the unique id identifier of message. **timestamp** is the time when this message was generated. **sourceID** is the unique id identifier of the source.
appendix b api reference — Definition Requests
appendix b api reference — CreateCollection
appendix b api reference — Interface:**
appendix b api reference — Description:**
appendix b api reference — Create a collection through CreateCollectionRequest.
appendix b api reference — Parameters:**
appendix b api reference — CreateCollectionRequest**
appendix b api reference — CreateCollectionRequest struct is shown as follows:
appendix b api reference — CreateCollectionRequest contains **MsgBase**, **db_name**, **collection_name** and serialized collection schema **schema**. **db_name** contains only a string named **collection_name**. Collection with the same collection_name is going to be created.
appendix b api reference — Collection schema contains all the base information of a collection including **collection name**, **description**, **autoID** and **fields**. Collection description is defined by the database manager to describe the collection. **autoID** determines whether the ID of each row of data is user-defined. If **autoID** is true, our system will generate a unique ID for each data. If **autoID** is false, users need to give each entity an ID when inserting.
appendix b api reference — Fields** is a list of **FieldSchema**. Each schema should include Field **name**, **description**, **dataType**, **type_params** and **index_params**.
appendix b api reference — FieldSchema struct is shown as follows:
appendix b api reference — Field schema** contains all the base information of a field including **fieldID**, **name**, **description**, **data_type**, **type_params** and **index_params**. **data_type** is an enum type to distinguish different data types. Total enum is shown in the last of this doc

appendix c system configurations — Milvus 能够通过配置文件、命令行选项、环境变量进行配置。
appendix c system configurations — 优先级顺序： 命令行选项 > 环境变量 > 配置文件 > 默认值
appendix c system configurations — 如果提供了配置文件，则其他的命令行选项和环境变量都将被忽略。
appendix c system configurations — 例如： `milvus run rootcoord --config-file milvus.yaml --log-level debug` 将忽略 `--log-level` 选项。
appendix c system configurations — 在控制台中使用以下语法运行 `milvus` 命令：
appendix c system configurations — `command`， `server type`， `flags` 分别表示为
appendix c system configurations — `command`： 指定要在程序上执行的操作。例如： `run`，`stop`
appendix c system configurations — `server type`：指定执行程序的类型。`server type` 有：
appendix c system configurations — `rootcoord`
appendix c system configurations — `querycoord`
appendix c system configurations — `querynode`
appendix c system configurations — `datacoord`
appendix c system configurations — `datanode`
appendix c system configurations — `indexcoord`
appendix c system configurations — `indexnode`
appendix c system configurations — `standalone`
appendix c system configurations — `mixture`
appendix c system configurations — `flags`：指定命令行选项。例如，你可以使用 `-f` 或者 `--config-file` 选项去指定配置文件路径。
appendix c system configurations — 当 `server type` 为 `mixture` 时，必须附加以下几个 `flag` 中的一个或多个，表示这几个服务在一个进程内启动
appendix c system configurations — `-rootcoord`
appendix c system configurations — `-querycoord`

proxy-reduce-cn — How Proxy Reduce the Multiple Search Results?
proxy-reduce-cn — Search Results 的组织形式
proxy-reduce-cn — 假设对于某个特定的 Search 请求，该 Search 请求 nq = 2，topk = 10，Proxy 收到来自 Query Nodes 的 4 份 Search Result。
proxy-reduce-cn — 每一份 Search Result 都是 nq \* topk 的二维结构，如下图所示，该结果表示用户输入了 nq 个向量，希望分别获取和这 nq 个向量最相似的 topk 个向量。
proxy-reduce-cn — ![search_result_format](./figs/nq_topk_search_results.png)
proxy-reduce-cn — 对于同一个 query，topk 个命中结果按照 score 降序，score 越大，表示命中结果与待查向量越相似。不同 query 之间命中结果互相独立。
proxy-reduce-cn — 因此我们下面讨论 Proxy 如何对结果进行归并也只关注一个 query 结果如何归并即可，对 nq 个 query 结果，循环遍历 nq 或者并行处理即可。
proxy-reduce-cn — 于是问题退化为，4 个长度为 topk(10) 的数组，每个数组降序排列，如何从这 4 个数组中得到其中最大的 10(topk) 个数。如下图所示：
proxy-reduce-cn — ![final_result](./figs/reduce_results.png)
proxy-reduce-cn — 该算法的伪代码如下：
proxy-reduce-cn — 该算法脱胎于归并排序算法的归并阶段，两者共同点是归并时结果已经排序，不同点是归并排序是归并两路结果，reduce 这里归并多路结果。
proxy-reduce-cn — 对比归并排序时使用两个指针记录两路结果的偏移量，proxy reduce 使用多个指针 locs 记录多路结果的偏移量。
proxy-reduce-cn — 具体到该例子，n 表示有 4 份结果需要归并，multiple_results 是四份 topk 的数组，locs 里面每一个 choiceOffset 记录了每一路的偏移量。
proxy-reduce-cn — 该偏移量对应的 score_this_way 记录了当前这一路的最大值，因此取下一个较大的 score 时只需要从这四个最大值里面挑一个即可。
proxy-reduce-cn — 这样子保证了我们每次取的结果都是剩余结果中最大的。
proxy-reduce-cn — 该算法最多只会线性扫描所有的 Search Results，因此该算法的时间复杂度为 n \* topk。
