how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — Guarantee Timestamp in Search Requests
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — [English Version of This Doc](./how-guarantee-ts-works.md)
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — 很多同学接触 Milvus 时都会对 Search 请求里面茫茫多的参数感到迷惑不解，尤其是为 Milvus 开
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — 发 sdk 客户端的同学。这个文档就会介绍 Search 请求里面一个比较特殊的参数——“Guarantee
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — Timestamp”，以下简称 “GuaranteeTs”。
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — Milvus 时钟机制
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — 像大多数分布式系统一样，Milvus 会为每一条进入系统的记录分配一个时间戳。与此同时，Milvus
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — 是一个存储计算分离的系统，数据持久化负载由 DataNodes 承担，最终会落盘到 MinIO/S3 之类的
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — 分布式对象存储中。Search 之类的计算任务由 QueryNodes 承担，计算链路会同时处理两类数据——
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — 批式数据以及流式数据。其中，批式数据不会再被更改，Search 请求会看到批式数据里面的所有数据。
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — QueryNodes 和 DataNodes 通过同一个订阅机制消费用户的插入请求，这些构成了流式数据。由于
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — 存在网络延迟，QueryNodes 往往不会持有最新的流式数据。如果没有其他保障，在流式数据上直接做
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — Search 会损失许多未消费的数据，降低查询精度，这个时候 GuaranteeTs 就派上用场了。
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — Milvus 通过时间戳水印来保障读链路的一致性，如下图所示，在往消息队列插入数据时，
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — Milvus 不光会为这些插入记录打上时间戳，还会不间断地插入同步时间戳，以图中同步时间戳
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — syncTs1 为例，当下游消费者（比如QueryNodes）看到 syncTs1，那么意味着 syncTs1 以前的
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — 数据已经全部被消费了，换句话说，比 syncTs1 时间戳还小的插入记录不会再出现在消息队列中。
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — 当然了，有的话，那肯定是系统有 bug，如果你发现了，还希望尽快告诉我们。
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — ![ts-watermask](./figs/guarantee-ts-ts-mask.png)
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — Guarantee Timestamp
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — 上面说了，QueryNodes 会不断从消息队列里面拿到插入记录以及同步时间戳，每消费到一个同步时间
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — 戳，QueryNodes 会把这个时间戳称为可服务时间——“ServiceTime”，有了上图，ServiceTime
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — 实际上就很好理解了，意味着 QueryNodes 能够看到 ServiceTime 以前所有的数据了。
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — 有了这个 ServiceTime，Milvus 根据不同用户对一致性以及可用性的需求，提供了 GuaranteeTs，
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — 用户可以指定 GuaranteeTs 告知 QueryNodes 我这次 Search 请求必须看到 GuaranteeTs 以前
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — 如下图所示，如果 GuaranteeTs 小于 ServiceTime，QueryNodes 可以立刻执行 Search 查询。
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — ![do-search-right-now](./figs/guarantee-ts-do-search-right-now.png)
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — 如果 GuaranteeTs 大于 ServiceTime，QueryNodes 必须从消息队列里持续消费同步时间戳，
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — 直到 ServiceTime 大于 GuaranteeTs 才能执行 Search 查询。
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — ![wait-for-service-time](./figs/guarantee-ts-wait-for-service-time.png)
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — 如果用户希望得到足够高的查询精度，对一致性有较高的要求，对查询时延不敏感，那么 GuaranteeTs
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — 应该尽可能大；反之，如果用户希望尽快得到搜索结果，对可用性有较高的要求，对查询精度有较高的
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — 容忍程度，那么 GuaranteeTs 可以不必特别大。
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — 如下图所示，不同的 GuaranteeTs 分别对应四种不同的一致性：
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — ![relationship-between-consistency-and-guaranteeTs](./figs/guarantee-ts-consistency-relationship.png)
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — 强一致性：GuaranteeTs 设为系统最新时间戳，QueryNodes 需要等待 ServiceTime 推进到
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — 当前最新时间戳才能执行该 Search 请求；
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — 最终一致性：GuaranteeTs 设为一个特别小的值（比如说设为 1），跳过一致性检查，立刻在当
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — 前已有数据上执行 Search 查询；
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — 有界一致性：GuaranteeTs 是一个比系统最新时间稍旧的时间，在可容忍范围内可以立刻执行查询；
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — 客户端一致性：客户端使用上一次写入的时间戳作为 GuaranteeTs，那么每个客户端至少能看到
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — 自己插入的全部数据。
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — Milvus 默认提供有界一致性，如果用户不传入 GuaranteeTs，那么会将 GuaranteeTs 设为系统
how-guarantee-ts-works-cn — 当前的最新时间戳。

chap02 schema — Different index types use different index params in construction and query. All index params are represented by the structure of the map. This doc shows the map code in python.

chap02 schema — IVF_FLAT
chap02 schema — IVF** (_Inverted File_) is an index type based on quantization. It divides the points in space into `nlist` units by the clustering method. During searching vectors, it compares the distance between the target vector and the center of all units, and then selects the `nprobe` nearest unit. Afterwards, it compares all the vectors in these selected cells to get the final result.
chap02 schema — IVF_FLAT is the most basic IVF index, and the encoded data stored in each unit is consistent with the original data.
chap02 schema — building parameters:
chap02 schema — nlist**: Number of cluster units.
chap02 schema — search parameters:
chap02 schema — nprobe**: Number of inverted file cells to probe.
chap02 schema — BIN_IVF_FLAT
chap02 schema — BIN_IVF_FLAT** is a binary variant of IVF_FLAT.
chap02 schema — building parameters:
chap02 schema — nlist**: Number of cluster units.
chap02 schema — search parameters:
chap02 schema — nprobe**: Number of inverted file cells to probe.
chap02 schema — PQ** (_Product Quantization_) uniformly decomposes the original high-dimensional vector space into Cartesian products of `m` low-dimensional vector spaces and then quantizes the decomposed low-dimensional vector spaces. Instead of calculating the distances between the target vector and the center of all the units, product quantization enables the calculation of distances between the target vector and the clustering center of each low-dimensional space and greatly reduces the time complexity and space complexity of the algorithm.
chap02 schema — IVF_PQ performs IVF index clustering, and then quantizes the product of vectors. Its index file is even smaller than IVF_SQ8, but it also causes a loss of accuracy during searching.
chap02 schema — building parameters:
chap02 schema — nlist**: Number of cluster units.
chap02 schema — m**: Number of factors of product quantization. **CPU-only** Milvus: `m ≡ dim (mod m)`; **GPU-enabled** Milvus: `m` ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32, 40, 48, 56, 64, 96}, and (dim / m) ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32}. (`m` x 1024) ≥ `MaxSharedMemPerBlock` of your graphics card.
chap02 schema — search parameters:
chap02 schema — nprobe**: Number of inverted file cells to probe.
chap02 schema — IVF_SQ8** does scalar quantization for each vector placed in the unit based on IVF. Scalar quantization converts each dimension of the original vector from a 4-byte floating-point number to a 1-byte unsigned integer, so the IVF_SQ8 index file occupies much less space than the IVF_FLAT index file. However, scalar quantization results in a loss of accuracy during searching vectors.
chap02 schema — building parameters:
chap02 schema — nlist**: Number of cluster units.
chap02 schema — search parameters:
chap02 schema — nprobe**: Number of inverted file cells to probe.
chap02 schema — IVF_SQ8_HYBRID
chap02 schema — An optimized version of IVF_SQ8 that requires both CPU and GPU to work. Unlike IVF_SQ8, IVF_SQ8H uses a GPU-based coarse quantizer, which greatly reduces the time to quantize.
chap02 schema — IVF_SQ8H is an IVF_SQ8 index that optimizes query execution.
chap02 schema — The query method is as follows:
chap02 schema — If `nq` ≥ `gpu_search_threshold`, GPU handles the entire query task.
chap02 schema — If `nq` < `gpu_search_threshold`, GPU handles the task of retrieving the `nprobe` nearest unit in the IVF index file, and CPU handles the rest.
chap02 schema — building parameters:
chap02 schema — nlist**: Number of cluster units.
chap02 schema — search parameters:
chap02 schema — nprobe**: Number of inverted file cells to probe.
chap02 schema — ANNOY** (_Approximate Nearest Neighbors Oh Yeah_) is an index that uses a hyperplane to divide a high-dimensional space into multiple subspaces, and then stores them in a tree structure.
chap02 schema — When searching for vectors, ANNOY follows the tree structure to find subspaces closer to the target vector, and then compares all the vectors in these subspaces (The number of vectors being compared should not be less than `search_k`) to obtain the final result. Obviously, when the target vector is close to the edge of a certain subspace, sometimes it is necessary to greatly increase the number of searched subspaces to obtain a high recall rate. Therefore, ANNOY uses `n_trees` different methods to divide the whole space, and searches all the dividing methods simultaneously to reduce the probability that the target vector is always at the edge of the subspace.
chap02 schema — building parameters:
chap02 schema — n_trees**: The number of methods of space division.
chap02 schema — search parameters:
chap02 schema — search_k**: The number of nodes to search. -1 means 5% of the whole data.
chap02 schema — HNSW** (_Hierarchical Navigable Small World Graph_) is a graph-based indexing algorithm. It builds a multi-layer navigation structure for an image according to certain rules. In this structure, the upper layers are more sparse and the distances between nodes are farther; the lower layers are denser and the distances between nodes are closer. The search starts from the uppermost layer, finds the node closest to the target in this layer, and then enters the next layer to begin another search. After multiple iterations, it can quickly approach the target position.
chap02 schema — To improve performance, HNSW limits the maximum degree of nodes on each layer of the graph to `M`.
chap02 schema — In addition, you can use `efConstruction` (when building index) or `ef` (when searching targets) to specify a search range.
chap02 schema — building parameters:
chap02 schema — M**: Maximum degree of the node.
chap02 schema — efConstruction**: Take the effect in the stage of index construction.
chap02 schema — search parameters:
chap02 schema — ef**: Take the effect in the stage of search scope, should be larger than `top_k`.
chap02 schema — RHNSW_PQ
chap02 schema — RHNSW_PQ** is a variant index type combining PQ and HNSW. It first uses PQ to quantize the vector, then uses HNSW to quantize the PQ quantization result to get the index.
chap02 schema — building parameters:
chap02 schema — M**: Maximum degree of the node.
chap02 schema — efConstruction**: Take effect in the stage of index construction.
chap02 schema — PQM**: m for PQ.
chap02 schema — search parameters:
chap02 schema — ef**: Take the effect in the stage of search scope, should be larger than `top_k`.
chap02 schema — RHNSW_SQ
chap02 schema — RHNSW_SQ** is a variant index type combining SQ and HNSW. It uses SQ to quantize the vector, then uses HNSW to quantize the SQ quantization result to get the index.
chap02 schema — building parameters:
chap02 schema — M**: Maximum degree of the node.
chap02 schema — efConstruction**: Take effect in the stage of index construction, search scope.
chap02 schema — search parameters:
chap02 schema — ef**: Take the effect in the stage of search scope, should be larger than `top_k`.
chap02 schema — NSG** (_Refined Navigating Spreading-out Graph_) is a graph-based indexing algorithm. It sets the center position of the whole image as a navigation point, and then uses a specific edge selection strategy to control the out-degree of each point (less than or equal to `out_degree`). Therefore, it can reduce memory usage and quickly locate the target position nearby during searching vectors.
chap02 schema — The graph construction process of NSG is as follows:
chap02 schema — Find `knng` nearest neighbors for each point.
chap02 schema — Iterate at least `search_length` times based on `knng` nearest neighbor nodes to select `candidate_pool_size` possible nearest neighbor nodes.
chap02 schema — Construct the out-edge of each point in the selected `candidate_pool_size` nodes according to the edge selection strategy.
chap02 schema — The query process is similar to the graph building process. It starts from the navigation point and iterates at least `search_length` times to get the final result.
chap02 schema — building parameters:
chap02 schema — search_length**: Number of query iterations.
chap02 schema — out_degree**: Maximum out-degree of the node.
chap02 schema — candidate_pool_size**: Candidate pool size of the node.
chap02 schema — knng**: Number of nearest neighbors
chap02 schema — search parameters:
chap02 schema — search_length**: Number of query iterations

chap05 proxy — Task Scheduler
chap05 proxy — Base Task Queue
chap05 proxy — _AddUnissuedTask(task \*task)_ will push a new task into _unissuedTasks_, while maintaining the list by timestamp order.
chap05 proxy — _TaskDoneTest(ts Timestamp)_ will check both _unissuedTasks_ and _unissuedTasks_. If no task found before _ts_, then the function returns _true_, indicates that all the tasks before _ts_ are completed.
chap05 proxy — Data Definition Task Queue
chap05 proxy — Data definition tasks (i.e. _CreateCollectionTask_) will be pushed into _DdTaskQueue_. If a task is enqueued, _Enqueue(task \*task)_ will set _Ts_, _ReqId_, _ProxyId_, then push it into _queue_. The timestamps of the enqueued tasks should be strictly monotonically increasing. As _Enqueue(task \*task)_ will be called in parallel, setting timestamp and queue insertion need to be done atomically.
chap05 proxy — Data Manipulation Task Queue
chap05 proxy — Insert tasks and delete tasks will be pushed into _DmTaskQueue_.
chap05 proxy — If an _insertTask_ is enqueued, _Enqueue(task \*task)_ will set _Ts_, _ReqId_, _ProxyId_, _SegIdAssigner_, _RowIdAllocator_, then push it into _queue_. The _SegIdAssigner_ and _RowIdAllocator_ will later be used in the task's execution phase.
chap05 proxy — Data Query Task Queue
chap05 proxy — Queries will be pushed into _DqTaskQueue_.
chap05 proxy — Task Scheduler
chap05 proxy — _scheduleDdTask()_ selects tasks in a FIFO manner, thus time order is guaranteed.
chap05 proxy — The policy of _scheduleDmTask()_ should target on throughput, not tasks' time order. Note that the time order of the tasks' execution will later be guaranteed by the timestamp & time tick mechanism.
chap05 proxy — The policy of _scheduleDqTask()_ should target on throughput. It should also take visibility into consideration. For example, if an insert task and a query arrive in a same time tick and the query comes after insert, the query should be scheduled in the next tick thus the query can see the insert.
chap05 proxy — _TaskDoneTest(ts Timestamp)_ will check all the three task queues. If no task is found before _ts_, then the function returns _true_, which indicates that all the tasks before _ts_ are completed.
chap05 proxy — Statistics
chap05 proxy — Time Tick
chap05 proxy — Time Tick
chap05 proxy — _Start()_ will enter a loop. On each _tickStep_, it tries to send a _TIME_TICK_ typed _TsMsg_ into _ttStream_. After each _syncInterval_, it synchronizes its _wallTick_ with _tsAllocator_ by calling _synchronize()_. When _currentTick + tickStep < wallTick_ holds, it will update _currentTick_ with _wallTick_ on next tick. Otherwise, it will update _currentTick_ with _currentTick + tickStep_.

appendix a basic components — A.2 Session
appendix a basic components — ServerID
appendix a basic components — The ID is stored in a key-value pair on etcd. The key is metaRootPath + "/session/id". The initial value is 0. When a service is registered, it is incremented by 1 and returned to the next registered service.
appendix a basic components — Registration
appendix a basic components — Registration is achieved through etcd's lease mechanism.
appendix a basic components — The service creates a lease with etcd and stores a key-value pair in etcd. If the lease expires or the service goes offline, etcd will delete the key-value pair. You can judge whether this service is available through the key.
appendix a basic components — key: metaRoot + "/session" + "/ServerName(-ServerID)(optional)"
appendix a basic components — value: json format
appendix a basic components — By obtaining the address, you can establish a connection with other services
appendix a basic components — If a service is exclusive, the key will not have **ServerID**. But **ServerID** still will be stored in value.
appendix a basic components — Discovery
appendix a basic components — All currently available services can be obtained by obtaining all the key-value pairs deposited during registration. If you want to get all the available nodes for a certain type of service, you can pass in the prefix of the corresponding key
appendix a basic components — Registration time can be compared with ServerID for ServerID will increase according to time.

appendix a basic components — A.6.1 Timestamp
appendix a basic components — Let's take a brief review of the Hybrid Logical Clock (HLC). HLC uses 64bits timestamps which are composed of a 46-bits physical component (thought of as and always close to local wall time) and an 18-bits logical component (used to distinguish between events with the same physical component).
appendix a basic components — <img src="./figs/hlc.png" width=400>
appendix a basic components — HLC's logical part is advanced on each request. The physical part can be increased in two cases:
appendix a basic components — A. when the local wall time is greater than HLC's physical part,
appendix a basic components — B. or the logical part overflows.
appendix a basic components — In either case, the physical part will be updated, and the logical part will be set to 0.
appendix a basic components — Keeping the physical part close to local wall time may face non-monotonic problems such as updates to POSIX time that could turn time backward. HLC avoids such problems, since if 'local wall time < HLC's physical part' holds, only case B is satisfied, thus monotonicity is guaranteed.
appendix a basic components — Milvus does not support the transaction, but it should guarantee the deterministic execution of the multi-way WAL. The timestamp attached to each request should
appendix a basic components — have its physical part close to wall time (has an acceptable bounded error, a.k.a. uncertainty interval in transaction scenarios),
appendix a basic components — and be globally unique.
appendix a basic components — HLC leverages physical clocks at nodes that are synchronized using the NTP. NTP usually maintains time to within tens of milliseconds over local networks in the datacenter. Asymmetric routes and network congestion occasionally cause errors of hundreds of milliseconds. Both the normal time error and the spike are acceptable for Milvus use cases.
appendix a basic components — The interface of Timestamp is as follows.

chap01 system overview — System Overview
chap01 system overview — In this section, we sketch the system design of Milvus, including the data model, data organization, architecture, and state synchronization.
chap01 system overview — Data Model
chap01 system overview — Milvus exposes the following set of data features to applications:
chap01 system overview — a data model based on schematized relational tables, in that rows must have primary keys,
chap01 system overview — a query language specifies data definition, data manipulation, and data query, where data definition includes create, drop, and data manipulation includes insert, upsert, delete, and data query falls into three types, primary key search, approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS), ANNS with predicates.
chap01 system overview — The requests' execution order is strictly in accordance with their issue-time order. We take Proxy's issue time as a request's issue time. For a batch request, all its sub-requests share the same issue time. In cases there are multiple proxies, issue time from different proxies are regarded as coming from a central clock.
chap01 system overview — The transaction is currently not supported by Milvus.
chap01 system overview — A batch insert/delete is guaranteed to become visible atomically.
chap01 system overview — Data Organization
chap01 system overview — <img src="./figs/data_organization.png" width=550>
chap01 system overview — In Milvus, 'collection' refers to the concept of a table. A collection can be optionally divided into several 'partitions'. Both collection and partition are the basic execution scopes of queries. When using the partition, users should know how a collection should be partitioned. In most cases, partition leads to more flexible data management and more efficient querying. For a partitioned collection, queries can be executed on the collection or a set of specified partitions.
chap01 system overview — Each collection or partition contains a set of 'segment groups'. The Segment group is the basic unit of data-to-node mapping. It's also the basic unit of a replica. For instance, if a query node failed, its segment groups will be redistributed across the other nodes. If a query node is overloaded, part of its segment groups will be migrated to underloaded ones. If a hot collection/partition is detected, its segment groups will be replicated to smooth the system load skewness.
chap01 system overview — 'Segment' is the finest unit of data organization. It is where the data and indexes are actually kept. Each segment contains a set of rows. In order to reduce the memory footprint during query execution and to fully utilize SIMD, the physical data layout within segments is organized in a column-based manner.
chap01 system overview — Architecture Overview
chap01 system overview — <img src="./figs/system_framework.png" width=800>
chap01 system overview — The main components, Proxy, WAL, query node, and write node can scale to multiple instances. These components scale separately for a better tradeoff between availability and cost.
chap01 system overview — The WAL forms a hash ring. Requests (i.e. inserts and deletes) from clients will be repacked by Proxy. Operations shared the identical hash value (the hash value of primary key) will be routed to the same hash bucket. In addition, some preprocessing work will be done by Proxy, such as static validity checking, primary key assignment (if not given by the user), timestamp assignment.
chap01 system overview — The query/write nodes are linked to the hash ring, with each node covering some portion of the buckets. Once the hash function and bucket coverage are settled, the chain 'proxy -> WAL -> query/write node' will act as a producer-consumer pipeline. Logs in each bucket are a determined operation stream. Via performing the operation stream in order, the query nodes keep themselves up to date.
chap01 system overview — The query nodes hold all the indexes in memory. Since building an index is time-consuming, the query nodes will dump their index to disk (store engine) for fast failure recovery and cross node index copy.
chap01 system overview — The write nodes are stateless. They simply transform the newly arrived WALs to binlog format, then append the binlog to the store engine.
chap01 system overview — Note that not all the components are necessarily replicated. The system provides failure tolerance by maintaining multiple copies of WAL and binlog. When there is no in-memory index replica and there occurs a query node failure, other query nodes will take over its indexes by loading the dumped index files, or rebuilding them from binlog and WALs. The links from query nodes to the hash ring will also be adjusted such that the failed node's input WAL stream can be properly handled by its neighbors.
chap01 system overview — State Synchronization
chap01 system overview — <img src="./figs/state_sync.png" width=800>
chap01 system overview — Data in Milvus have three different forms, namely WAL, binlog, and index. As mentioned in the previous section, WAL can be viewed as a determined operation stream. The other two data forms keep themselves up to date by performing the operation stream in time order.
chap01 system overview — Each of the WAL is attached with a timestamp, which is the time when the log is sent to the hash bucket. Binlog records, table rows, index cells will also keep that timestamp. In this way, different data forms can offer consistent snapshots for a given time T. For example, requests such as "fetch binlogs before T for point-in-time recovery", "get the row with primary key K at time T", "launch a similarity search at time T for vector V" perform on binlog, index respectively. Though different data forms of these three requests are performed, they observe identical snapshots, namely all the state changes before T.
chap01 system overview — For better throughput, Milvus allows asynchronous state synchronization between WAL and index/binlog/table. Whenever the data is not fresh enough to satisfy a query, the query will be suspended until the data is up-to-date, or timeout will be returned.
chap01 system overview — Stream and Time
chap01 system overview — In order to boost throughput, we model Milvus as a stream-driven system.

20211221-retrieve entity — Support to retrieve the specified entity from a collection
20211221-retrieve entity — Background
20211221-retrieve entity — In Milvus, a collection has multiple fields, mainly there are two kinds of fields: vector field and scalar field. We call a row an entity, one entity encapsulates multiple vectors and scalar values.
20211221-retrieve entity — When creating a collection, you can specify using the auto-generated primary key, or using the user-provided primary key.
20211221-retrieve entity — If a user sets to use the user-provided primary key, each entity inserted must contain the primary key field. Otherwise, the insertion fails.
20211221-retrieve entity — The primary keys will be returned after the insertion request is successful.
20211221-retrieve entity — Milvus currently only supports primary keys of the int64 type.
20211221-retrieve entity — QueryNode subscribes to the insert channel and will determine whether to use the data extracted from the insert channel or data processed by DataNode to provide services according to the status of a segment.
20211221-retrieve entity — Support to retrieve one or more entities from a collection through primary keys
20211221-retrieve entity — Support to retrieve only some fields of an entity
20211221-retrieve entity — Consider backward file format compatibility if a new file is defined
20211221-retrieve entity — Non-Goals
20211221-retrieve entity — How to deal with duplicate primary keys
20211221-retrieve entity — How to retrieve entity by non-primary key
20211221-retrieve entity — Detailed design
20211221-retrieve entity — When the DataNode processes each inserted entity, it updates the bloomfilter of the Segment to which the entity belongs. If it does not exist, it creates a bloomfilter in memory and updates it.
20211221-retrieve entity — Once DataNode receives a Flush command from DataCoord, it sorts the data in the segment in ascending order of primary key, records the maximum and minimum values of a primary key, and writes the segment, statistics and bloomfilter to the storage system.
20211221-retrieve entity — Key of binlog file: `${tenant}/insert_log/${collection_id}/${partition_id}/${segment_id}/${field_id}/_${log_idx}`
20211221-retrieve entity — Key of statistics file: `${tenant}/insert_log/${collection_id}/${partition_id}/${segment_id}/${field_id}/stats_${log_idx}`
20211221-retrieve entity — Key of bloom filter file: `${tenant}/insert_log/${collection_id}/${partition_id}/${segment_id}/${field_id}/bf_${log_idx}`
20211221-retrieve entity — QueryNode maintains a mapping from primary key to entities in each segment. This mapping updates every time an insert request is processed.
20211221-retrieve entity — After receiving the Get request from the client, the Proxy sends the request to the `search` channel and waits for the result returned from the `searchResult` channel.
20211221-retrieve entity — The processing flow after QueryNode reads the Get request from `search` channel:
20211221-retrieve entity — Search for the existence of the requested primary key in the mapping of the `Growing` status segment, and return directly if found;
20211221-retrieve entity — If the primary key exists in any mapping of `Growing` segments, return the results;
20211221-retrieve entity — Load statistics and bloomfilter of all `Sealed` segments;
20211221-retrieve entity — Convert the statistics into an inverted index from Range to SegmentID for each `Sealed` segment;
20211221-retrieve entity — Check whether the requested primary key exists in any inverted index of `Sealed` segment, return empty if not found;
20211221-retrieve entity — [optional] Use the bloomfilter to filter out segments where the primary key does not exist;
20211221-retrieve entity — Use binary search to find the specified entity in each segment where the primary key may exist;
20211221-retrieve entity — When the primary key does not exist in specified collection( and partitions), Milvus will return an empty result, which is not considered as an error.
20211221-retrieve entity — Both bloomfilter files and statistical information files belong to Binlog files and follow the Binlog file format.
20211221-retrieve entity — https://github.com/milvus-io/milvus/blob/master/docs/developer_guides/chap08_binlog.md
20211221-retrieve entity — Two new types of Binlog are added: BFBinlog and StatsBinlog.
20211221-retrieve entity — BFBinlog Payload: Refer to https://github.com/milvus-io/milvus/blob/1.1/core/src/segment/SegmentWriter.h for storage methods
20211221-retrieve entity — StatsBinlog Payload: Json format string, currently only contains the keys `max`, `min`.
20211221-retrieve entity — A new Get API
20211221-retrieve entity — DropCollection / ReleaseCollection / DropPartition / ReleasePartition requests need to clear the corresponding statistics files and bloomfilter files in the memory
20211221-retrieve entity — The name of the binlog file has been changed from `${log_idx}` to `_${log_idx}`
20211221-retrieve entity — Each binlog adds a stats file
20211221-retrieve entity — Each binlog adds a bloomfilter file
20211221-retrieve entity — Test Plan
20211221-retrieve entity — Testcase 1
20211221-retrieve entity — In the newly created collection, insert an entity with a primary key of 107, call the Get interface to query the entity with a primary key of 107, and each field of the retrieved entity is exactly the same as the inserted entity.
20211221-retrieve entity — Testcase 2
20211221-retrieve entity — In the newly created collection, insert a record with a primary key of 107, call the Get interface to query the record with a primary key of 106, and the retrieved record is empty.
20211221-retrieve entity — Testcase 3
20211221-retrieve entity — In the newly created collection, insert the records with the primary keys of 105, 106, 107, call the Get interface to query the records with the primary keys of 101, 102, 103, 104, 105, 106, 107, the retrieved result only contains the records with primary keys of 105, 106, 107.
20211221-retrieve entity — Testcase 4
20211221-retrieve entity — In the newly created collection, insert a record with a primary key of 107, call the Flush interface, and check whether there are stats and bloomfilter files on MinIO.

20230918-datanode remove datacoord dependency — MEP: Datanode remove dependency of `Datacoord`
20230918-datanode remove datacoord dependency — Current state: "Accepted"
20230918-datanode remove datacoord dependency — ISSUE: https://github.com/milvus-io/milvus/issues/26758
20230918-datanode remove datacoord dependency — Keywords: datacoord, datanode, flush, dependency, roll-upgrade
20230918-datanode remove datacoord dependency — Remove the dependency of `Datacoord` for `Datanodes`.
20230918-datanode remove datacoord dependency — Motivation
20230918-datanode remove datacoord dependency — Datanodes shall be always be running even when the data coordinator is not alive
20230918-datanode remove datacoord dependency — If datanodes performs `sync` during rolling upgrade, it needs datacoord to change the related meta in metastore. If datacoord happens to be offline or it is during some period of rolling-upgrade, datanode has to panic to ensure there is no data lost.
20230918-datanode remove datacoord dependency — Flush operation is complex and error-prone due since the whole procedure involves datacoord, datanodes and grpc
20230918-datanode remove datacoord dependency — This proposal means to remove the dependency of datacoord ensuring:
20230918-datanode remove datacoord dependency — the data is integrate and no duplicate data is kept in records
20230918-datanode remove datacoord dependency — no compatibility issue during or after rolling upgrade
20230918-datanode remove datacoord dependency — `Datacoord` shall be able to detect the segment meta updates and provides recent targets for `QueryCoord`
20230918-datanode remove datacoord dependency — Design Details
20230918-datanode remove datacoord dependency — The most brief description if this proposal is to:
20230918-datanode remove datacoord dependency — Make `Datanode` operating the segment meta directly
20230918-datanode remove datacoord dependency — Make `Datacoord` refresh the latest segment change periodically
20230918-datanode remove datacoord dependency — Preventing multiple writers
20230918-datanode remove datacoord dependency — There is a major concern that if multiple `Datanodes` are handling the same dml channel, there shall be only one `DataNode` could update segment meta successfully.
20230918-datanode remove datacoord dependency — This guarantee is previously implemented by singleton writer in `Datacoord`: it checks the valid watcher id before update the segment meta when receiving the `SaveBinlogPaths` grpc call.
20230918-datanode remove datacoord dependency — In this proposal, `DataNodes` update segment meta on its own, so we need to introduce a new mechanism to prevent this error from happening:
20230918-datanode remove datacoord dependency — {% note %}

20230918-datanode remove datacoord dependency — If a `datanode` finds the lease id is revoke or updated, it shall close the flowgraph/pipeline and cancel all pending operations instead of panicking.

20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — Root Coordinator recovery on power failure
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — Basic idea
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — `RootCoord` (Root Coordinator) reads meta from etcd when it starts.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — `RootCoord` needs to store the `position` of the msgstream into etcd every time it consumes the msgstream.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — `RootCoord` reads the `position` of msgstream from etcd when it starts up, then it seeks to the specified `position` and re-consumes the msgstream.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — Ensure that all messages from the msgstream are processed in an idempotent fashion, so that repeated consumption of the same message does not cause system inconsistencies.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — `RootCoord` registers itself in etcd and finds out if the dependent `DataCoord(Data Coordinator)` and `IndexCoord(Index Coordinator)` are online via etcd.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — Specific tasks
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — Read meta from etcd
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — `RootCoord` needs to load meta from etcd when it starts, this part is already done.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — `dd requests` from grpc
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — The `dd requests`, such as create_collection, create_partition, etc., from grpc are marked as done only if the related meta has been written into etcd.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — The `dd requests` should be sent to `dd msgstream` when the operation is done.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — There may be a fault here, that is, the `dd request` has been written to etcd, but it has not been sent to `dd msgstream` yet, then the `RootCoord` has crashed.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — For the scenarios mentioned in item 3, `RootCoord` needs to check if all `dd requests` are sent to `dd msgstream` when it starts up.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — `RootCoord`'s built-in scheduler ensures that all grpc requests are executed serially, so it only needs to check whether the most recent `dd requests` are sent to the `dd msgstream`, and resend them if not.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — Take `create_collection` as an example to illustrate the process
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — When `create collection` is written to etcd, 2 additional keys are updated, `dd_msg` and `dd_type`.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — `dd_msg` is the serialization of the `dd_msg`.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — `dd_type` is the message type of `dd_msg`, such as `create_collection`, `create_partition`, `drop_collection,` etc. It's used to deserialize `dd_msg`.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — Update the meta of `create_collection`, `dd_msg` and `dd_type` at the same time in a transactional manner.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — When `dd_msg` has been sent to `dd msgstream`, delete `dd_msg` and `dd_type` from etcd.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — When the `RootCoord` starts, first check whether there are `dd_msg` and `dd_type` in etcd. If yes, then deserialize `dd_msg` according to `dd_type`, and then send it to the `dd msgstream`. Otherwise, no processing will be done.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — There may be a failure here, that is, `dd_msg` has been sent to the `dd msgstream` , but has not been deleted from etcd yet, then the `RootCoord` crashed. In this case, the `dd_msg` would be sent to `dd msgstream` repeatedly, so the receiver needs to count this case.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — `create index` requests from grpc
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — In the processing of `create index`, `RootCoord` calls `metaTable`'s `GetNotIndexedSegments` to get all segment ids that are not indexed.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — After getting the segment ids, `RootCoord` calls `IndexCoord` to create index on these segment ids.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — In the current implementation, the `create index` requests will return after the segment ids are put into a go channel.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — The `RootCoord` starts a background task that keeps reading the segment ids from the go channel, and then calls the `IndexCoord` to create the index.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — There is a fault here, the segment ids have been put into the go channel in the processing function of the grpc request, and then the grpc returns, but the `RootCoord`'s background task has not yet read them from the go channel, then `RootCoord` crashes. At this time, the client thinks that the index is created, but the `RootCoord` does not call `IndexCoord` to create the index.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — The solution for the fault mentioned in item 5:
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — Remove the go channel and `RootCoord`'s background task.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — In the request processing function of `create index`, the call will return only when all segment ids have been sent `IndexCoord`.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — Some segment ids may be sent to `IndexCoord` repeatedly, and `IndexCoord` needs to handle such requests.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — New segment from `DataCoord`
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — Each time a new segment is created, the `DataCoord` sends the segment id to the `RootCoord` via msgstream.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — `RootCoord` needs to update the segment id to the collection meta and record the position of the msgstream in etcd.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — Step 2 is transactional and the operation will be successful only if the collection meta in etcd is updated.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — So the `RootCoord` only needs to restore the msgstream to the position when recovering from a power failure.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — Flushed segment from `data node`
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — Each time the `DataNode` finishes flushing a segment, it sends the segment id to the `RootCoord` via msgstream.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — `RootCoord` needs to fetch binlog from `DataCoord` by id and send a request to `IndexCoord` to create an index on this segment.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — When the `IndexCoord` is called successfully, it will return a build id, and then `RootCoord` will update the build id to the `collection meta` and record the position of the msgstream in etcd.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — Step 3 is transactional and the operation will be successful only if the `collection meta` in etcd is updated.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — So the `RootCoord` only needs to restore the msgstream to the position when recovering from a power failure.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — Failed to call external grpc service
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — `RootCoord` depends on `DataCoord` and `IndexCoord`, if the grpc call failed, it needs to reconnect.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — `RootCoord` does not listen to the status of the `DataCoord` and `IndexCoord` in real time.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — Add virtual channel assignment when creating a collection
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — Add a new field, "number of shards" in the `create collection` request. The "num of shards" tells the `RootCoord` to create the number of virtual channels for this collection.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — In the current implementation, virtual channels and physical channels have a one-to-one relationship, and the total number of physical channels increases as the number of virtual channels increases; later, the total number of physical channels needs to be fixed, and multiple virtual channels share one physical channel.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — The name of the virtual channel is globally unique, and the `collection meta` records the correspondence between the virtual channel and the physical channel.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — Add processing of time synchronization signals from Proxy node
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — A virtual channel can be inserted by multiple proxies, so the timestamp in the virtual channel does not increase monotonically.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — All proxies report the timestamp of all the virtual channels to the `RootCoord` periodically.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — The `RootCoord` collects the timestamps from the proxies on each virtual channel and gets the minimum one as the timestamp of that virtual channel, and then inserts the timestamp into the virtual channel.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — Proxy reports the timestamp to the `RootCoord` via grpc.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — Proxy needs to register itself in etcd when it starts, `RootCoord` will listen to the corresponding key to determine how many active proxies there are, and thus determine if all of them have sent timestamps to `RootCoord`.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — If a proxy is not registered in etcd but sends a timestamp or any other grpc request to `RootCoord`, `RootCoord` will ignore the grpc request.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — Register service in etcd
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — `RootCoord` needs to register itself with etcd when it starts.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — The registration should include IP address, port, its own id and global incremental timestamp.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — Remove the code related to Proxy service
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — `Proxy service` related code will be removed.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — The job of time synchronization which is done by `Proxy service` is partially simplified and handed over to the `RootCoord` (subsection 2.8).
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — Query collection meta based on timeline
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — Add a new field of `timestamp` to the grpc request of `describe collection`.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — `RootCoord` should provide snapshot on the `collection mate`.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — Return the `collection meta` at the point of timestamp mentioned in the request.
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — Timestamp of `dd operations`
20220105-root coordinator recovery on power failure — `RootCoord` response is to set the timestamp of `dd operations`, create collection, create partition, drop collection, drop partition, and send this timestamp into `dml msgstream`.

20211214-milvus hybrid ts — The Organization of TSO
20211214-milvus hybrid ts — The type of TSO is `uint64`. As shown in the figure below, TSO was organized by two parts:
20211214-milvus hybrid ts — physical part;
20211214-milvus hybrid ts — logical part;

geometry — Background
geometry — Milvus is a high-performance vector database widely used in fields such as image retrieval, recommender systems, and semantic search. With the increasing integration of scenarios such as LBS (location-based service), MultiModal Machine Learning retrieval, and driverless technology **spatial awareness** and **semantic retrieval** requirements, users increasingly need to be able to perform vector searches in "geographical context".
geometry — Currently, Milvus only supports numerical, string, and vector type fields, **lacking native understanding and index support for geographical information**. This limits its capabilities in emerging spatial computing applications.
geometry — Requirement
geometry — The following is a typical use case that combines geographic information with vector retrieval:
geometry — _Perform vector search under spatial constraints_
geometry — I would like to search for products, stores, and images that are within 1 kilometer of me and semantically most similar.
geometry — Example Industries:
geometry — Local services (such as Ele.me, Uber)
geometry — Map content recommendation (e.g., AutoNavi Maps recommendation)
geometry — E-commerce scenarios (LBS advertising, nearby same-item retrieval)
geometry — Security surveillance (tracking similar faces near a given location)
geometry — In addition to being combined with vector retrieval, supporting Geographic Information System (GIS) can also meet many common requirements for geographic information-based analysis. For example, heat map analysis, planning transportation routes, and planning market locations through statistical analysis, etc.
geometry — Sometimes, users may also choose different coordinate systems to analyze geographic data from different perspectives based on different usage scenarios. And since geographic data usually comes from third-party platforms (maps, remote sensing, testing, etc.), with diverse data formats, it is necessary to support at least WKT and WKB, and GeoJson, GeoHash and other data formats can be added as needed later.
geometry — Based on the above requirements, it is necessary to provide support for the geospatial data structure in Milvus, including the definition of its core data types, various query operators, index optimization, etc. The following details the feasible implementation plan from several aspects.
geometry — Implementation Plan
geometry — Data Type
geometry — Geo Spatial DataType is a data structure used to describe geospatial information. In the SFA (Simple Feature Access) standard developed by the OGC, the following common geometric types are defined:
geometry — Point: Represents a two-dimensional coordinate, usually representing different objects depending on the scale
geometry — LineString: An ordered collection composed of two or more points, often used to represent rivers, roads, etc.
geometry — Polygon: Represents a planar region that can have "holes".
geometry — MultiPoint: A collection of multiple points
geometry — MultiLineString: A collection of multiple line strings
geometry — MultiPolygon: A collection of multiple polygons
geometry — GeometryCollection: A collection composed of all the above geometries
geometry — The input and output of these data types have two representation methods in the SFA standard: WKT (Well Known Text) and WKB (Well Known Binary). The former is a human-readable format, such as: `POINT (0 0)` , `MULTILINESTRING ((0 0, 1 1), (2 2, 3 3))` , etc., while the latter is a binary format for efficient storage.
geometry — In Milvus, we do not need to manually define the above data types. Instead, we can introduce third-party libraries, wrap the geometric classes provided by third-party libraries in Milvus, and then perform unified processing on geometric data and provide a unified processing interface externally.
geometry — Common third-party libraries include GEOS, GDAL, etc. Among them, GEOS (Geometry Engine - Open Source) is an open-source geometric computation library that adheres to the OGC SFA standard. OGR, on the other hand, is a wrapper library for the geos library and some functions such as coordinate transformation and other geographic coordinate types. It has now been integrated into GDAL, which contains many contents unrelated to geographic information, such as grating processing. For the scalability of the geographic information system, we choose to use the OGR library encapsulated by GDAL. Meanwhile, for the sake of simplicity, we need to remove the extra parts we don't need (such as grating processing) during compilation.
geometry — Coordinate System
geometry — Commonly used coordinate systems include WGS 84, the international standard for latitude and longitude; Web Mercator, the standard for web maps; etc.
geometry — The underlying layer of GEOS has no coordinate system and only performs operations on geometric shapes in the Cartesian set (plane coordinate system). However, the WKT information input by the user may be based on latitude and longitude information, and when the scale is large enough, there will be a problem of excessive error caused by direct conversion between spherical coordinates and plane coordinates.
geometry — Therefore, when high-precision calculations are required, it is necessary to first use the coordinate transformation function provided by GDAL for conversion before performing the calculations.
geometry — Query Operator
geometry — Common query operators include:
geometry — Topological Relationships
geometry — These functions are used to determine whether there is a certain topological relationship (such as intersection, inclusion, coverage, etc.) between two geometric objects, based on the logical relationship between the shape and position of spatial objects.
geometry — | Function Name | Description |
geometry — | --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
geometry — | `ST_Contains(A, B)` | Determine **whether A completely contains B (excluding the boundary)** , and there is at least one common point in the interiors of A and B. For example: whether a city contains a park. |
geometry — | `ST_Covers(A, B)` | Determine **whether A covers B**, i.e., all points of B are inside or on the boundary of A. |
geometry — | `ST_Equals(A, B)` | Determine **whether A and B represent the same geometric object** , i.e., have the same coordinate sequence and type. |
geometry — | `ST_Intersects(A, B)` | Determine **whether A and B have at least one common point** , which is the most commonly used spatial relationship judgment function. |
geometry — | `ST_Overlaps(A, B)` | Determine **whether A and B overlap**, i.e., they have the same dimension (e.g., both are faces or both are lines), and their regions partially coincide, but neither completely contains the other. |
geometry — | `ST_Touches(A, B)` | Determine **whether A and B only touch at the boundary**, but do not intersect internally. For example: the boundary of adjacent plots. |
geometry — | `ST_Within(A, B)` | Determine **whether A is completely inside B** and that A and B have at least one common point in their interiors. It is `an alias for ST_Contains(B, A)`. |
geometry — Index Optimization
geometry — To speed up querying, it is necessary to create an index for geographic information data. In a standard database, whether scalar or vector, indexes are built based on the values of the indexed columns, but it is different for spatial indexes because the database cannot directly index the values of geometric fields, that is, the geometric objects themselves. Therefore, it is necessary to index the **bounding box** of geometric objects. The following example is from the PostGIS documentation:
geometry — ![_images/bbox.png](https://postgis.net/workshops/zh_Hans/postgis-intro/_images/bbox.png)
geometry — In the figure above, the number of lines intersecting the yellow star is **1** , which is the red line. However, the range boxes intersecting the yellow box include the red and blue ones, a total of 2.
geometry — The database solves the problem of "what line intersects with the yellow star" by first using a spatial index to solve the problem of "what bounding box intersects with the yellow bounding box" (which is very fast), and then "what line intersects with the yellow star". The above process only applies to the spatial features of the first test.
geometry — For large data tables, this "two-pass method" of indexing first and then performing local precise calculations can fundamentally reduce the amount of query computation.
geometry — Common indexing methods include: R-Tree, QuadTree, GeoHash, S2, H3, etc.
geometry — For each spatial object, a Minimum Bounding Rectangle (MBR) is established, and these MBRs are recursively organized into a tree structure. The internal nodes of the tree contain the MBRs of multiple sub-nodes, which are used to quickly filter out irrelevant regions; leaf nodes store the actual spatial objects. When performing a spatial query, the R-Tree first uses the MBRs for quick filtering to find the set of objects that may meet the conditions, and then conducts precise spatial relationship judgments, thereby significantly improving query efficiency.
geometry — QuadTree：
geometry — Its core idea is to divide the entire space into four quadrants, with each quadrant continuing to be recursively divided until the number of objects contained within each region is less than the set threshold. Each node represents a spatial region, and leaf nodes store actual data objects. When performing a query, the QuadTree starts from the root node, sequentially checks which sub-nodes intersect with the query range, and recursively enters these sub-nodes, ultimately finding matching objects in the leaf nodes. This structure is simple to implement and suitable for scenarios such as image processing and map tile systems, but it may encounter imbalance issues when dealing with high-density or unevenly distributed data, affecting performance.
geometry — geohash：
geometry — The basic principle of geohash is: recursively divide the Earth's surface using a quadtree, where each division assigns a binary bit to the resulting sub-region, and finally a hash string for a specific region is given through base32/64 encoding. When querying, input the latitude and longitude, calculate its geohash, then specify the desired prefix length to match (e.g., 6 digits), and the algorithm will return regions with matching prefixes.
geometry — This indexing method is suitable for nearest neighbor search. And the longer the prefix, the more precise the match. However, it performs poorly at the "boundary", i.e., there may be cases where neighbors at the junction of rectangular regions do not have the same prefix.
geometry — Its core idea is to project the Earth's surface onto the six faces of a cube, with each face further recursively divided into small cells (referred to as Cells) in a quadtree structure. Each cell has a unique 64-bit integer ID (CellID) and supports up to 30 levels of resolution. The division at each level maintains the Hilbert curve order to ensure spatial locality. When performing queries, a set of spatial cells covering these geometries can be generated based on points, lines, or polygons, enabling efficient operations such as range queries and intersection judgments. This structure has a rigorous mathematical foundation, supports global seamless stitching, avoids boundary issues in traditional planar divisions, and is particularly suitable for complex scenarios such as high-precision spatial analysis, map tile systems, polygon coverage, and spatial aggregation. Although its implementation is relatively complex, it provides rich API support and is suitable for application systems requiring precise spatial operations.
geometry — The core idea is to divide the Earth's surface into a series of regular hexagonal grids (hexagons), with most regions being regular hexagons except for the polar regions. The entire division uses the Icosahedron unfolding method to form a hierarchical hexagonal grid system, with each layer having a different resolution (a total of 15 layers). Each hexagonal cell is assigned a unique 64-bit integer ID, which contains information such as the cell's layer information, parent cell path, and position offset. When performing queries, data in the surrounding area can be quickly obtained by finding the neighbors of a certain hex (up to 6), the K-ring range, etc. This structure is naturally suitable for neighborhood analysis and heat map display, with good spatial uniformity and aggregation capabilities. H3 performs particularly well in scenarios such as spatial aggregation, spatial connection, and path planning.
geometry — The geos library provides support for R-Tree and Quad-Tree. s2 and h3 each have their own officially provided libraries. GeoHash, on the other hand, requires additional third-party library support.
geometry — First, focus on the R-Tree index and S2 index:
geometry — The R-Tree index is the index type used by PostGIS to support spatial relationship query functions such as ST_XXX defined in the OGC standard. In actual development, you can directly create an R-Tree object, insert data, serialize it, and write it to disk.
geometry — The S2 index library does not support standard geographic information SQL query statements, but these functions can be simulated through its provided APIs. S2 provides `S2ShapeIndex` as the core index structure, which is used to manage geometric objects such as points, lines, and polygons, and supports various spatial query operations such as efficient inclusion judgment, nearest neighbor search, and intersection detection. At the same time, S2 provides serialization and deserialization functions. It should be noted that the S2 library uses its own defined spatial data types rather than the OGC standard WKT/WKB, and manual conversion is required.
geometry — Note: Not all spatial functions will use indexes!**
geometry — Functions that support the use of spatial indexes in PostGIS include:
geometry — ST_Within,ST_DWithin,ST_Intersects,ST_Contains,ST_Covers,ST_Overlaps,ST_Crosses,ST_Equals

geometry — The usage method can be roughly inferred from the pymilvus example.
geometry — Calculate the search results:
geometry — Combining the above possible usage scenarios, in the query and deletion scenarios, for the filter and output_field fields, it is necessary to support calculation during query and return the calculation results.

primarykey index — Primary Key Index Design Document
primarykey index — Introduction
primarykey index — This document outlines the design of Milvus' primary key indexing system, which enables fast lookups of string or integer primary keys across multiple segments. The index will be loaded in the Delegator and persisted in S3 storage.
primarykey index — Objectives and Benefits
primarykey index — Deduplication**: Identify duplicate data during write operations, automatically converting them to Insert + Delete operations
primarykey index — Accelerate Partial Updates**: Improve performance of partial upsert and point query operations
primarykey index — Optimize Delete Forwarding**: Reduce Bloom Filter check overhead in the Delegator during Delete operations
primarykey index — Design Overview
primarykey index — Core Components
primarykey index — BBhash**: A space-efficient hash structure that maps keys to a continuous range of integers without collisions. The master branch works with Plain Old Data types (POD), while the "alltypes" branch supports other types including strings.
primarykey index — Value Array**: A memory-mapped array storing segment position information for each primary key.
primarykey index — Architecture Details
primarykey index — BBhash**:
primarykey index — BBhash is a minimal perfect hash library for static key collections, capable of mapping each key to a unique, compact integer index. For example:
primarykey index — "user123" → 0
primarykey index — "user456" → 1
primarykey index — "user789" → 2
primarykey index — For string primary keys, BBhash processes the raw byte sequence directly without type conversion and supports variable-length strings. Key features include:
primarykey index — No need to store original strings
primarykey index — Full content hashing reduces collision probability
primarykey index — Extremely low memory usage
primarykey index — Value Array**:
primarykey index — This array stores segment metadata for each primary key. It can be accessed directly using the BBhash mapping result, providing **O(1)** query efficiency:
primarykey index — example code**
primarykey index — Index Structure Illustration
primarykey index — BBhash Workflow
primarykey index — BBhash (Bin Bloom Hash) maps keys to unique indices through multi-level hash functions:
primarykey index — The first level hash attempts to map all keys to non-conflicting positions
primarykey index — For keys with conflicts, a next-level hash function is used for remapping
primarykey index — This process iterates until all keys are mapped without conflicts
primarykey index — Value Array Storage Structure
primarykey index — Each entry in the value array contains:
primarykey index — Segment ID (pointing to the segment containing the primary key)
primarykey index — ![Primary Key Index Structure](bucket.png)
primarykey index — For L1 Segments, we don't need primary key indexing and can use Bloom Filters for approximate filtering with false positives. For L2 Segments, we build PK → Segment mappings for data under each bucket. Note that false positives still exist here due to: 1. Data that has been deleted, and 2. BBhash's small probability of false positives (approximately 1/2³² ≈ 2.3×10⁻¹⁰).
primarykey index — Memory Efficiency**:
primarykey index — BBhash: 2–4 bits/key (1B keys ≈ 250–500MB)
primarykey index — Value Array: ~4 bytes/key (Segment ID)
primarykey index — Total: ~4.5 bytes/key → 1B keys ≈ 4.5GB
primarykey index — mmap implementation allows the operating system to load and reclaim memory as needed, supporting billion-scale datasets
primarykey index — Performance Analysis
primarykey index — Index Building Performance
primarykey index — Single-thread Performance**: BBhash constructs a minimal perfect hash function (MPHF) for 100 million keys in about 10 seconds on a single thread, processing approximately 10 million keys/second
primarykey index — Multi-thread Scalability**: Using 8 threads, building an MPHF for 1 billion keys takes about 35 seconds, averaging approximately 28.57 million keys/second
primarykey index — Billion-scale Construction Feasibility**:
primarykey index — On a 32-core server, theoretical time to build a 1 billion key index is about 10-15 seconds
primarykey index — In actual testing, end-to-end time including data reading and index construction reaches 1 minute
primarykey index — Peak memory usage does not exceed 16GB
primarykey index — Query Performance Comparison
primarykey index — Single Primary Key Index vs. Multiple Bloom Filters**:
primarykey index — Query Latency**:
primarykey index — Primary Key Index: ~200 nanoseconds per query
primarykey index — ,000 Bloom Filters: Sequential querying required, average latency ~10,000 × 10 nanoseconds = 0.1 milliseconds
primarykey index — Performance Gap**: Primary key index query speed is approximately 500 times faster than the Bloom filter approach
primarykey index — Throughput**:
primarykey index — Primary Key Index: ~10-20 million queries per second per node
primarykey index — Bloom Filter Approach: ~1,000 queries per second per node
primarykey index — Advantage**: Primary key index supports higher query loads in high-concurrency scenarios
primarykey index — Precision Comparison
primarykey index — BBhash Precision**:
primarykey index — Actual implementation may have an extremely small probability of hash collisions, but far lower than Bloom filters
primarykey index — Bloom Filter Precision**:
primarykey index — Single Bloom filter false positive rate is typically set to 0.1%
primarykey index — Cumulative false positive rate when querying 10,000 Bloom filters approaches 100%
primarykey index — Additional Considerations
primarykey index — Performance validation, including index construction and querying, comparing BBhash and other libraries such as CMPH
primarykey index — Whether BBHash can also replace Bloom filters for individual Segments
primarykey index — How to handle false positives - ignore? verify in each segment
primarykey index — Value index redundancy fields for point query optimization, such as recording additional offset information or even fields

20211223-knowhere design — What's Knowhere
20211223-knowhere design — Concepts
20211223-knowhere design — Vector index is a time-efficient and space-efficient data structure built on vectors through a certain mathematical model. Through the vector index, we can efficiently query several vectors similar to the target vector.
20211223-knowhere design — Since accurate retrieval is usually very time-consuming, most of the vector index types of Milvus use ANNS (Approximate Nearest Neighbors Search). Compared with accurate retrieval, the core idea of ANNS is no longer limited to returning the most accurate result, but only searching for neighbors of the target. ANNS improves retrieval efficiency by sacrificing accuracy within an acceptable range.
20211223-knowhere design — What can Knowhere do
20211223-knowhere design — Knowhere is the vector search execution engine of Milvus. It encapsulates many popular vector index algorithm libraries, such as faiss, hnswlib, NGT, annoy, and provides a set of unified interfaces. In addition, Knowhere also supports heterogeneous computing.
20211223-knowhere design — Framework
20211223-knowhere design — ![Knowhere framework](graphs/knowhere_framework.png)
20211223-knowhere design — For more index types and heterogeneous support, please refer to the vector index document.
20211223-knowhere design — Major Interface
20211223-knowhere design — Data Format
20211223-knowhere design — The vector data used for index and query is stored as a one-dimensional array.
20211223-knowhere design — The first `dim * sizeof(data_type)` bytes of the array is the first vector; then `row_num -1` vectors are followed.
20211223-knowhere design — Sequence
20211223-knowhere design — Create index
20211223-knowhere design — ![create index sequence](graphs/create_index.png)
20211223-knowhere design — ![knn query sequence](graphs/knn_query.png)
20210521-datanode recovery design — DataNode Recovery Design
20210521-datanode recovery design — update: 5.21.2021, by [Goose](https://github.com/XuanYang-cn)
20210521-datanode recovery design — update: 6.03.2021, by [Goose](https://github.com/XuanYang-cn)
20210521-datanode recovery design — update: 6.21.2021, by [Goose](https://github.com/XuanYang-cn)
20210521-datanode recovery design — What's DataNode?
20210521-datanode recovery design — DataNode processes insert data and persists insert data into storage.
20210521-datanode recovery design — DataNode is based on flowgraph; each flowgraph cares about only one vchannel. There are data definition language (DDL) messages, data manipulation language (DML)
20210521-datanode recovery design — messages, and timetick messages inside one vchannel, FIFO log stream.
20210521-datanode recovery design — One vchannel only contains DML messages of one collection. A collection consists of many segments, hence
20210521-datanode recovery design — a vchannel contains DML messages of many segments. **Most importantly, the DML messages of the same segment can appear anywhere in vchannel.**
20210521-datanode recovery design — What is the real meaning of DataNode recovery?
20210521-datanode recovery design — DataNode is stateless, but vchannel has states. DataNode's statelessness is guaranteed by DataCoord, which
20210521-datanode recovery design — means the vchannel's state is maintained by DataCoord. So DataNode recovery is no different from starting.
20210521-datanode recovery design — So what's DataNode's starting procedure?
20210521-datanode recovery design — Objectives
20210521-datanode recovery design — Service Registration
20210521-datanode recovery design — DataNode registers itself to etcd after grpc server started, in *INITIALIZING* state.
20210521-datanode recovery design — Service Discovery
20210521-datanode recovery design — DataNode discovers DataCoord and RootCoord, in *HEALTHY* and *IDLE* state.
20210521-datanode recovery design — Flowgraph Recovery
20210521-datanode recovery design — The detailed design can be found at [datanode flowgraph recovery design](20210604-datanode_flowgraph_recovery_design.md).
20210521-datanode recovery design — After DataNode subscribes to a stateful vchannel, DataNode starts to work, or more specifically, flowgraph starts to work.
20210521-datanode recovery design — Vchannel is stateful because we don't want to process twice what's already processed, as a "processed" message means its
20210521-datanode recovery design — already persistent. In DataNode's terminology, a message is processed if it's been flushed.
20210521-datanode recovery design — DataCoord tells DataNode stateful vchannel info through RPC `WatchDmChannels` so that DataNode won't process
20210521-datanode recovery design — the same messages over and over again. So flowgraph needs the ability to consume messages in the middle of a vchannel.
20210521-datanode recovery design — DataNode tells DataCoord vchannel states after each flush through RPC `SaveBinlogPaths`, so that DataCoord
20210521-datanode recovery design — keeps the vchannel states updated.
20210521-datanode recovery design — Some interface/proto designs below are outdated, will be updated soon
20210521-datanode recovery design — DataNode no longer interacts with etcd except service registering
20210521-datanode recovery design — DataCoord rather than DataNode saves binlog paths into etcd
20210521-datanode recovery design — ![datanode_design](graphs/datanode_design_01.jpg)
20210521-datanode recovery design — DataCoord RPC Design
20210521-datanode recovery design — DataNode with collection with flowgraph with vchannel designs
20210521-datanode recovery design — The winner
20210521-datanode recovery design — ![datanode_design](graphs/collection_flowgraph_relation.png)
20210521-datanode recovery design — ![datanode_design](graphs/collection_flowgraph_1_n.png)
20210521-datanode recovery design — O4-1.** DataNode scales flowgraph 2 Day
20210521-datanode recovery design — Change `WatchDmChannelsRequest` proto.
20210521-datanode recovery design — DataNode consists of multiple DataSyncService, each service controls one flowgraph.
20210521-datanode recovery design — DataNode Init -> Register to etcd -> Discovery data service -> Discover master service -> IDLE
20210521-datanode recovery design — WatchDmChannels -> new dataSyncService -> HEALTH
20210521-datanode recovery design — `WatchDmChannels:`
20210521-datanode recovery design — If `DataNode.vchan2Sync` is empty, DataNode is in IDLE, `WatchDmChannels` will create new dataSyncService for every unique vchannel, then DataNode is in HEALTH.
20210521-datanode recovery design — If vchannel name of `VchannelPair` is not in `DataNode.vchan2Sync`, create a new dataSyncService.
20210521-datanode recovery design — If vchannel name of `VchannelPair` is in `DataNode.vchan2Sync`, ignore.
20210604-datanode flowgraph recovery design — DataNode Flowgraph Recovery Design
20210604-datanode flowgraph recovery design — update: 6.4.2021, by [Goose](https://github.com/XuanYang-cn)
20210604-datanode flowgraph recovery design — update: 6.21.2021, by [Goose](https://github.com/XuanYang-cn)

20210604-datanode flowgraph recovery design — A. One message stream to one vchannel, so there are one start and one end position in one message pack.

json storage — JSON Storage Design Document
json storage — Data Model Design
json storage — Data Layering
json storage — Dense Part
json storage — A set of "core fields" (such as primary keys and commonly used metadata) that are present in most records.
json storage — Sparse Part
json storage — Additional attributes that appear only in some records, potentially involving unstructured or dynamically extended information.
json storage — JSON Splitting and Mapping
json storage — Dense Field Extraction
json storage — When parsing JSON, predefined dense fields are extracted and mapped to independent columns in Parquet. A method similar to Parquet Variant Shredding is used to flatten nested data.
json storage — Sparse Data Preservation
json storage — Fields not included in the dense part are stored in a sparse data field. They are serialized using BSON (Binary JSON) format, leveraging its efficient binary representation and rich data type support, with the result stored in a Parquet BINARY type field.
json storage — Storage Strategy
json storage — Columnar Storage for Dense Data
json storage — Schema Definition**: Create independent columns in Parquet for each dense field, explicitly specifying data types (such as numeric, string, list, etc.).
json storage — Query Performance**: Columnar format is suitable for large data scanning and aggregation operations, improving query efficiency, especially for vectors, indexes, and frequently queried fields.
json storage — Row Storage for Sparse Data
json storage — BSON Storage**:
json storage — Serialize sparse data as BSON binary format and store it in a single binary column of the Parquet file.
json storage — BSON format not only compresses more efficiently but also preserves complete data type information of the original data, avoiding numerous null values and file fragmentation issues.
json storage — Parquet Schema Construction
json storage — Columnar Part**: Build a fixed schema based on dense fields, with each field having a clear data type definition.
json storage — Row Part**: Define a dedicated field (e.g., `sparse_data`) for storing sparse data, with type set to BINARY, directly storing BSON data.
json storage — Hybrid Mode**: When writing, dense data is filled into respective columns, and remaining sparse data is serialized as BSON and written to the `sparse_data` field, achieving a balance between query efficiency and storage flexibility.
json storage — Integration and Implementation Considerations
json storage — Data Classification Strategy
json storage — Density Classification**:
json storage — Classify fields as dense or sparse based on their frequency of occurrence in records (e.g., greater than 30% for dense), while considering data type consistency. If a field has multiple data types, we should treat data types that appear in more than 30% of records as dense fields, with the remaining types stored as sparse fields.
json storage — Dynamic Extension**:
json storage — For dynamically extended fields, regardless of frequency, store them in the BSON-formatted sparse part to simplify schema evolution.
json storage — Indexing for Sparse Data Access
json storage — Sparse Column Key Indexing
json storage — To accelerate BSON parsing, an inverted index stores BSON keys along with their offsets and sizes or values if they are of numeric type.
json storage — Value Data Structure Diagram
json storage — | Valid | Type | Row ID | Offset/Value |
json storage — |:-----:|:-----:|:------:|:------------:|
json storage — | 1bit | 4bit | 27bit | 16 offset, 16bit size |
json storage — bit Structure Breakdown**:
json storage — Bit 1 (Valid)**: 1 bit indicating data validity (1 = valid, 0 = invalid).
json storage — Bits 2-5 (Type)**: 4 bits representing the data type.
json storage — Bits 5-31 (Row ID)**: 27 bits for the row ID, uniquely identifying the data row.
json storage — Bits 32-64 (Last 32 bits)**:
json storage — If **Valid = 1**: Last 32 bits store the actual data value.
json storage — If **Valid = 0**: Last 32 bits are split into:
json storage — First 16 bits (Offset)**: Indicates the data offset position.
json storage — Last 16 bits (Size)**: Indicates the data size.
json storage — The column key index is optional, and can be configured at table creation time or modified later through field properties.
json storage — Example Data
json storage — Example JSON Records
json storage — Dense Data:**
json storage — The field `id` is considered dense.
json storage — Sparse Data:**
json storage — Record 1: `attr1`, `attr2`
json storage — Record 2: `attr1`, `attr3`
json storage — Record 3: `attr1`, `attr4`, `attr5`
json storage — Parquet File Storage
json storage — Schema Representation
json storage — | Column Name | Data Type | Description |
json storage — |--------------|-----------|-------------|
json storage — | **id** | int64 | Dense column storing the integer identifier. |
json storage — | **sparse_data** | binary | Sparse column storing BSON-serialized data of all remaining fields. |
json storage — | **sparse_index** | binary | Index column storing key offsets for efficient parsing. |
json storage — Stored Data Breakdown
json storage — Dense Column (`id`)**:
json storage — Row 1: `1`
json storage — Row 2: `2`
json storage — Row 3: `3`
json storage — Sparse Column (`sparse_data`)**:
json storage — Row 1:** BSON representation of `{"attr1": "value1", "attr2": 100}`
json storage — Row 2:** BSON representation of `{"attr1": "value2", "attr3": true}`
json storage — Row 3:** BSON representation of `{"attr1": "value3", "attr4": "extra", "attr5": 3.14}`
json storage — Sparse Index (`sparse_index`)**:
json storage — Row 1:** Index entries mapping `attr1` and `attr2` to their respective positions in `sparse_data`.
json storage — Row 2:** Index entries mapping `attr1` and `attr3`.
json storage — Row 3:** Index entries mapping `attr1`, `attr4`, and `attr5`.
json storage — In an actual system, the sparse data would be serialized using a BSON library (e.g., bsoncxx) for a compact binary format. The example above demonstrates the logical mapping of JSON data to the Parquet storage format.
